#103087. Tech Report: US affordable artists' housing initiatives hobbled by uneven regulation and oversight

Tech Report: US affordable artists' housing initiatives hobbled by uneven regulation and oversight

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2255 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, “Affordability” is on the lips of every American.
  • Sources indicate that national non-profits such as Artspace and the Community Arts Stabilization Trust (Cast) arrived in the state recently, participating in the many funding programmes supporting this effort.
  • “We were floored,” artists Emilie Dundee Odeile and Ken Lee Chapin tell The Art Newspaper, when their work Goodnight Moon: A Fiber Tale drew more than 10,000 visitors to Trinidad, a town of 8,000 people near Colorado’s southern border.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, “Affordability” is on the lips of every American. In Colorado, over 35% of residents spend more than 30% of their income on housing, which is considered a cost burden by the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (Hud). The state is responding by allocating $300m annually to the State Affordable Housing Fund. A niche area of this investment is the development of affordable housing for artists and creative districts.

Sources indicate that national non-profits such as Artspace and the Community Arts Stabilization Trust (Cast) arrived in the state recently, participating in the many funding programmes supporting this effort. Both non-profits market affordable housing for artists, but in the absence of artist certification programmes such as those in Boston, Upcoming York and now San Francisco, restricting available affordable housing to artists could run the risk of violating fair housing laws. There are also few mechanisms for cities and states to ensure their public funding delivers long-term solutions for artists’ housing and creative spaces.

“We were floored,” artists Emilie Dundee Odeile and Ken Lee Chapin tell The Art Newspaper, when their work Goodnight Moon: A Fiber Tale drew more than 10,000 visitors to Trinidad, a town of 8,000 people near Colorado’s southern border. The artists used around 152 miles of yarn to bring the famous children’s book to life in a 2023 exhibition.

“We started our RV-life, one-year road trip experiment,” Chapin says. “We were on our way to Santa Fe, and went through Trinidad”—and they never left. Goodnight Moon and another project by Odeile debuted at Space to Create, a state-led initiative to produce creative workforce housing and studios in rural Colorado.

Trinidad was the first municipality identified by the Colorado Office of Economic Development and International Trade (OEDIT) for public investment through the establishment of a creative district, in 2015. Today, 37 creative districts exist across the state. Next door to Space to Create on Trinidad’s historic Main Street, Artspace manages residences for artists.

According to recent reports, artspace develops and operates workforce housing across 23 states, including seven projects in Colorado. Each project markets itself “for those in the creative sector” and offers residential space that “prioritises creative use”. But without a formal certification programme to identify artists in Colorado or any of the local municipalities it operates in, it is unclear how Artspace can legally give preference to artist applicants over members of the general public.

Poet and editor Michele McDannold lived in Artspace’s complex in Michigan City, Indiana, for nearly four years and at the organisation’s Honolulu location for seven months. She arrived in Trinidad in 2020, but noticed a substantial difference in the artist preference process at that location compared to the properties she had been in previously. In Michigan City, she indicates, “I had to give a presentation to a board of practicing artists and participate in an interview.” In Trinidad, she was only asked to submit information for income eligibility. McDannold has only encountered five artists across the property’s 40 units during her three-year stay. The result of not prioritising artist applicants appeared to be that there were almost no artist residents.

Industry observers note that “When it came time to organise or participate in something like [open studios or a gallery night],” McDannold says, “neighbours were like, ‘What? Why are you bothering me?”.

Artspace did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s multiple requests for comment. The Artspace Trinidad leasing office stated that it does not track the number of artist residents at that location.

It has been revealed that affordable housing is a broad term that lives on a spectrum of interpretation and regulation. According to the federal government, household affordability is based on the regional or area median income (AMI). What a property owner can charge a tenant is determined by Hud’s AMI calculations, but a lender can set the contractual terms of the tax credit, loan or grant, whether private or public. Under US Treasury regulations, a housing unit generates a low-income housing tax credit (LIHTC) only if it is available for general-public use. However, in 2008 the Housing and Economic Recovery Act added a provision to the Internal Revenue Service’s tax code stating that general-public use is not violated if preference is given to tenants involved in artistic or literary activities. Even so, some cities maintain their own artist certification programmes for affordable housing.

Recent findings suggest that A 2023 affordable housing audit by Denver’s Department of Housing Stability expressed concerns that priority access to housing could violate the federal Fair Housing Act. While the report specifically focused on the Denver city council’s move to prioritise displaced households or people at risk of displacement, it highlighted the fact that prioritising seniors and veterans also requires better systems for monitoring and evaluation. Each time a person, such as an artist, is prioritised for affordable housing access, the county must track data such as the number of units allocated, eligibility requirements, types of document accepted as evidence of eligibility, the selection process, and the parties responsible for implementation and monitoring the property and rent levels.

Municipal governments are concerned about incurring fair housing lawsuits, especially if state and county laws contradict or fail to reaffirm the 2008 tax code revision. Cities considering allocating affordable housing units for artists can be faced with having to develop significant compliance procedures. This patchwork of rules, requirements and compliance regimes helps explain why creating and maintaining affordable housing for artists can be very complicated, costly, and look different in different cities and regions. According to the Center for an Urban Future, US cities have created just 2,804 units of dedicated housing for artists in the last decade.

According to recent reports, the soaring windows of 210 East Street in Trinidad must have caught the eye of the developer Dana Crawford when she first visited the elegant century-old school building. Crawford, who died in January 2025, was a celebrated preservationist in the region, known for saving Denver’s historic Larimer Square and redeveloping the city’s Union Station. There were minimal requirements attached to the $4m community revitalisation grant Crawford received for the redevelopment of 210 East Street into 17 affordable live-work spaces for artists. An open records request reveals the terms of the grant for the property only ask for progress reports on the number of housing units and jobs created.

The Former East Street School building in Trinidad, Colorado has been converted to housing and marketed as affordable for artists, among others Photo: Community Arts Stabilization Trust.

Sources indicate that for the 210 East Street project, Crawford procured three different tax credits, the $4m community revitalisation grant and $1.8m in private financing, but the most restrictive terms were attached to last-minute funding from the city of Trinidad. In 2022 Crawford applied to the city’s Housing Now incentive programme to help cover the $125,000 cost of redesigning five units. The city approved the request on the condition of a two-year workforce housing deed restriction, requiring rent rates to be limited to 80% of AMI starting in 2023.

Crawford also sought $1.9m in funding from an impact investor, Greenland CDF. The funding from Greenland was contingent on signing a Community Benefit Agreement (CBA), a binding contract that requires the borrower to produce a social benefit with enforceable penalties. The details of the agreement are not public and expired earlier this year.

Less than five years after Crawford received a total of $7.5m in public funding for 210 East Street, the property was acquired by Cast. There are no existing public terms that legally require Cast to deliver affordable housing to artists, or even general housing.

Cast operates a non-profit real estate development strategy around creative spaces and affordability. Recently, the organisation expanded that strategy to housing in Colorado.

Sources indicate that “Our model as a non-profit is to reset the floor of affordability,” states Ken Ikeda, Cast’s chief executive. “If we could do that without debt, through grants, then that would keep it that way in perpetuity.”.

Presently, Ikeda adds, Cast is only required to deliver the private terms of the $1.9m grant the organisation received from the Colorado Health Foundation to acquire 210 East Street. Rent at the complex is currently between 55% and 80% of AMI, and according to a spokesperson for the organisation, five current residents are artists. The Art Newspaper was only able to verify that one resident is an artist, and that person remarked they know of no others.

In a recent development, half a mile from 210 East Street are three properties that have received significant public funding in exchange for affordable artists’ housing. In 2019 ownership of two addresses on Main Street and one on Elm Street were transferred to Artspace by the city of Trinidad. In exchange for that real estate and a $715,000 promissory note by the Colorado Housing Finance Authority in 2022, Artspace must deliver housing units within or below 40% to 60% of AMI for 35 years, and preserve the historic facade of the Main Street properties for 15 years. If it fails to maintain this commitment, it must repay the borrowed funds.

The vastly different requirements for the Artspace and Cast properties in Trinidad, and the strings attached (or not) to their public and private funding reflect the wildly different standards and requirements for organisations creating and operating affordable artists’ housing.

The 444 17th Street building in Denver, the future site of a multi-use affordable housing and cultural hub for artists, to be operated by Community Arts Stabilization Trust Photo: Community Arts Stabilization Trust.

It has been revealed that A vibrant art and culture scene boosts local businesses and helps create jobs, according to the Denver Downtown Development Authority (DDDA), a city initiative to revive a downtown core where the vacancy rate has remained at or above 30% since the Covid-19 pandemic. In 2025 and 2026 the DDDA awarded $114.5m in financing for fresh housing and $4.45m for art-related initiatives—including a $1.35m grant to Cast to convert 6,300 sq. ft of vacant office and retail space into affordable artists’ studios, a cinema and gallery. The city council approved the terms of the property’s sale to Cast in September.

In a recent development, “We are going to make it affordable no matter what, because that is our aim and objective,” Ikeda claims of the project in Denver, which has been vacant since 2021. Cast estimates the art space will open in the summer of 2027.

Sources indicate that representatives for the city did not clarify how it defines “affordable” in the context of commercial real estate, but noted that the city has the first right to purchase the property for $1 for the next ten years if Cast decides to sell. In the meantime, municipal support will be released in phases as Cast reaches a series of build-out milestones.

Sources indicate that while Denver finds its footing on affordable housing for artists and Newly introduced York has not added any units in a decade, San Francisco’s first dedicated affordable artists’ housing is on track to open in 2028. The Artist Hub on Market, at 1687 Market Street, will have 94 units of housing, rehearsal space and a theatre. Rent will be set between 30% and 80% of the AMI, depending on the size of the unit and number of occupants, which equates to annual income of between $46,440 and $167,120 for tenants.

A rendering of the future Artists Hub on Market project in San Francisco Courtesy Artists Hub on Market and Mercy Housing California.

Launching alongside the Market Street property is a new artist certification programme for San Francisco, facilitated by the Mayor’s Office of Housing and Community Development. Artists can achieve certification by documenting at least $10,000 in annual income from their art practice, showing proof of a public art commission or grant in the previous three years, or submitting a portfolio of work for review. Once certification is awarded, artists can enter the lottery for units at Artist Hub on Market; any units unclaimed by artists in the lottery will be opened to general-public use through the city’s affordable housing system.

Of the Artist Hub on Market project’s $140m in funding, $100m came from a single anonymous donor and, according to a source familiar with the terms of the deal, implementing the artist certification programme was a condition of the funding.

It has been revealed that the inconsistent regulation of properties that receive public funding for affordable artists’ housing and cultural spaces risks undermining such projects’ longevity and disappointing the communities they were meant to serve. Recently, a $400,000 low-interest loan from the DDDA to Denver Immersive Repertory Theater (Dirt) went into default after Dirt’s alleged failure to make rent payments less than a year after it was awarded the loan and before its project ever opened to the public. According to reporting by Denverite, the loan’s rate surges from 3% to 15% when loan proceeds are shown to not be used for their intended purpose, though it is unclear what assets the city will be able to claw back from the project’s founders.

Affordable housing for artists is an emerging sector entangled with various local governments’ goals, which include attracting business, lowering housing costs by adding units and retaining creative workers. Ikeda describes every affordability project as a funding “butterfly” due to the unique risks and complexity of the capital and terms assembled. But, he adds, they are worth the trouble: “There is something magical about artist-only housing and live-work environments.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last month, scientists and photographers all over the world competed in the 52nd annual Nikon Small World Photomicrography Competition, revealing an incredible, often unseen microscopic world. Photomicrography has gone to space thanks to a joint experiment by NASA and Encapsulate Inc.

NASA’s newest Image of the Day reveals patient-derived gastric tumor samples in extreme microscopic detail, captured as part of the novel Encapsulate-1 scientific study.

The photo, captured last week aboard the International Space Station (ISS), shows cancer cells suspended in microgravity. Scientists at Encapsulate believe that a microgravity-induced model of metastasis may help save early-stage cancer patients and prevent the spread of cancer cells inside the body.

Industry observers note that the initiative, developed jointly by Encapsulate Inc., a Connecticut-based medical startup working on biochips, and NASA, received a $3.63 million grant last year through NASA’s In Space Production Applications (InSPA) program. The goal is to better study, understand, and eventually predict cancer cell metastasis in a microgravity environment unique to space.

According to recent reports, “This grant represents a bold step forward in how we approach cancer research,” Dr. Armin Rad, CEO and co-founder of Encapsulate, said last year. “We are honored to partner with NASA and explore the unique advantages of space-based research in advancing cancer diagnostics and precision medicine.”.

Extensive, highly advanced scientific research has taken place aboard the International Space Station since it rolled out nearly three decades ago. According to NASA, more than 4,000 experiments have been conducted on the ISS as it orbits roughly 260 miles above Earth.

Many biology and biotechnology experiments—including cutting-edge medical studies—have been performed in orbit. For example, NASA astronaut Christina Koch, who went to the Moon aboard the famed Artemis II mission earlier this year, studied amyloid protein aggregations aboard the ISS that scientists believe may cause Alzheimer’s disease. Fellow NASA astronaut Serena Auñón-Chancellor worked on developing more effective cancer treatments as part of a study with Angiex Cancer Therapy.

According to recent reports, medical treatments take a long time to develop, of course, but it’s entirely possible that the cancer cell research underway aboard the ISS could save many lives down the road. Medical science breakthroughs routinely happen in labs on Earth, but sometimes they happen in space.

Image creditsEncapsulate Inc., NASA.

  • In a recent development, photographers routinely look for Adobe Lightroom alternatives for their RAW photo organization and processing needs, hoping to avoid Adobe’s subscription fees.
  • Billed as “the spiritual successor to Aperture and Lightroom,” PixelLoupe is right now on version 1.4.2 and is compatible with macOS 27 or later.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PixelLoupe is a free, open-source photography app built natively for macOS that promises many of Adobe Lightroom’s photo editing and asset management tools.

In a recent development, photographers routinely look for Adobe Lightroom alternatives for their RAW photo organization and processing needs, hoping to avoid Adobe’s subscription fees. On Mac, many also miss Aperture. PixelLoupe aims to answer both calls as a Lightroom alternative that channels Apple’s defunct software.

Billed as “the spiritual successor to Aperture and Lightroom,” PixelLoupe is right now on version 1.4.2 and is compatible with macOS 27 or later. Its overall layout closely mirrors Adobe Lightroom Classic, offering separate Library and Develop modules, a wide array of RAW editing sliders, folder-based hierarchies, local adjustments, AI-powered tools, and presets. The app is built on Apple’s own RAW image engine, Core Image, and its Metal graphics and compute API.

Sources indicate that pixelLoupe promises non-destructive RAW processing, organizational features like catalogs and collections, ratings and flags, keyword and IPTC metadata support, and advanced image adjustments. It even lets users import their Lightroom Classic catalogs, preserving valuable presets, camera profiles, and smart collections. Assuming the accompanying .xmp files are present, basic image edits carry over, too. Lightroom users will also find PixelLoupe’s keyboard shortcuts familiar, as they remain unchanged.

Beyond essential adjustments like sliders, tone curves, and HSL controls, the latest version of PixelLoupe includes AI-powered Assisted Culling, one-click subject selection and masking, and AI relighting.

Sources indicate that the app also includes more specialized tools, such as photo merging for focus stacking, panoramas, and HDR photography, alongside a web gallery builder for easy online sharing. That is an impressive feature set for a completely free program. Because it is open source, people can also modify and tinker with the software as they see fit.

There are some caveats to consider, though. PixelLoupe is a solo-developer project that debuted just last month, meaning its development was almost certainly heavily aided by AI coding tools. The Github page specifically mentions Claude, a go-to AI tool for solo devs. While AI-assisted coding is commonplace even among major, established developers these days, it’s understandable that some people may be wary of upstart projects like this.

The app’s newness also means there is a risk that some features won’t work as expected. On the plus side, it’s free, so trying it carries no financial risk. Open-source photo editing apps have been popular for a long time, and there are plenty of interesting choices on macOS these days, including the well-known app Darktable. Another popular option is RawTherapee. PetaPixel also maintains a guide to the best free RAW editing programs available, which will be updated early next year.

Recent findings suggest that until then, photographers are welcome to try PixelLoupe to see if it fits their workflow on macOS 27. It’s available through Pixegen and on GitHub.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Grand Theft Auto VI player notes he received a 30-day suspension from PlayStation Network’s social features for sharing a photograph he took in the game.

The player, who uses the name DerrickGott007 on X (formerly Twitter), says he received a notification from PlayStation Safety informing him that his account had been temporarily restricted for violating the platform’s Code of Conduct. The notice cited the sharing of “pornographic or obscene content” as the reason for the suspension.

Industry observers note that according to Derrick, the image was captured using GTA VI’s built-in camera feature and showed a nudist resort within the game. The location, which is apparently a nudist colony, is a beachside area near the main protagonist’s house featuring non-player characters who are either fully or partially nude. TweakTown notes that some players have referred to the location as Tiki Touchdown.

Following the suspension, Derrick warned other players about sharing similar images through PlayStation Network messaging, writing: “Do not, I repeat, do not send any photos taken with the in-game camera across the PSN messaging network that contain nudity.”.

DO NOT, I REPEAT DO NOT SEND ANY PHOTOS TAKEN WITH THE IN GAME CAMERA , ACROSS THE PSN MESSAGING NETWORK THAT CONTAIN NUDITY. I JUST GOT A 30 DAY PSN SOCIAL FEATURES BAN FOR SENDING MY FRIEND A PHOTO OF THE NUDIST COLONY IN GTA6 THAT I FOUND. https://t.co/vsoIjmpGrt.

— DerrickGott007💎 (@derrickgott007) November 20, 2026.

Industry observers note that sony’s Community Code of Conduct prohibits owners from sharing, requesting, accessing, distributing, or storing “material that is obscene, pornographic, or illegal.” The policy does not appear to distinguish between content created outside a game and images captured from within one. As a result, the player’s actions may fall under the platform’s existing restrictions, despite the image originating from GTA VI itself.

As Engadget points out, the rules are murky. Sony is apparently comfortable selling a game that contains such content to customers, but not with those customers sharing it with friends. At best, it’s inconsistent; at worst, it’s hypocritical.

Recent findings suggest that derrick says that the 30-day ban not only stops him from messaging his friends but also prevents him from playing multiplayer games such as Call of Duty. If he falls foul of Sony’s rules again, he could face more restrictions.

Industry News: Book of Birkenstock: Inside Bureau Borsche's Editorial Design

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bureau Borsche turns 250 years of Birkenstock into the Book of Birkenstock, a 130-metre timeline across 608 pages of archive and image.
  • The book reads as one long strip of history.
  • Industry observers note that the layout was not placed by hand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bureau Borsche turns 250 years of Birkenstock into the Book of Birkenstock, a 130-metre timeline across 608 pages of archive and image.

The book reads as one long strip of history. More than 1,000 photographs, illustrations, and documents sit on a continuous timeline that runs from 1774 to 2024, and images cross the gutter from one page to the next so the story never breaks. A hundred historical events sit alongside the timeline, with notes on the social conditions of each era, and a 60-page index at the back sorts everything by model, country, and document type. What holds it together is restraint: the pages stay pale, the captions stay small, and the archive does the talking.

Industry observers note that the layout was not placed by hand. Bureau Borsche built the book from a dedicated online database of 2,500 archived objects, each tagged with year, type, category, location, and shoe model, and pulled the material through an API. Column widths, cropping, and DPI were decided by custom code and rendered in the browser with JavaScript, so the grid flexes around the material instead of forcing the material into a fixed frame.

Page numbers were placed automatically, and the index pages generated themselves from the same data, with references pointing back to the pages they came from. The final step exported every page as a single-page PDF. It is design systems thinking applied to a book: the rules are written once, and 608 pages follow them.

Recent findings suggest that three paper stocks divide the book into sections, and each one changes how the images sit. The archival section prints on yellow-tinted, semi-transparent paper, so the documents feel thin and handled. The middle section, photographs and advertisements, sits on glossy greyish stock. The final section moves to bright white glossy paper, the kind used for fashion magazines and art catalogs.

Sources indicate that the cover keeps the same quiet register. It is blind-stamped on extra rough cardboard, carrying the first recorded mention of a Birkenstock shoemaker, from a church file dated 1774, with only the year printed in small black type at the centre. The spine does the loud work instead: the wordmark runs down it in heavy black capitals, with Steidl at the foot.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sabine Marcelis has nominated Swedish Girls as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project sponsored by Kohler. In this interview, we learn why the design duo deliberately play into stereotypes.

The steady emergence of Swedish Girls has not been lost on prolific Dutch designer Marcelis, who nominated the collective as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design over the next 20 years.

“I really like how they work with existing industrial production processes, yet the result very much speaks to the current culture,” Marcelis told Dezeen, explaining her selection.

Josefin Zachrisson and Mira Bergh run multidisciplinary studio Swedish Girls between Stockholm and Milan, creating furniture, installations and set design.

Industry observers note that the duo met during their studies at Sweden’s Beckmans College of Design, where they graduated in 2019. They bonded over a desire to make work “without hierarchies” and maintain creative control of the studio’s output, which they prefer to call their ever-expanding “universe”.

The Big Bang for Swedish Girls was the selection of their collective’s tongue-in-cheek name, chosen after their first exhibition outing at Milan design week.

For experimental platform Alcova in 2021, Zachrisson and Bergh unveiled their ongoing metal rod Seats System project (pictured left).

Originally a single piece of modular seating without a defined front or back, the project has evolved into more metal pieces that follow the same design language, including a fruit bowl and a candle holder.

Industry observers note that “We overheard people talking about our furniture, asking who made it, and others were like, ‘ah, it was those Swedish girls’, and we felt a bit belittled by it,” recalled Zachrisson. The duo had previously made work under their own names.

“The Swedish girl has obviously become a phenomenon,” added Bergh. “You know, blonde, sexy. But when we were talking about it, we also found it really funny because it’s so stereotypical. We thought we’d call ourselves Swedish Girls because everybody else was already calling us that.”.

In a recent development, humour is intrinsic to Zachrisson and Bergh’s interdisciplinary practice. Even their website, admired by Marcelis, was playfully designed as a Swedish Girls-branded Google search engine. It is meant to look like the internet itself, complete with mock web pages listing each of the collective’s projects.

“We got the idea when we rolled out the name Swedish Girls,” the pair explained.

“A professor from Beckmans called and noted that we should change our name because when she Googled ‘Swedish Girls’, the search result was not exactly art and design,” they added.

“We thought that was so funny and decided to make Google about us instead of changing our name.”.

Another of the duo’s wit-inflected projects is Only Fans, an installation presented at Gothenburg’s Röhsska design museum in 2024 during local music festival Way Out West.

Dubbed “a multidimensional art experience about fan culture” in all its forms, the installation included 25 electric fans, selected as a riff on adult content platform OnlyFans, where women are often the subject of scrutiny.

“The installation was interactive, so that visitors could stand in the middle of the fans in a hysterical storm,” remarked Bergh.

It has been revealed that our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things. But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life.

Alongside the fans, the collective presented seven laser-cut steel chairs emblazoned with I <3 Swedish Girls, along with a fanzine and female mannequins wearing “metal merch” designed by Zachrisson and Bergh.

“Our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things,” considered Zachrisson.

Recent findings suggest that “But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life,” she continued. “It feels like a way to approach it that makes it accessible.”.

According to recent reports, “Sometimes it’s hard because we get these questions like, ‘are you a feminist?'” added the designer. “But it’s inherently political to be a woman moving through the world. Our work is just reacting to our reality.”.

The pair is keen to highlight that although they make furniture, “social values are always a starting point” for their projects.

“We really want to have a practice that feels purposeful,” said Zachrisson, considering the significance of partnering with institutions like design museums.

“We’ve realised that showing work in public spaces is the most important thing,” she continued.

Recent findings suggest that “Especially because the materials and processes we use have become quite expensive. So we want to put our pieces in public spaces so that everyone can take part in some way.”.

“You meet all different kinds of people, and we talk to them and grow from it,” added Bergh.

Recent findings suggest that the hardest thing is to earn money. We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money.

Despite Swedish Girls’ various collaborations and recurring presence at Milan design week, seven years after leaving Beckmans, Bergh and Zachrisson continue to work in cafes and supermarkets to fund their design practice.

The duo are hyperaware of the difficulties faced by emerging creatives, especially those like themselves who, as they put it, “want to listen to your gut and be close to the process”.

In a recent development, “The hardest thing is to earn money,” stated Bergh. “We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money on very quick timelines. I feel like we should have more respect.”.

Sources indicate that “You don’t get paid in a way where you as two people can survive,” added Zachrisson. “But all these years of working and keeping our creative integrity is paying off in every way except financially.”.

When it comes to building their studio, the designers consider themselves to be playing the long game.

“Long term, it’s an investment to do it this way because we have now created a context where we can feel freedom and gain respect, which is why we were so happy when Sabine nominated us,” said Zachrisson.

“You can measure success in so many different ways and with this we feel respected, and that is so valuable.”.

The duo stated funding that they won from Sweden’s Konstnärsnämnden arts council after graduating gave them a significant leg up when they were just starting out.

Zachrisson and Bergh are concerned that scholarships like theirs have been scarcer across Sweden in recent years thanks to the country’s right-wing administration, which came into power in 2022 and has only just been voted out of office.

In a recent development, “All the artists we have talked to have felt an extreme difference in that time,” noted Zachrisson. “The share of the total budget allocated to culture has not been this low in 26 years.”.

Still, the pair are confident and excited about what’s to come.

According to recent reports, “It comes in handy that we have a broad practice,” said Bergh. “We have plans for the future to make it easier for ourselves to be designers.”.

According to recent reports, “I like how they surprise with their projects and feel like we have only seen chapter one of their story,” concluded Marcelis. “And I can’t wait to discover the next chapter.”.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Industry observers note that picture this: you're standing at the gate for your Boston weekend trip, and the person next to you just swiped their credit card for $280 to book the exact same seat you're sitting in — a seat that cost you 7,500 Avios and maybe $5.60 in taxes. That's the British Airways Avios short-haul sweet spot in action, and once you see it, you can never unsee it. This is the redemption the ChooseFI community quietly uses to stretch their points further than almost any other domestic award. While everyone else is chasing first-class international awards (which are spectacular, don't get us wrong), this sweet spot lets you turn a modest points balance into a steady stream of nearly free regional flights — year-round, on American Airlines metal, with zero fuel surcharges. Here's the math that makes it click: A last-minute nonstop flight from New York (JFK/LGA) to Boston Logan or Los Angeles (LAX) to San Francisco typically runs anywhere from $150 to $300 in cash. You're paying that for roughly a one-hour flight — the kind of trip where by the time the flight attendant hands you a drink, you're already starting your descent. British Airways prices that same flight at a flat **7,500 Avios**. At a $200 cash fare, that's **2.67 cents per point (CPP)** — well above the standard valuation most programs offer for domestic economy. At a $300 last-minute fare, you're looking at **4 cents per point**, which is exceptional for any award program, let alone a simple domestic booking. The pricing inefficiency is hiding in plain sight: British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart**, which means short flights cost proportionally fewer points. The U.S. domestic short-haul zone (under 650 miles) sits at 7,500 Avios one-way — a price that hasn't ballooned with inflation the way cash fares have. Every time airfare spikes for a holiday weekend or a last-minute booking, your Avios redemption looks better and better. For the FI-minded traveler, this redemption is pure arbitrage: you're converting transferable points that cost you perhaps 1–1.5 cents each to earn into travel worth 2–4 cents each in real-world value. That's a 2–4x return, consistently, on routes you'd likely be flying anyway.

The magic here lives inside British Airways' distance-based award chart — and understanding why it's structured this way is the 'aha moment' that turns a confusing loyalty program into a tool you actually want to use.

According to recent reports, most U.S. airline programs (Delta, United, American) have largely abandoned distance-based pricing in favor of dynamic or zone-based awards that tend to price popular routes higher. British Airways never fully made that switch for partner awards. Their Avios chart still prices flights primarily by the number of miles flown between origin and destination. A flight under 650 miles costs 7,500 Avios one-way in economy — full stop. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday in February or the Sunday after Thanksgiving. The chart price holds.

The Partner Piece: Why You're Booking AA, Not BA.

Here's the critical nuance that trips up fresh consumers: British Airways charges notoriously high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights. We're talking $300–800+ in carrier-imposed fees on top of the Avios. That would completely wipe out the value of this redemption. But when you book American Airlines-operated flights through British Airways Avios, those surcharges disappear entirely. AA does not pass fuel surcharges to partner award bookings. Your out-of-pocket cost is typically just the government taxes — often $5–15 each way.

This is the non-negotiable rule: always book AA metal through British Airways Avios, not BA-operated flights.

The 355-day booking window means you can transfer and book nearly a full year in advance — critical for holiday travel or high-demand routes.

According to recent reports, british Airways allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. That means you could theoretically fly into one city and out of a nearby city without paying for two separate awards — useful if you're exploring a region and want flexibility. For short domestic hops, this opens up creative itinerary options that pure point-to-point programs don't allow.

You're searching for American's own award inventory — the same inventory British Airways can see and book. If AA shows saver-level availability (the lowest award tier), British Airways will almost certainly be able to book it too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A photographer didn’t expect to see her camera again after it plunged 150 feet off a cliff in Arkansas — until a well-known photographer stepped in.

KY3 reports that on November 19, Heinrichs was hiking on Hawksbill Crag in the Upper Buffalo Wilderness.

Hawksbill Crag is a magnet for photographers thanks to the unusual way it juts out over the oak-hickory forest.

Heinrichs was doing just that, taking photos near Hawksbill Crag with her Nikon D750 mounted on a tripod.

“I turned around for maybe five seconds or so and turned back around to my camera and I saw it falling off the side of a cliff,” Heinrichs tells KY3. “About 150 feet down.”.

Industry observers note that the problem? One of the tripod legs wasn’t locked properly, causing it to fall over. This is normally bad enough without the camera going over a huge cliff.

Recent findings suggest that “It was heartbreaking,” adds Heinrichs. “I could just feel my heart sink and drop when it happened.”.

The photographer turned to a local Facebook page, Our Buffalo River, explaining that she “had a camera mishap” and that her D750 was now at the bottom of Hawksbill Crag.

Tim Ernst, a wilderness and nature photographer who is based in northern Arkansas, saw the post and responded.

“Hey, I got an excuse to run out to the Crag,” Ernst tells KY3. “So that was an easy call on my part. I literally jumped up and took off and headed to the Crag.”.

And it turns out that Heinrichs is a fan of Ernst, who is a well-established photographer whose work has appeared in National Geographic and the Fresh York Times.

In a recent development, “I’ve followed Tim Ernst for years,” says Heinrichs. “And so for him to be the one to reach out and do that it, I was starstruck a little bit.”.

It has been revealed that ernst found the camera sitting on a pile of leaves. However, it wasn’t in great shape.

“I immediately knew it was not good because the lens that was on it had actually separated,” indicates Ernst.

In a recent development, it appears the camera is beyond repair, but Heinrichs claims she’s grateful to Ernst for reaching out and trying. She does proposal to replace the camera.

Exhibition celebrates Delftware, the Dutch art form that became the ‘Ikea of its day’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that on a tour of ceramics displays in museums across Europe ahead of a landmark latest Delftware exhibition she was organising, Suzanne Lambooy realised they all had something in common: they were empty of people.
  • But for Lambooy, ceramics are all about human connection, and she was determined to do something different.
  • “Delftware is so much fun, and we’re going to prove that,” she says.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that on a tour of ceramics displays in museums across Europe ahead of a landmark latest Delftware exhibition she was organising, Suzanne Lambooy realised they all had something in common: they were empty of people. “There was no one there because ceramics can feel cold and distanced,” she says. “They can be hard to bring alive, because the makers are anonymous, and [the objects are] often displayed in glass cases.”.

But for Lambooy, ceramics are all about human connection, and she was determined to do something different. The result, Blue Loves You: The Magic of Delftware, opens this month at the Kunstmuseum in The Hague, where she is the curator of decorative arts. It will, she states, be “the biggest and most comprehensive Delftware exhibition ever”. Equally importantly, she promises it will be captivating and enjoyable.

“Delftware is so much fun, and we’re going to prove that,” she says. “We want to show the love craftspeople put into these pieces. It has inspired, and it continues to inspire, so many craftmakers—we’ll give them a platform.”.

Natasja Sadi's Suikerbloemen (2024) Courtesy of Kunstmuseum Den Haag, photo: Studio Roodenburch.

Around 1,000 objects, including vases, teapots, plates, wall plaques and tiles, will be on display at the Kunstmuseum, which has one of the largest collections of the art form that is perhaps the best-known cultural export of the Netherlands. Also on show in Blue Loves You will be Delftware-inspired pieces, including the blue dress worn by Queen Máxima of the Netherlands for her husband’s 2013 investiture, its bodice embroidered with Delft-derived flowers. “There’s a lot more to it than blue and white fridge magnets,” Lambooy claims.

Sources indicate that although the porcelain is known for its characteristic colouring, the show will include examples of both white and multicoloured Delftware. It will explore its history, dating back to the 17th century. The form was originally a high-end Chinese import, displayed in the wealthiest homes. But when factories started to make their own version of it in Delft, it was transformed.

“It became an on-trend, functional brand that was affordable for every home and on every budget: it was the Ikea of its day,” says Lambooy, whose co-curator for the long-term show is the television presenter Janny van der Heijden (who is also a judge on the country’s version of The Great British Bake Off).

Ceramics in Blue Loves You, “the biggest and most comprehensive Delftware exhibition ever” Courtesy of Kunstmuseum Den Haag.

Recent findings suggest that the quintessential Delftware piece was the tulip pyramid, some of the best examples of which were made for King William III, born in The Hague, and his English wife Queen Mary II, who were the joint monarchs of England, Scotland and Ireland in the late 17th century. “Mary exported Delftware to Britain—she was the most notable woman in its history,” Lambooy says.

The porcelain’s connections to Dutch colonialism will also be explored, with exhibits including an installation of sugar flowers by the floral artist Natasja Sadi, whose family are originally from the former Dutch colony of Suriname and whose ancestors were enslaved.

• Blue Loves You: The Magic of Delftware, Kunstmuseum, The Hague, 28 November-31 December 2029.

Recent findings suggest that U.S. first lady Melania Trump is selling digital photos of herself shot by influential fashion photographer Ellen von Unwerth for $150.

In a recent development, melania made the announcement of the sale of “exclusive” photographs taken by von Unwerth in a post on X (the platform formerly known as Twitter) on Sunday. The launch coincides with the release of MELANIA: The Series, a new two-part production focusing on the wife of President Donald Trump, which debuted on Amazon Prime Video on November 20.

— MELANIA TRUMP (@MELANIATRUMP) November 22, 2026.

In a recent development, according to the product listing on Melania’s official website for the “PhotoArchival Digital Edition”, she collaborated with von Unwerth over a two-day photo shoot “to develop the visual narrative” of the images. The photographs are being sold for $150 as a digital album delivered in the form of a movie file.

According to a report by Newsweek, buyers are also required to have a cryptocurrency wallet on the Solana blockchain to store the digital collectible. While customers can presently pay by credit card, they must connect their cryptocurrency wallet to Melania’s website before completing the purchase.

“Melania Trump is launching PhotoArchival Digital Edition, an exclusive collection of digital photographs by internationally acclaimed fashion photographer Ellen von Unwerth,” the announcement on X states. “The collection presents a visual portrait of Mrs. Trump, showcasing von Unwerth’s distinctive artistry. Its release coincides with the debut of MELANIA, The Series, a new two-part production streaming on Amazon Prime Video.”.

Von Unwerth also shot the photography for Melania, the documentary about the first lady released in January, and some of the images featured in the $150 PhotoArchival Digital Edition appear to be the same. One of von Unwerth’s black-and-white photographs indicates Melania wearing a fitted suit, sitting in a chair with her legs crossed and looking directly at the camera. Another image shows Melania standing beside a mirror in a strapless black dress as someone holds a clapperboard in the shot.

The release of Melania’s digital photo collection follows a recent interview in which von Unwerth, one of the most sought-after fashion photographers working today, claimed that “there’s no money left” in the industry.

  • It has been revealed that saeedi is an internationally recognized photojournalist who has won numerous awards for his coverage of Afghanistan, including a Lucie Award and the Robert F.
  • According to a report by the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), Saeedi was arrested at his home in Tehran on September 9.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Getty Images is demanding the release of veteran Iranian photojournalist Majid Saeedi, a regular contributor to the photo agency who has been detained in Iran for more than two months.

It has been revealed that saeedi is an internationally recognized photojournalist who has won numerous awards for his coverage of Afghanistan, including a Lucie Award and the Robert F. Kennedy Journalism Award. His images have been published in The New York Times, The Washington Post, and Life magazine. Saeedi also received second prize in the 2013 World Press Photo Contest’s Contemporary Problems category.

According to a report by the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), Saeedi was arrested at his home in Tehran on September 9. More than two months after his arrest, Iranian authorities have yet to disclose whether the freelance photojournalist faces any charges or which agency is holding him, despite repeated efforts to obtain this information. Saeedi is believed to be detained in Kerman, a city in southeastern Iran, although his location has not been officially confirmed.

The CPJ and Getty Images have now urged Iranian authorities to release the award-winning photojournalist immediately and unconditionally. They say that the lack of information surrounding his detention has raised serious concerns about his safety, as well as the increasing threats facing independent journalists in Iran.

Sources indicate that “Holding Majid Saeedi for more than two months, with no official confirmation of any charges, is unacceptable,” Getty Images VP of Global News Pancho Bernasconi claims. “Journalism is not a crime. We join CPJ in demanding Iranian authorities account for Majid’s whereabouts and release him immediately and unconditionally.”.

“For more than two months, Majid Saeedi’s family has been left in the dark about his whereabouts, the reason for his detention, and whether he is safe. No journalist should simply disappear into state custody, while Iranian authorities refuse to tell their family what has happened,” CPJ Regional Director Sara Qudah says in a further statement. “Majid’s detention is part of a broader campaign to intimidate and silence journalists in Iran — he must be released immediately and unconditionally.

Saeedi has previously been arrested on several occasions in connection with his photographic coverage of politically sensitive events and their aftermath, including in 2009, 2021, and June 2025. According to CPJ, the photographer’s latest detention comes amid an escalating crackdown on independent journalism in Iran, where authorities have increasingly resorted to arrests and lengthy prison sentences to suppress critical reporting.

Previously, PetaPixel reported on two female photographers, prominent photojournalist Yalda Moaiery and 18-year-old artist Shaghayegh Afshar, who were sentenced to a combined 24 years in prison in Iran. Meanwhile Tahmineh Monzavi, an acclaimed Iranian documentary photographer, was sentenced to 74 lashes for documenting an Iranian female singer’s concert.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Insta360 has confirmed a winter upgrade for the X6 360-degree camera that ties footage to activity data in the popular ski and snowboard app Slopes, linking the footage to GPS data without needing a dedicated GPS accessory.

Industry observers note that slopes is a popular ski and snowboard app that provides digital trail maps for thousands of resorts worldwide. Because it is tied to a smartphone, the app tracks GPS data and provides riders with detailed information about their runs beyond just standard fitness data, such as top speed, average speed, lift versus run times, and more.

Sources indicate that the Insta360 X6 now pairs with the Slopes app through the Insta360 app, providing riders with the ability to tie their footage to the data Slopes records. For example, “footage and data help riders review their progress and revisit moments from their season, from a favorite descent to a family ski day,” Insta360 explains.

“Riders can also connect their phone to X6 using the camera’s new Phone GPS Link feature. Once connected, X6 records GPS data with each shot, with no separate import step or dedicated GPS accessory required.”.

Because the X6 captures 360-degree video, riders can combine that footage with the additional data provided by Slopes for specific cuts, like terrain or friends, as well as the ability to highlight specific runs.

Industry observers note that “AI Director can identify highlights and assemble an edit,” Insta360 explains. “Dedicated skiing and snowboarding templates give riders another quick way to turn the day’s footage into a video they can share. When filming a friend, InstaFrame 2.0 keeps the selected skier or snowboarder in frame and produces a ready-to-share 4K flat video. With supported settings, 360 Video Backup also saves the full 360 degree view, so riders can go back and choose a different angle from the same run.”.

Sources indicate that the update to the Insta360 app, which allows the X6 to pair with the Slopes app, is free and will be available starting November 24. The integration will require a firmware update to the X6 as well, but that is performed through the app per usual. Slopes also requires a separate subscription.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Curving ceilings sweep down to frame the two small gardens that flank this home in Kerala, India, designed by local architecture studio Fictional Project.
  • Named Interstitial Living, the home in the village of Adoor was designed for a family of four who wanted to feel connected to the outside, in particular the lush greenery surrounding the site.
  • This led Fictional Project to pull the home’s built volume back to create space for two planted yards on either side, overlooked by the home’s pared-back and open interiors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Syam Sreeshylam.

Curving ceilings sweep down to frame the two small gardens that flank this home in Kerala, India, designed by local architecture studio Fictional Project.

Named Interstitial Living, the home in the village of Adoor was designed for a family of four who wanted to feel connected to the outside, in particular the lush greenery surrounding the site.

This led Fictional Project to pull the home’s built volume back to create space for two planted yards on either side, overlooked by the home’s pared-back and open interiors.

“The residence is careful not to overpower, becoming one with the landscape,” the studio told Dezeen.

Interstitial Living is organised around a bedroom at its centre, which is housed within a cubic volume finished in cement plaster.

A small window in this bedroom overlooks a potted tree within a cut-out in the floor of the adjacent living room, which faces the yard to the west through a row of full-height windows above a built-in timber bench.

On the opposite side of the home, the kitchen overlooks the eastern yard through a row of windows above its countertops. Both these spaces are defined by the curving white-plastered ceilings overhead, which sweep down from the centre of the home.

“The scale of the residence allows for intimate working spaces in the kitchen and a welcoming living room, all accentuated by the dynamic nature of the roof. The other spaces negotiate the private/public nature of the indoors,” the studio explained.

“The concavity of the roof creates a visual connection to the outdoors, becoming a marker that emerges from within the site.”.

Recent findings suggest that “It breaks the rigidity of a traditional sloping roof, helping create fluid indoor spaces. Nothing here is built or conceived in isolation, but rather as interconnected systems,” it added.

The smaller first floor contains a second bedroom, bathroom and a study area, which overlook the living space below from a steel-framed landing and internal windows.

While the internal finishes were kept minimal, the exterior of the home and its boundary walls were built using terracotta-toned textured blocks, which the studio described as introducing a sense of “groundedness and warmth”.

Other dwellings in Kerala recently featured on Dezeen include a home by InLe Architects framed and shaded by two large mango trees and a farmhouse by Evolving Radical Aesthetics that is built into a hillside above a carved-out, open-air temple.

Photography by Syam Sreeshylam.

📖 Baca
Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

From the margins to the mainstream: the growing market for illustration art

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1183 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The illustration art market began in the 1960s when, according to Roger Reed, a Manhattan-based independent art dealer in this field, works used in children’s storybooks, product advertising and magazine covers “were taken out of their context in publishing and sold just as paintings”.
  • In a recent development, lucas and fellow filmmaker Steven Spielberg have been some of the largest collectors of the original art created by illustrators for decades, but many others have caught up.
  • “A lot of the work of illustrators was pooh-poohed by the art world, because they were illustrators,” notes the New York-based American art dealer Debra Force, “but you don’t hear that so much anymore.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The illustration art market began in the 1960s when, according to Roger Reed, a Manhattan-based independent art dealer in this field, works used in children’s storybooks, product advertising and magazine covers “were taken out of their context in publishing and sold just as paintings”. Some six decades later and the apotheosis of that market has arrived with the recent opening of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles, the $1bn creation of film-maker George Lucas (Star Wars and Indiana Jones) devoted to children’s book art, fantasy art, cartoon images, movie posters, film stills and magazine illustrations, as well as works distinguished as fine art by the likes of Paul Cadmus, Diego Rivera and Carrie Mae Weems.

In a recent development, lucas and fellow filmmaker Steven Spielberg have been some of the largest collectors of the original art created by illustrators for decades, but many others have caught up. Today, the interest in works by Norman Rockwell, N.C. Wyeth, J.C. Leyendecker, Howard Pyle, Maxfield Parrish, Jessie Willcox Smith, John Held Jr and Charles Dana Gibson, among many others, has mushroomed—and in some cases prices have shot up from almost zero to millions of dollars.

“A lot of the work of illustrators was pooh-poohed by the art world, because they were illustrators,” notes the New York-based American art dealer Debra Force, “but you don’t hear that so much anymore.”.

In a recent development, certainly, one doesn’t hear that at the major auction houses where works by Rockwell, Parrish, Wyeth and Leyendecker frequently bring the highest prices in American art sales. Norman Rockwell (1894-1978) leads the pack, with his 1951 painting for a Saturday Evening Post cover, Saying Grace, fetching $46m at a 2013 Sotheby’s auction and his 1957 oil painting The Rookie (Red Sox Locker Room) sold for $22.5m at a 2014 auction at Christie’s. The 1922 painting Daybreak by Maxfield Parrish(1870-1966) earned $7.6m at a Christie’s sale in 2006, while a 1943 tempera on panel, Portrait of a Farmer, by N.C. Wyeth (1882-1945) brought $5.9m at Sotheby’s in 2018. Football Hero, the 1914 painting for a Saturday Evening Post cover by J.C. Leyendecker (1874-1951), brought $4.1m at a Heritage Auctions sale in 2021, and the 1907 painting Captain Keitt by Howard Pyle (1853-1911) for the frontispiece of his novel The Ruby of Kishmoor earned $702,000 at a 2004 sale at Sotheby’s.

It has been revealed that “There’s definitely a hierarchy,” states Aviva Lehmann, the deputy chair of fine art at Heritage Auctions, which sold Rockwell’s 1943 work So You Want to See the President! in 2025 to the White House Historical Association for $7.2m.

Sources indicate that however, “Rockwell’s success has not been at the expense of these other illustrators”, says Skye Lacerte, an illustration art specialist at Swann Auction Galleries in New York. “Rather, it has helped establish a broader market in which collectors and museums are beginning to take the entire field seriously.” She notes that “immediately recognisable” images from magazine covers and illustrations from famous books like Alice in Wonderland, The Wind in the Willows, or L. Frank Baum’s Oz books are highly sought after, as well as advertising art for “companies like Coca-Cola, TWA and Cadillac because those images have become part of American cultural experience”.

Recent findings suggest that besides the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, there is the Brandywine River Museum of Art in Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania; the Norman Rockwell Museum in Stockbridge, Massachusetts; the Eric Carle Museum of Picture Book Art in Amherst, Massachusetts; and the National Museum of American Illustration in Newport, Rhode Island. That last museum was founded in 1998 by Judy Goffman Cutler, the owner of Manhattan’s American Illustrators Gallery, who claims to have sold Lucas “hundreds” of original paintings by the top book and magazine illustrators. “I sold him his first Rockwell—it was called Going Out,” she says—a 1933 painting that was used on the cover of the Saturday Evening Post. For reasons of “client confidentiality”, she declines to say how many works in the illustration field she has sold to Lucas, only noting that “I built his collection”.

Industry observers note that other museums that aren’t wholly devoted to illustration or storytelling art also have collections of this type of work, most notably the Newly introduced Britain Museum of American Art in Connecticut and the Delaware Art Museum in Wilmington. The New Britain Museum has almost 1,800 works in its Sanford B.D. Low Illustration Collection, named in honour of the institution’s first director who himself had been an illustrator and invited illustrators he knew to donate works for a collection. They include such artists as Willcox Smith, Everett Raymond Kinstler, Stevan Dohanos, Walter Wick and William Steig.

“Interest in illustration art doesn’t begin and end with Rockwell, and the awareness of illustration art as art is definitely increasing,” says Lisa Williams, head of curatorial affairs at the New Britain Museum.

In a recent development, N.C. Wyeth’s Victory Garden (1943) © N.C. Wyeth.

In a recent development, others agree. “I have no doubt that the collective appreciation for the category will continue to grow thanks to its elevation by these museums,” states Quincie Dixon, head of sale in Christie’s American art department. She adds that “private collectors make up the bulk of this market, but perhaps that will change now that there are museums on both coasts dedicated to the category”.

Specialised museums and collections reflect a growing prominence, but they might also be keeping these works segregated. Goffman Cutler states that it is her “goal to have museums include American illustration art in their American art galleries”, which the occasional museum has done, but not many and not too often.

Industry observers note that A spokesperson for the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, notes that the “collection includes art from American artists of many backgrounds, including quite a few who have worked as illustrators, among them Winslow Homer, Childe Hassam, William Glackens, Joseph Leyendecker, Charles Sheeler” and some others. Having worked as illustrators doesn’t mean that their illustration work is what the museum shows, and the Leyendecker is not currently “on view”. Both New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, own paintings by Parrish that are not displayed in their American art galleries, but the Art Institute of Chicago has hung its Rockwell, The Dugout (1948), in one of the Arts of Americas galleries, and the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas, has hung Rockwell’s 1943 work Rosie the Riveter (which the museum purchased from a private collector in 2009) next to Charles Willson Peale’s George Washington (around 1780-82) and works by John Singleton Copley and James Peale Sr in its Visions of America galleries. “In the same section of the gallery as Rosie the Riveter,” indicates a museum spokesperson, “are Susie J. Lee’s Johnny [2013], Kerry James Marshall’s Our Town [1995] and a new commission by artist Teri Greeves.”.

It seems the greatest test for illustration art is no longer garnering record prices, but if it can enter—and hold its own within— the art historical canon.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • TTArtisan has unveiled the AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH., a newly introduced ultra-wide-angle lens for full-frame Sony and Nikon mirrorless cameras.
  • Industry observers note that TTArtisan says its fresh lens is built for landscapes, architecture, and night-sky photography, all common applications for ultra-wide lenses.
  • Industry observers note that the AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TTArtisan has unveiled the AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH., a newly introduced ultra-wide-angle lens for full-frame Sony and Nikon mirrorless cameras. Better still, it’s very affordable.

Industry observers note that TTArtisan says its fresh lens is built for landscapes, architecture, and night-sky photography, all common applications for ultra-wide lenses. With its f/2.8 aperture, it should work well for astrophotography, though real-world performance will depend on how well it controls optical aberrations. For its part, TTArtisan promises “excellent aberration control” alongside “outstanding resolution,” even when shooting wide open.

Industry observers note that the AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH. lens has 16 optical elements arranged in 10 groups, including a pair of aspherical elements and three extra-low dispersion (ED) elements. The aperture diaphragm features just six blades, a relatively low count by modern standards, though it should produce distinct sunstars.

Many ultra-wide lenses are big, heavy, and difficult to use with traditional front filters, but the TTArtisan AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH. is an exception. It weighs between 336 and 349 grams (11.85 to 12.31 ounces) and measures 72 to 74 millimeters (2.83 to 2.91 inches) long, with the Nikon Z-mount version being slightly heavier and longer than the Sony E-mount variant. The lens accepts common 82mm front filters, which is great news for landscape photographers who want to use circular polarizing and neutral-density filters. Because the front element is bulbous, mounting filters requires an extending filter-thread adapter, though TTArtisan includes one in the box and it adds minimal bulk.

It has been revealed that the autofocus-equipped lens focuses as close as 0.18 meters (7.1 inches), making it well suited for emphasizing close-up foreground elements. Given its ultra-wide 122-degree field of view, though, it’s clearly not a macro lens. TTArtisan states the lens uses a high-performance stepping motor and supports eye- and face-detection autofocus modes on compatible cameras.

Speaking of compatibility, TTArtisan states the lens works seamlessly on Nikon Z-mount bodies, while some older Sony E-mount cameras have limited functionality. The Sony a7 III, for example, is fully compatible for photo modes but only partially compatible for video. The original a7 and a7 II also lack full compatibility. TTArtisan notes that autofocus performance may be limited on certain bodies, while firmware updates are in development for others. More compatibility details are available on the tech giant’s website.

The TTArtisan AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH. lens is available to preorder now for Nikon Z and Sony E-mount cameras at $489.

Recent findings suggest that although TTArtisan does not list an L-Mount version for sale, one is referenced on the product page. Since the company already makes several lenses for L-Mount, it is reasonable to expect the AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH. to arrive in that third mount down the road.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dual Roomâs poster design for Maison Saint-Gervais pairs Matthieu Croizierâs photography with nine shifting typefaces across two seasons.

It has been revealed that nine floors of 1960s architecture in central Geneva hold rehearsals, scientific research, film screenings, performances, installations, and exhibitions under one roof. Dual Room didnât flatten Maison Saint-Gervais into a single polite house font. For the 2025/26 and 2026/27 seasons, the studio built its poster design series around Matthieu Croizierâs photography and a nine-family type roster. According to Fonts In Use, the lettering draws from six Kyiv Type Foundry cuts (KTF Rublena, KTF Tiemann, KTF Labyrinth, KTF Roman, KTF Jermilov, and KTF Compact, several still unreleased) alongside Maxitypeâs Selecta, Teletext, and MX Claw. Thatâs a crowded toolkit for one cultural venue. Still, the street run hangs together.

Sources indicate that season-wide anchor sheets set the baseline before individual highlights break loose. On the amber-backlit 2026/27 poster, a performer stands in dark silhouette while translucent outlined Maison Saint-Gervais lettering runs flat across the torso. On the companion 2025/26 F4 sheets, bright red institutional type slices dead center across a seated figure in a pinstripe suit lifting one shoe, and again across two athletes draped shoulder-to-shoulder. Even the red subscription poster pulls a crisp edge trick. Maison Saint-Gervais crosses the vertical borders of the centered white ticket card and flips polarity on contact, turning from black on red outside to red on white inside. Nothing gets wasted.

Once individual highlights step forward, the lettering turns restless on purpose. Chaos BALLAD jams heavy blackletter inside a red banner next to a hollow serif outline above two stacked portraits of a white-painted clown. Les Trois Soeurs mirrors red capitals backward along the top and bottom of a cyan sidewalk frame, while Impossible drags a thin red strikethrough across a high-contrast serif title. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nirvana fans have raised over $94,000 for the photographer who shot the cover of the band’s debut album Bleach, to cover her medical expenses as she enters hospice care.
  • Recent findings suggest that tracy Marander, the photographer behind the cover of Bleach and Kurt Cobain’s former girlfriend, has been battling cancer for four years.
  • Marander’s family rolled out a GoFundMe campaign to help cover her medical expenses, which has raised $94,101 toward its $100,000 goal at the time of writing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nirvana fans have raised over $94,000 for the photographer who shot the cover of the band’s debut album Bleach, to cover her medical expenses as she enters hospice care.

Recent findings suggest that tracy Marander, the photographer behind the cover of Bleach and Kurt Cobain’s former girlfriend, has been battling cancer for four years. Last week, Marander’s family declared that the photographer was suspending her cancer treatment and entering hospice care.

Marander’s family rolled out a GoFundMe campaign to help cover her medical expenses, which has raised $94,101 toward its $100,000 goal at the time of writing. Hundreds of Nirvana fans have accompanied their donations with tributes to the photographer and her contribution to the band’s legacy.

It has been revealed that cobain’s widow Courtney Love also urged her followers to donate to the GoFundMe campaign in support of Marander in an Instagram post, calling the photographer “the unsung hero of Nirvana” who believed in the band’s lead singer “before he believed in himself.” In her post, Love describes the American medical system as “broken” and called on people to give what they could, adding “P.S. Kurt owed Tracy a lot of rent.”.

A post shared by Courtney Love Cobain (@courtneylove).

Released in June 1989, Bleach was the debut studio album by Nirvana. Marander shot the iconic photograph that ended up becoming the album cover art during a Nirvana concert at Reko/Muse art gallery in Olympia, Washington, on April 1, 1989. Marander’s image shows the band performing live, with Cobain’s hair falling across his face, alongside guitarist Jason Everman, who did not play on the album despite appearing on its cover.

Lisa Orth, a graphic designer at the local music newspaper The Rocket, inverted the light and dark tones of Marander’s photograph to give it the appearance of a film negative. According to Nirvana: Taking Punk to the Masses by Jacob McMurray, Orth designed the album cover in keeping with the signature aesthetic of the band’s record label Sub Pop, which favored plain backgrounds, bold lettering, and striking photography. The cover also gave rise to Nirvana’s now-famous logo almost by accident, when Orth asked The Rocket’s typesetter Grant Alden to set the band’s name in whatever typeface was already installed on the typesetting machine.

Although Bleach received positive reviews from critics, it failed to enter the charts when it was first released. However, the album became popular when it was internationally reissued in 1992 following the commercial success of Nirvana’s second album Nevermind, released in 1991.

According to Nirvana biographer Michael Azerrad, Marander was Cobain’s first serious romantic partner and inspired him to write the song About a Girl. Their relationship lasted around three years before Cobain ended it in 1990. Marander recalled how Cobain encouraged her to develop her photographic talents, but the demands of working full-time and financially supporting him left her with little time to pursue her own creative interests.

Recent findings suggest that “Near the end, we started fighting more and more,” Marander tells Azerrad in his 1993 book Come as You Are, according to reports. “He wanted me to be artistic, and I didn’t have time to be artistic. I was driving an hour to work and an hour back from work. I was supporting him.”.
