💡 Key Takeaways
  • Towers of concrete drainage tubes and colourful exposed steel elements are among the eclectic features of House Tropicália, a “very personal” London residence recently extended by local architecture studio CAN.
  • Located in Catford, the project responds to a brief with “two distinct strands” – one relating to the functional elements of the project, and the other to its expressive and atmospheric qualities.
  • Functionally, CAN was asked to introduce a fresh kitchen and dining space that felt connected to the garden, alongside two new bedrooms on the first floor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Jim Stephenson.

Towers of concrete drainage tubes and colourful exposed steel elements are among the eclectic features of House Tropicália, a “very personal” London residence recently extended by local architecture studio CAN.

Located in Catford, the project responds to a brief with “two distinct strands” – one relating to the functional elements of the project, and the other to its expressive and atmospheric qualities.

Functionally, CAN was asked to introduce a fresh kitchen and dining space that felt connected to the garden, alongside two new bedrooms on the first floor.

Meanwhile, the design was required to be an expression of the interests and experiences of its clients – designer Fabiane Lee-Perrella, television producer Robin Lee-Perrella and their two sons.

“The atmospheric side of the brief was to somehow encapsulate the clients’ diverse visual tastes and architectural memories from their pasts,” CAN founder Mat Barnes told Dezeen.

“This resulted in the eclecticism of the project; one that is very personal to the clients.”.

Visual references given to CAN included modernist Brazilian architecture projects such as Lina Bo Bardi’s SESC Pompéia in São Paulo, as well as industrial architecture, David Hockney paintings and Moroccan riads.

The resultant design inspired the project’s name, House Tropicália, which nods to the late 1960s Tropicália movement that celebrated bold ideas and rebelled against accepted norms.

“We reject the idea that a project needs to be driven by a single, homogeneous idea or material,” remarked Barnes.

“Instead, we celebrate the complexity, diversity and even contradiction inherent in our clients’ tastes and design references,” he continued.

“We see these different influences not as competing ideas, but as an opportunity to create something individual and ultimately more meaningful.”.

The focal point of the project is its highly unique rear elevation, with features including two towers of engineering drainage tubes, which break through a red-steel canopy that extends over the patio.

Meanwhile, bright blue and red fibre-cement panels decorate its elevation, alongside portions of textured raked render and exposed concrete, punctured by irregular shapes.

Details also include a metal sawtooth roof at first-floor level, alongside a bright yellow screen facing the neighbouring property to prevent overlooking.

Finally, at ground level, a full-width set of doors open onto a patio with a winding perimeter, referencing the designs of Brazilian landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx.

“It brings together a mix of materials, forms and ideas drawn from the huge range of references the clients shared with us,” remarked Barnes. “I think it captures the character and personalities of the clients brilliantly.”.

Industry observers note that inside, the back half of the ground floor has been rearranged to maximise its connection to the rear garden. This is where the fresh open-initiative kitchen, dining and living space is positioned.

Meanwhile, at the front of the ground floor, the studio has created a secondary dining area and living space, and a children’s playroom in the original lounge.

According to recent reports, above, a void on the north side of the first floor has been filled to add a main bedroom suite, complete with an ensuite and roof terrace. Another bedroom has also been added.

The roof terrace has a walk-on, diamond-shaped skylight, which sits directly above the dining table.

According to recent reports, interior finishes echo the eclecticism of the exterior, with a bold mix of colours, materials and textures. This includes exposed steel joists and trusses, and a colourful timber kitchen with contrasting black tiles.

Walls of ceramic tiles on the ground floor have shell-like forms, handmade by Fabiane Lee-Perrella with glazing that shifts from pink to blue hues.

A microcement floor runs throughout the ground floor and incorporates pebble inlay that evokes a river and is a nod to the water feature at SESC Pompéia.

CAN hopes the project will highlight the importance of challenging the “established or standard way of doing things in a particular city or context”.

“We think it’s vital to look beyond the usual architectural references and draw inspiration from unexpected places, whether that be sculpture, set design, or even infrastructure,” Barnes said.

“These disciplines can offer entirely different ways of thinking about space, material and form. Ultimately, it’s about exposing clients to these different ways of doing things.”.

CAN, known fully as Critical Architecture Network, was founded by Barnes in 2016. Its previous projects include the equally bold house extensions Druid Grove and Mountain View.

Photography by Jim Stephenson.

The most dramatic reaction I've read came from Igor Sarzyński, creative director on Cyberpunk 2. Reported on Shift Delete, he posted on Bluesky on Saturday evening, two days after launch, and started with "GTA VI-induced-open-world-game-dev-depression is real", then called it "probably the single greatest artistic achievement in history" and "a technological and creative miracle".

Industry observers note that as our sister site GamesRadar+ covered, Sarzyński isn't the only CD Projekt Red game dev impressed. Joint CEO Michał Nowakowski called the game a masterpiece and said it's "unbelievably hard" to achieve what Rockstar has. Witcher 4 director Sebastian Kalemba said he'd love to lose a whole weekend to it, although he's busy hunting monsters for now.

In a recent development, @RockstarGames created a masterpiece that I am planning to explore in the coming weeks and months. Massive congratulations to the whole team who worked on the game. It is unbelievably hard to achieve what you just did. Hats off to all of youNovember 19, 2026.

Over at Naughty Dog, Michael Barclay, who has 19 years in the industry and is working on Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet, said GTA 6 looks to him like "a Bugatti Veyron would to a nervous Victorian child".

Recent findings suggest that push Square picked up on how Barclay was impressed by the lighting specifically, which he explained is mostly dynamic, yet he says it looks as good as, if not better than, most baked lighting. That's a significant deal in an open world where the weather and time of day never stop changing.

Tim Soret of Odd Tales (The Last Night) joined the thread, saying he can't work out how Rockstar gets so many draw calls, hair simulations and volumetric lights running at once.

I’ve made video games for 19 years and GTA VI appears to me as a Bugatti Veyron would to a nervous Victorian child.November 20, 2026.

None of this surprises anyone who's seen how Rockstar builds its world. As I reported earlier, Rockstar's art team designs buildings by imagining who actually lives in them. And then there's the fact that the animators spend months on small details, like how Lucia opens a door with her hip in a natural way when her hands are full.

VP of art Miriam Bellard states they ask whether a place is messy or tidy, and "what is their taste?" The range runs from industrial and scruffy to decadent and dangerous.

So it seems the people who made GTA 6 are as stunned as everyone else by what they've achieved. As GamesRadar+ reported, Rockstar production coordinator Navya Manaswitha reacted to the reviews by saying she's "truly grateful to be a part of this masterpiece".

Industry observers note that I've already argued Rockstar has bucked the AI trend in how it made the game, and GTA 6 is proof that human creativity is still the most impressive technology we have. It seems most game devs agree.

It has been revealed that in 2022, Iraq’s National Museum in Baghdad reopened after being closed for three years following political unrest. Then in 2024, the museum closed again, this time for renovations. Now, it’s scheduled to open on December 1.

The Art Newspaper reported that the museum will open with several new galleries, such as the Abbasid and Islamic galleries. There will also be specially curated wings.

Industry observers note that the museum will display artifacts including winged bulls (lamassu) and stone carvings depicting legendary Assyrian monarchs, ancient clay tablets and historical prisms recording legal codes, calligraphic friezes, stone carvings, glassworks, and mosaics that have been recovered and restored. According to the newspaper Iraqi News, the museum’s doors are opening to domestic visitors, international tourists, and researchers from around the world. Related Articles Iraqi Archaeologists Arrested Amid Growing Concerns Over State Corruption Researchers Confirm Location of Lost City of Alexandria on the Tigris.

Sources indicate that the reopening of the museum has been a long time coming. In 2003, the National Museum was the subject of looting during the US-led invasion. Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq’s Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, has stated that reopening the museum in December, rather than January 2027, is a priority, and that he also has looks for “a new building that befits the historical and civilizational value of Iraq.”.

Paul Collins, the keeper of the Middle East Department at the British Museum, told the Art Newspaper that the reopening of the museum “is an important moment, reflecting Iraq’s strong commitment to preserving its world-renowned cultural heritage and promoting heritage tourism.”.

As Iraq rebuilds itself after years of political unrest, the museums’ opening is a big step for the country’s cultural sector.

Recent findings suggest that the Abbasid Palace in Baghdad opened its doors on November 15, and Iraq’s first Jewish museum, the Shamash Museum, opened its doors on October 22. Many of Iraq’s museums are also close to its large-scale monuments that are part of the city’s charm, such as the Al-Shaheed Monument designed by Iraqi sculptor Ismail Fatah al-Turk, the Monument to the Unknown Soldier designed by Khaled al-Rahal and Marcello D’Olivo, and the Saving Iraqi Culture Monument designed by Mohammed Ghani Hikmat.

Industry observers note that relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

Industry observers note that each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

It has been revealed that from those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:.

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

Recent findings suggest that research reveals that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Recent findings suggest that lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

According to recent reports, if the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of newly introduced love into a warm, enduring attachment.

According to recent reports, hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the issues head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

Significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

If you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

It has been revealed that you know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Sources indicate that every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

According to recent reports, after an inaugural edition last year, the Bukhara Biennial will return to Uzbekistan in 2027, this time with “The Long Welcome” as a theme (after 2025’s theme of “Recipes for Broken Hearts”). As announced this past summer, the artistic director for the next edition—slated to open September 3 and run through November 21—is Kulapat Yantrasast, the revered architect behind museum projects for institutions including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Louvre, Harvard Art Museums, and the Art Institute of Chicago (as well as others while he worked for Tadao Ando). Related Articles John Lennon Drawings to be Animated, Pace Gallery Trims Artist Roster, and More: Morning Links for June 4, 2026 Kulapat Yantrasast Named Artistic Director of Next Bukhara Biennial.

“At a time when the world needs dialogue and understanding more than ever, culture can bring people together and open space for a shared future,” Bukhara Biennial commissioner Gayane Umerova stated in a press release announcing the theme, which will be organized around four parts: Local Hospitality, Co-Creation, Resilience and Biodiversity, and Living Heritage. “For centuries, Bukhara welcomed travelers, craftspeople and merchants from across the world, and that openness shaped its identity. Through the biennial, we want to carry this legacy forward through contemporary art, so that it becomes part of life in the city, creates opportunities for its residents and leaves a lasting cultural legacy.”.

Yantrasast added: “The Long Welcome celebrates the spirit of hospitality that made Bukhara worth crossing continents to reach, and worth returning to again and again. When people welcome you into their city, you want to give something back. My hope is that an artist who returns to Bukhara years from now will find that something they made with people here has become part of everyday life.”.

Along with news of the theme, the Bukhara Biennial revealed its first slate of artists to exhibit work in the city, which will also host the 19th Annual Conference of UNESCO Creative Cities next year. Below, see the artists enlisted.

Atelier Manferdini uses digital glitches to shape tile-and-metal facade of Virginia power station

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (469 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Dave Huh unless stated.
  • California-based studio Atelier Manferdini has created an expressive facade system for an electrical substation in Virginia, USA, using metal and colourful tile to represent the flow of electrical power within.
  • Called InVisible, the project was carried out for Dominion Energy, an electricity provider that was updating the substation in Crystal City, Northern Virginia, just outside of Washington DC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Dave Huh unless stated.

California-based studio Atelier Manferdini has created an expressive facade system for an electrical substation in Virginia, USA, using metal and colourful tile to represent the flow of electrical power within.

Called InVisible, the project was carried out for Dominion Energy, an electricity provider that was updating the substation in Crystal City, Northern Virginia, just outside of Washington DC.

Atelier Manferdini founder Elena Manferdini, who is Italian and teaches at Sci-Arc in Los Angeles, said that her studio sought to translate the largely functional structure into something more human.

“Critical infrastructure is essential to our cities, yet the Dominion Energy substation is fundamentally designed for machines rather than people,” Manferdini told Dezeen.

“With inVisible, we wanted to explore this dichotomy, transforming a purely functional structure into something meaningful to the surrounding community,” she continued.

“While the interior responds to the needs of machines, the exterior becomes an opportunity to engage with people through color, pattern, and perception, creating a dialogue between infrastructure and the human scale of the city.”.

The substation converts power into different voltages to facilitate the transmission of energy, and the patterns on the sculptural facade were computationally designed to represent that process.

Atelier Manferdini used programming site Processing, which came out of the MIT Media Lab in the early 2000s, to design the colourful tile band that lines the bottom of the structure.

This pattern incorporates 10 colours and tiles of three different sizes, two, four, and six inches across – a reference to voltages – along with “glitches” in the program to create the graphic.

It recalls the Boogie Woogie works of modernist artist Piet Mondrian, which were based on the rhythms of cities.

Above the ceramic pattern, the studio placed massive gridded aluminium panels.

The panels create a ventilated facade system, set at different distances from the exterior walls and stacked where they meet so that sunlight passes through different densities in the gridded pattern, creating a variable light effect.

“The folds catch light and cast shadows, allowing the surface to shift with the time of day and the viewer’s position,” stated the studio.

At night, the panels are backlit by programmable LEDs.

Overall, the studio said that it considers the contrast between the monochromatic metal and colour tile patterns a unified image.

“Quiet and metallic above, saturated and granular below, the two bands form a unified architectural composition,” said the studio, with the unseen machines humming with electricity inside.

Other creative takes on infrastructure include a power station in China that Schmidt Hammer Lassen shrouded with steel lamellas and topped with a walkway, as well as a sculptural stormwater facility in Toronto by GH3, a Canadian studio well known for its aesthetic treatment of otherwise overlooked infrastructure.

Photography by Dave Huh unless stated.

  • Sources indicate that the more than 1,000 documents, photographs, drawings, letters, and reports that make up the archive were collected and saved for decades by Annemarie Kusserow, one of 11 children from a Jehovah’s Witness family that lived in the town of Bad Lippspringe in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany.

Recent findings suggest that five years after the Jehovah’s Witnesses sued the German government over ownership of an archive tracing one family’s persecution by the Nazi regime, the files have been returned to the religious organization, reports the Upcoming York Times. Jehovah’s Witnesses were targeted by the Nazis specifically for their refusal to salute Hitler, display the swastika flag, or serve in the military; 4,500 were sent to concentration camps, and 1,800 died during the Nazi era.

Sources indicate that the more than 1,000 documents, photographs, drawings, letters, and reports that make up the archive were collected and saved for decades by Annemarie Kusserow, one of 11 children from a Jehovah’s Witness family that lived in the town of Bad Lippspringe in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. According to an oral history published by the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum, the Kusserow home was searched by the Gestapo 20 times, and the Kusserow parents, Hilda and Franz, were the first to be arrested, in the mid-1930s. The children eventually ended up in prisons, concentration camps, or training schools. Two brothers, Wilhelm and Wolfgang, were murdered by the Nazis, and another survived the war but died shortly after from tuberculosis contracted at Dachau. Related Articles Hamburg Culture Prize Renamed After Namesake's Nazi Ties Emerge Switzerland's Bührle Foundation Reaches Settlement with Heirs of Jewish Collector Who Owned Prized Manet.

It has been revealed that at the time of her death in 2005, Annemarie Kusserow’s will stated that her family’s archive should go to the Jehovah’s Witnesses. But one of her brothers, Hans Werner Kusserow, had the archive in his possession at the time, and in 2009 he sold it to the Bundeswehr Military History Museum in Dresden. This was “especially troubling,” the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ official website notes, given that her brothers lost their lives due to their pacifism.

Industry observers note that the parties came to an “amicable agreement” on November 19, which was formalized the following day by the Higher Regional Court of Cologne. The museum and the Jehovah’s Witnesses agreed to keep the details of the settlement private. A Kusserow relative told the Fresh York Times it is “a great relief that at last we will have these precious documents back where Annemarie always wanted them.”.

Industry observers note that vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

These machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:.

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he claims.

As Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study showed that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe claims this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he says.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

Recent findings suggest that “Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe says. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”.

In a recent development, nobbe claims WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he notes.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe states.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he notes.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thelma Golden, the director and chief curator of the Studio Museum in Harlem, will step down from her position in late 2027, the museum declared Tuesday.

The announcement coincides with Golden’s 20th anniversary in the role, which she assumed in 2006, and comes just one year after the museum reopened in a new, purpose-built building after a seven-year closure. The new $125 million building was designed by architect David Adjaye and provides 82,000 square feet across seven floors, including a 139-seat public lobby, a rooftop terrace, education spaces, a library, and a cafe. It received rave reviews upon its reopening. Related Articles Zohran Mamdani Spends a Birthday to Remember at the Studio Museum in Harlem Time Magazine Publishes its First Art 100 List, Featuring Artists, Museum Leaders, Dealers and More--See Who Made the Cut.

Kathryn C. Chenault, chair of the museum’s board of trustees, said in a statement that the board has formed a search committee to identify Golden’s successor and has retained an international executive search firm to assist. Golden will remain in her post until a replacement is hired.

While Golden’s departure was not entirely expected, it is not unusual for museum directors to exit their positions after a major renovation or expansion. Lisa Phillips revealed in September 2025 that she would leave her role as director of the Upcoming Museum after its reopening, and Janne Sirén, director of the Buffalo AKG Art Museum, said in April that he would step down following the museum’s 2023 expansion.

“I know this is the right moment to begin this transition—and as I look ahead to fresh projects and opportunities, I also look back with gratitude toward the many people whose achievements have been my bedrock,” Golden stated in a statement. “I think of my teachers, mentors, and professional colleagues; the long line of Directors, Trustees, and donors who established the Studio Museum and made it thrive; half a century’s worth of endlessly dedicated staff members, audiences, and beloved Harlem neighbors; and above all the generations of artists who have enlightened us. Together, they are an expansive community I cherish that will continue to inspire and enable the next leader of the Studio Museum.”.

Industry observers note that before becoming director of the Studio Museum, Golden worked there as a curatorial fellow. She then joined the Whitney Museum of American Art in 1988 as a curatorial assistant and held several curatorial positions there, co-organizing the 1993 Whitney Biennial and organizing the landmark 1994 exhibition “Black Male: Representations of Masculinity in American Art.” In 2000, she returned to the Studio Museum as deputy director for exhibitions and programs under then-director Lowery Stokes Sims. When Sims stepped down in 2005, Golden was named as her successor.

In a recent development, golden has been credited with raising the profile of the Studio Museum through numerous groundbreaking exhibitions, including 2001’s “Freestyle”. Organized with curator Christine Y. Kim, the show featured 28 emerging Black artists whose work the curators described as “post-Black.” Among the artists championed in that show were Mark Bradford, Rashid Johnson, and Julie Mehretu.

In 2023, Golden won the Dorothy and Lillian Gish Prize, which carries a $250,000 award and recognizes a person who has made a significant contribution to the arts.

Speaking to ARTnews in 2020, Golden described what the Studio Museum meant to her and other young Black creatives:.

Recent findings suggest that [At the Studio Museum], they begin their careers and are able to not only get real professional experience but to form a mission and get a vision of real museum work. I say this as someone whose career is the result of those early experiences at the Studio Museum. It cannot be overstated how significant it was for me, as a 19-year-old art history/African-American studies double major from Smith College, to encounter Dr. Mary Schmidt Campbell, art historian and director of the Studio Museum. I can’t tell you what it meant for me, after over a decade as a curator at the Whitney, to become chief curator at the Studio Museum and to work for Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims, a pioneer in the museum field.

Robert Pattinson's James Bond will be different – should the brands be different too?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (921 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that robert Pattinson is the newly introduced James Bond and brings with him a host of luxury deals and an audience that’s grown up alongside him.
  • It has been revealed that robert Pattinson has only just got the coveted job as the most famous secret agent on earth, and there’s already speculation around who’ll cut his first dinner jacket.
  • There’s a little bit of danger in Pattinson’s acting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that robert Pattinson is the newly introduced James Bond and brings with him a host of luxury deals and an audience that’s grown up alongside him. Matt Kerr, Global Executive Creative Director at Marks, shares what he feels brands will need to do to belong in his version of Bond’s world.

It has been revealed that robert Pattinson has only just got the coveted job as the most famous secret agent on earth, and there’s already speculation around who’ll cut his first dinner jacket. Craig wore Tom Ford, but Pattinson has enjoyed a longstanding relationship with Dior. I’m interested in who gets the job, of course – but I’d like to see what Pattinson does in the suit first.

There’s a little bit of danger in Pattinson’s acting. He has this laid-back British cool thing going on, but there’s also a bit of an awkward edge to him – he’s a bit of a conundrum, and I’d s say there’s something of Fleming’s Bond in that. So, for an agency taking a brief or a brand handing one out, I’d start there. What would this particular Bond choose, and when would we get to see why he chose it?

Industry observers note that fleming was deliberate in showcasing what Bond would buy – he understood his protagonist and the pleasure his audience would get from finding out. The Sea Island cotton shirt, the Rolex, the Aston Martin. You could read the books as a shopping list for a certain idea of British masculinity. The list was interesting because it belonged to a man who had his reasons for choosing things.

Recent findings suggest that take the silver Aston Martin in Goldfinger. An iconic scene is Bond flipping open the top of the gearstick and sending his passenger through the roof. I couldn’t tell you how long the badge was in shot. But the car still got the punchline. Yes, you can hand over some serious investment to get your car brand into a Bond film, but it’s the association with the scene and the interaction with the hero that people buy into.

I’d give a watch brand the same brief. For No Time to Die, Omega developed the Seamaster Diver 300M 007 Edition with input from Daniel Craig and the filmmakers, then put it on sale to the public. Craig wanted a lightweight watch that felt right for a military man, so Omega made it in titanium. That’s where I’d start with Pattinson too. Work out what his Bond would choose and why. If the audience can see why he’d wear it, they’ve got a reason to want one for themselves.

Industry observers note that brands also need to think about the audience. Yes, Bond is the ultimate masculine icon, but Pattinson is an icon to women in their thirties because they grew up with him. For the teen girl who saw the first Twilight movie at 15, Pattinson is her pin-up. And if he stays with the franchise for the best part of a decade – which seems to be the norm – that young girl will be in her forties. So, I’d have that in mind when I was briefing the campaign.

According to recent reports, take a hotel partnership. There’s a familiar version of that ad where a man books a weekend so he can spend it feeling like Bond. According to Nielsen data, women influence 70 to 80% of consumer spending, so maybe brands should ask what a hotel brand could offer a woman who has followed Pattinson for years and fancies booking the weekend herself. Give her a detail to spot at check-in and let it pay off later that evening. She gets to have some of the fun Bond has in the film. If the partnership carries through to another film, the hotel can give her something different to come back for.

I’d keep the gun barrel iconography and every word of the slick one-liner, “Bond, James Bond”, but I’d give Pattinson room to play with the pause. We know the line so well that we’ll hear the difference. And I’d make this the rule for every brand partner. Make it make sense for Bond but show me what makes it right for Pattinson’s Bond.

In a recent development, when the first design concepts come in, I’d put my thumb over the 007 mark. If the cufflink shot underneath could sell any Saville Row suit, I’d send the team back to the drawing board. It must fit this latest era of Bond - something that Craig’s or Connery’s might have passed on.

Some of the old partnerships will still fit. Others will need to go or evolve with the way he plays Bond and the audience that will spend the next decade watching him. For a brand planning its next five to ten years, the next Bond film might be the last great monoculture event.

According to recent reports, matt Kerr is a Global Executive Creative Director at Marks with more than 20 years’ experience shaping brands and leading creative teams. His work spans brand identity, packaging, campaigns and digital experiences for clients including LEGO, Diageo, Reckitt and Haleon. At Marks, he has helped transform the agency’s strategic design offering and leads creative standards across a global community of more than 500 designers.

Over the next month, we will reveal the architects and designers who will have the biggest impacts over the next 20 years, as selected by some of the biggest names in architecture and design from the past 20 years.

We started the series with an interview with Harry Nuriev, who was selected by Bjarke Ingels. We then interviewed Lanza Atelier, Freya Tangelder and Swedish Girls, who were selected by Frida Escobedo, Nendo and Sabine Marcelis, respectively.

In a significant week for Dezeen, we also unveiled the winners of the 2026 Dezeen Awards winners at a ceremony in London.

We we revealed the architecture, design and interior project winners, including the Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi (pictured), along with the six designers of the year.

A group of Harvard GSD students also aimed to draw attention to another Donald Trump-backed scheme in Washington DC, by proposing alternative designs to his planned arch.

The two proposals for the planned site of the arch replaced the proposed structure with an expansive pool of water.

Also in the US, looks by SHoP Architects for a supertall skyscraper in Miami, which is backed by Serbian tennis player Novak Djokovic, were revealed.

The 320-metre-tall skyscraper will have a ribbed design and include amenity facilities developed by the tennis player.

In less serious news, American fast-food chain Chipotle launched a range of hoodies all with a hidden, insulated pocket for sneaking burritos into cinemas.

The tongue-in-cheek clothing was designed to keep concealed burritos warm to allow for illicit snacking at the movies.

Popular projects on Dezeen this week include a “surreal” house in rural China, a pink commercial building in Mexico and a Cotswolds barn renovation.

#102993. Industry News: Toot Toot! 6 Tips to Prevent Protein Farts

Industry News: Toot Toot! 6 Tips to Prevent Protein Farts

📅 30 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (711 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets.
  • According to recent reports, protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant!
  • And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets. They happen because of how proteins are digested. But(t) don’t worry! We have some tips to help you say goodbye to those pungent protein toots without giving up your gains.

According to recent reports, protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant! They’re generally due to upping your protein intake from supplements like protein shakes.

And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.

Farts consist of different gases. The most stinky odors usually come from your gut bacteria, producing sulfur-containing compounds as they break down food. The main culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which gives off a characteristic rotten egg smell, yum!

But why do your protein choices lead to thunder from down under?

Well, there’s not much evidence that a high-protein diet causes protein farts. However, there’s some anecdotal evidence that supplementary protein — like protein bars, protein shakes, and powder powders — increases flatulence, but it’s likely due to non-protein ingredients like lactose.

Supplements containing whey protein or casein are derived from milk and are high in lactose, which can increase flatulence. If your body can’t properly digest lactose, it ends up in your colon, where bacteria feast on it, producing — you guessed it — more gas and cheek flapping.

Recent findings suggest that so, whey protein can throw a curveball for those who are lactose intolerant or sensitive. Surprisingly, it might also stir up digestive drama even for folks who typically handle dairy like champs, potentially due to additives like fart-inducing sweeteners or thickeners.

It has been revealed that some people may also have more significant complications digesting protein. Proteins are substantial, complex molecules — breaking them down is no small task for your gut. Plant-based protein supplements, like those based on soya beans, may also worsen flatulence.

FYI: Another reason why flatulence is common with protein powders and supplements is due to the addition of artificial sweeteners in the powders and bars, like sugar alcohols, sucralose, sorbitol, xylitol, and stevia.

If you’re looking to continue your protein regimen without becoming a walking, talking whoopee cushion, here are some strategic adjustments you can make:.

Industry observers note that don’t just dive into the deep end with your protein intake — wade in slowly. Gradually increasing the amount of protein you consume allows your digestive system to adjust without getting overwhelmed. This step-by-step approach can help minimize the likelihood of excessive gas.

It has been revealed that keep the water flowing. Drinking plenty of water is crucial as it helps your digestive system handle higher protein levels more efficiently. Proper hydration aids in the breakdown and absorption of nutrients, which can help prevent gas buildup.

Sometimes, your body needs a little extra help. Enzyme supplements like Beano or Lactaid can be game-changers, especially if you consume proteins that your body struggles with. These supplements help break down proteins and lactose, making digestion smoother and less gassy.

Variety isn’t just the spice of life — it can also be the solution to your protein fart problems. If whey protein tends to upset your stomach, explore other options like plant-based or animal-based proteins that might be easier to digest. Diversifying your protein sources can also ensure you get a broad range of nutrients.

What you blend your protein powder with can make a big difference. If you’re whipping up a protein shake, be mindful of adding high-fiber fruits and vegetables, as these can also increase gas production. Try to find a balance that allows you to enjoy the benefits of protein and fiber without the extra flatulence.

Sources indicate that introducing probiotics into your diet can improve your gut health, which can help manage and reduce gas production. Whether through supplements or probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, or sauerkraut, boosting your gut flora can aid in better overall digestion and less discomfort from gas.

Protein farts are a rather windy side effect of a high-protein diet, but they don’t have to knock you off course. Try easing into your protein consumption, staying hydrated, diversifying your protein sources, and integrating enzyme supplements or probiotics to max those gains, minus the stink bombs!

#102992. “It’s such an obvious partnership” – how D&D and World of Warcraft finally joined forces, according to the lead designer

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1906 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Creativebloq ↗ Open Full Page

“It’s such an obvious partnership” – how D&D and World of Warcraft finally joined forces, according to the lead designer

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this month, two imaginary worlds collide as the legendary tabletop roleplaying game Dungeons & Dragons joins forces with the wildly popular MMORPG, World of Warcraft.The two fantasy franchises have crossed paths before, albeit obliquely, with Warcraft: The Roleplaying Game in 2003, a standalone RPG that was compatible with D&D's 3rd Edition ruleset.
  • Sources indicate that D&D: World of Warcraft is a lavish 256-page hardback book that takes you back to the magical realm of Azeroth and enables you to explore it in the context of your D&D games.
  • The new book contains a wealth of new illustrations alongside art that has been carefully selected from World of Warcraft's vast archives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this month, two imaginary worlds collide as the legendary tabletop roleplaying game Dungeons & Dragons joins forces with the wildly popular MMORPG, World of Warcraft.The two fantasy franchises have crossed paths before, albeit obliquely, with Warcraft: The Roleplaying Game in 2003, a standalone RPG that was compatible with D&D's 3rd Edition ruleset. The upcoming D&D: World of Warcraft gameplay expansion book, however, is the first full-blooded crossover to bring the different species, settings and magical items of Warcraft to the beloved D&D 5E ruleset. "It's such an obvious partnership that it was only a matter of time before it finally happened," admits Senior Game Designer James Wyatt, who led the project for D&D publishers' Wizards of the Coast. "Fundamentally, this book is about playing D&D in the world of Azeroth, and giving you the tools you need to do that.".

Sources indicate that D&D: World of Warcraft is a lavish 256-page hardback book that takes you back to the magical realm of Azeroth and enables you to explore it in the context of your D&D games. The upcoming volume contains 13 WoW-themed character classes for you and your friends to play as, including staples such as Death Knights and Druids, Warlocks and Warriors. It's also chock full of lore that will enable you to devise a rich background for your characters, as well as a wide range of professions and gear that will help them on their adventures. "I like to tell players that they can make a character whose backstory is unique, entirely unlike any other character with the same species," indicates Wyatt, of the book's flexibility. "You can play a Night Elf with the Sailor background, perhaps having grown up ferrying passengers between Auberdine and Rut'theran, never venturing into the heights of Teldrassil – unlike every Night Elf in the MMO. Or you might choose the Entertainer background for your Orc, deciding that you were part of a small, unloved theater company in Orgrimmar for years before deciding to seek your fortune as an adventurer instead. The possibilities are limitless!".

The new book contains a wealth of new illustrations alongside art that has been carefully selected from World of Warcraft's vast archives. "When I came in, I was like, okay, do we have the resources to do this all from scratch, or are we picking out some of the art [from the archives]?" says Jaramillo. "From there it was about figuring out which artists we would have and what type of visuals we would like to include, because World of Warcraft has several different styles of illustration, right from the beginning, like Chris Metzen's sketches [most of which hail from the early, pre-MMO versions of Warcraft – ed.] and then going through the Alex Horley work to more modern stuff, with Billy Christian and Andrey Kuzinskiy." In total the book contains work by more than 50 artists. In terms of the methods and materials used, the book was a real mix with Jaramillo stating that, while most of the artists worked in PhotoShop and Procreate, some painted with oils and then touched the images up digitally.

Sources indicate that in short, it's a perfect blend of these two iconic games, though adapting an online game into a pen and paper RPG was no simple task. "Different parts of the game presented very different challenges," states Wyatt. "And even each WoW class demanded a different set of solutions as we tried to express that class in D&D terms. The result is a book that I think pushes our design across the board to new levels, and challenges our team to continue to innovate and explore the reaches of what we can do in D&D design."Of course, ImagineFX is first and foremost a digital art magazine and we're excited about the visuals in the book as much as we are the game itself. D&D: World of Warcraft does not disappoint on that level – it's a genuinely lavish affair, with every chapter filled with gorgeous, evocative images that celebrate World of Warcraft's long history. Art Director Sergio Jaramillo led the design of the book in what sounds like a dream gig for the veteran WoW player."I joined the D&D team around two years ago," he explains. "By that time [Wizards of the Coast and WoW-owners Blizzard] were already thinking about getting this project prepped. As I was joining the team, my creative director asked me, 'Is there anything that we're working on that you might be interested in?' and immediately I said, 'Warcraft!' That is my jam. I was very familiar with the world, so it was a no-brainer for me.".

Another consideration that the art team needed to bear in mind was that Dungeons & Dragons books have an established format. "We had to have a visual UX layout," claims Jaramillo. "The experience of the book needs to feel like it's a D&D book. With the chapter opener images, if it's a class [chapter] then it needs to feel like that class. The species pages need to inform what different types of characters you might find in a species." So, for example, the image used to illustrate the section on the Orcs is rendered in reds and greens, to reflect the creatures’ different skin tones in the video game. Sometimes, however, a hole would need to be filled with the creation of an all-new image. "For the professions we found a [picture of] a guide fishing, but we needed at least one Horde image too, so that it didn't look like we're skewed towards just the Alliance," Jaramillo explains. "So we added an image of an undead gathering some shrooms. It was a case of getting the right images that we needed for the game. We had access to all these gorgeous pieces of art and we definitely dug deep into the archives of Blizzard.".

It has been revealed that of course, a significant part of the appeal of both Dungeons & Dragons and Warcraft is losing yourself in a richly-detailed fantasy world. The locations of Azeroth remain a vital part of the WoW experience, arguably more so in this tabletop form where players are relying on the imagination of their DM, rather than graphics, to guide them through an adventure. To help make the dungeons accurate to the game, Wyatt played through the MMORPG's various dungeons, trying to map them out, while Jaramillo worked with cartographers Damien Mammoliti and Marc Moureau. "Their style of art is a little bit different," says Jaramillo. Mark is a bit more comic book-ish, in the work that he does, it's more lines, and Damien is very painterly. So it was like, OK, how do we make these maps and styles look similar and inform [the players] that they belong to World of Warcraft. So we put them on parchment that is very reminiscent of the WoW maps. That's the bridge between these two artists and between D&D and WoW.".

One of the earliest locations that players will encounter in the book is the dank Blackfathom Deeps, a fallen temple of Elune that has been defiled by the sinister Twilight's Hammer, evil worshippers of the Old Gods. It's Wyatt's favourite dungeon in the book."Blackfathom Deeps holds a special place in my heart for a couple of reasons," he claims. "My first WoW character was a Night Elf, and I spent months steeped in the aesthetic of the Night Elf regions of the world, including Teldrassil, Darkshore, and Ashenvale (where Blackfathom Deeps is located). I love the colors, the landscapes, and the music of those regions, and the hints of the sweeping history of the Night Elves I got as I adventured through those areas. It was also one of the only dungeons that I actually played as part of a group in those early years, where mostly I was exploring the world solo or with my daughter.".

Sources indicate that wyatt hopes that D&D players who have never experienced the MMORPG before will find inspiration for their own campaigns. "Any of the monsters in the bestiary chapter of this book can be dropped into a D&D campaign on any world," he notes. "My hope is that D&D players who pick up this book will realize that Azeroth is a really cool world that has a lot to offer as a setting for D&D campaigns!"And as for those gamers who grew up with WoW and who are coming to D&D for the first time? "I want them to recognize the feeling of being in Azeroth, almost like you were sitting down and hearing the 'Legends of Azeroth' main title for the first time again. And then at the same time to realize with delight that this is an opportunity to explore the world in a whole upcoming way. This is an Azeroth where you can talk to anyone you meet, interact with anything you see, go anywhere you want to, and try anything you can imagine. I can't wait to hear about the stories our players and DMs tell with this material.".

According to recent reports, when it comes to selecting Sergio Jaramillo's favourite image from D&D: World of Warcraft, the Art Director notes that he cannot pick just one from the wealth of gorgeous visuals contained in the upcoming book. "I'll give you three instead," he laughs. "One from the species, one from miscellaneous stuff, and one from the final characters in the book." From the species, Jaramillo chooses an old WoW favourite. "I have to go with the image of the Pandaren. That piece, as soon as it came in, I was like, 'Oh, this just feels right.'"When it comes to the miscellaneous pile, he chooses something more imposing. "I would have to go with the only new class image that we commissioned for the book, the Dracthyr Evoker," he says of a glorious picture of a fearsome and imposing dragon painted by Andrey Kuzinskiy. "That's just great. I really love the energy in that piece."Finally, for the characters, he chooses an image by Alex Horley of a character known in the game as 'the daughter of the sea'. "I think it would have to be the picture of Jaina Proudmoore. Alex just did a really amazing job on that piece.".

As you might expect, Easter eggs for both games are littered throughout the new book, though both Jaramillo and Wyatt are coy about where you might find them. "The Easter Egg Hunt is less exciting if I tell you where to find them," says the latter, though he points to the piece of art used to illustrate the sections on mounts and companion creatures, noting "The mount and the companion should be recognizable" to fans."I wish I had more time to add even more Easter eggs to this," says Jaramillo. Asked for an example of one that he did manage to sneak in, he highlights a neat nod to D&D. "The art that we picked for the warlock class chapter is of a Gnome. That was just perfect because our warlock art in the D&D book is also a Gnome. So it's like okay, that’s nice. It just fits.".

D&D: World of Warcraft is published by Wizards of the Coast, and is out now.

How YouTube, LEGO, Pokémon, and McDonald's are winning with Gen Alpha

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that what unites the brands that kids love the most?
  • According to recent reports, brands that resonate with Gen Alpha are often seen to be building affinity with the next generation of consumers.
  • Recent findings suggest that but the benefits of engaging Gen A audiences can often be seen sooner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that what unites the brands that kids love the most? Autonomy, discovery, sharing and collecting are recurrent themes, according to Beano Brain's 2026 Coolest Brands report.

According to recent reports, brands that resonate with Gen Alpha are often seen to be building affinity with the next generation of consumers. It's true that many connections formed with brands today will continue throughout adolescence and adulthood.

Recent findings suggest that but the benefits of engaging Gen A audiences can often be seen sooner. Our Gen Alpha: Born to Shop research from earlier this year found that the UK’s 7-to 14-year-olds had £94 million worth of pocket money to spend on the high street.

Autonomy and self-discovery really matter to Gen Alpha, and we see this across some of the most popular brands that ranked in our research.

It’s no surprise when you consider that kids’ lives are still primarily spent following schedules and rules set by adults. Creating a space for them to explore their own interests gives them that freedom and ‘grown-up’ feeling.

According to recent reports, youTube – the number one coolest brand for the past three years – is a perfect example of this. The platform lets kids follow creators, explore latest hobbies and move naturally between quick clips and long-form content. And importantly YouTube serves up content focussed on kids’ interests that simply isn’t available anywhere else – certainly not in traditional media.

The same is true of TikTok (#9), which also enters the top ten for the first time this year. But despite the apparent appeal of social media brands, even here kids are increasingly trying to gain control concerned with doomscrolling and other negative online experiences, 49% of 7-14-year-olds having actively taken time off social media; a third of those taking a break wanted more time for hobbies and interests.

YouTube and TikTok are popular with younger audiences because they offer a chance for kids to explore and provide them with a sense of an owned space. But the crucial contradiction for brands to understand is that kids don’t want to spend all their time there and that sense of freedom isn’t limited to a screen.

Sources indicate that food, drink, and retail brands consistently score highly in our reports because they lead on innovation for example offering a range of limited-edition flavours and experiences for kids to explore. They’re also inherently shareable and must be experienced offline, - attributes of shareability and real-life experiences are loved by kids.

In a recent development, this is backed up by kids’ preferred shopping habits. In Gen Alpha: Born to Shop, more than two thirds (68%) of kids preferred real shops to shopping online, while 90% preferred shopping with someone.

Retail, and particularly QSRs, offer kids affordable spaces for kids and tweens to spend time with family or friends. This is one reason McDonald's has risen to number two, and why food and drink brands in general account for 29% of our Top 100; they offer the chance for shared real-life experiences kids crave.

The return of toys and physical play also came through strongly.

Analogue toys and collectables tap into kids' love of building, trading, and sharing physical items. LEGO (#6), another top ten brand, not only appeals to kids' creativity, but also, through partnerships, allows kids to collect different sets and get imaginative in a hands-on way.

Pokémon (#34) is another brand that’s ‘cool’ this year. Its cards and merchandise give it a collectible and shareable real-world presence to reinforce the online games and TV highlights, properties that may have been the introduction to Pokémon for kids.

It is these shareable and collectable traits that play into the popularity of food and retail brands. For McDonalds, Happy Meal collaborations give children another reason to anticipate a visit, bringing familiar characters and collectable formats into the experience.

In a recent development, youTube, LEGO, Pokémon, and McDonald's all share some of the same attributes of discovery, autonomy, shareability, and collectability. In this context, what may seem like ‘surprise’ inclusions in the list – the discount stores Home Bargains (#88) and B&M (#83) – make sense. ‘Coolness’ is not a trend; it’s embedded in your brand's personality and the brand experience.

Industry observers note that the lesson is not that every brand needs a viral moment or partnership to be ‘cool’. It is that lasting relevance starts with listening to what children want to do and how they want to feel, rather than where to reach them.

Recent findings suggest that gen Alpha’s choices may still surprise us. But the motivations behind them should not.

Helenor is an award-winning researcher in the kids and family insights field. With over 30 years of experience in kids media, Helenor is an authority on kids, authoring one of the first white papers establishing key Gen Alpha behaviours.

Helenor designed and manages Beano Brain's unique ethnographic kids panel which means she has her ear to the ground when it comes to all things newly introduced and emerging. Her thorough knowledge means she has unrivalled knowledge about what drives kids and their parents, the rhythm of their lives and what they think is cool (or not).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck.
  • From a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti. If you’ve ever scrambled for scarves or turtlenecks, welcome to the kissing booth of knowledge! Join us as we navigate the lifecycle of hickeys, from their eye-catching start to their subtle fade, and learn how to speed up their departure.

Recent findings suggest that A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck. This intense suction causes the tiny blood vessels under the skin, a.k.a. capillaries, to burst and release blood into the surrounding tissues. The immediate result? An unmistakable red or purple mark that gradually shifts to a darker shade as it heals.

From a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing. They showcase the skin’s sensitivity and the body’s rapid response to minor vascular injury. Not so romantic when you think about it scientifically, right? But hey, it’s all part of the human experience of showing affection — or something like that.

Sources indicate that when you get a hickey, your body starts a healing process that resembles how it deals with other bruises. Here’s a more detailed look at each stage of a hickey’s life cycle.

It has been revealed that immediately after the passionate moment, a hickey appears on the skin, screaming in shades of bright red or deep purple. This initial coloration is due to blood from the ruptured capillaries pooling beneath the skin’s surface in response to the suction. It’s your skin’s way of signaling that there’s been some minor internal damage in that area.

As the hickey begins to heal, it undergoes a whole wardrobe of color transformations, showcasing your body’s metabolic process at work.

Initially, the hickey darkens as the blood begins to oxidize. Then, after a few days, the body starts to break down and reabsorb the blood, so it turns lighter — going from blue to green to brown and, finally, mellow yellow. This rainbow journey reflects the breakdown of hemoglobin, the iron-containing substance in the blood, into biliverdin and bilirubin.

Recent findings suggest that finally, your hickey starts to ghost you. Over a week or two, depending on factors like your skin type, overall health, how severe the hickey was., and how your body rides the healing waves, the last traces of your hickey fade into nothing.

During this stage, the body’s immune system clears away the remaining by-products of the broken-down blood. White blood cells swoop in like a cleanup crew at a festival, gobbling up and digesting the debris in a process called phagocytosis, while increased blood flow to the area helps to flush out the remnants.

In a recent development, need a hickey gone yesterday? Here’s how to help your hickey heal. Start with a cold pack — grab a spoon from the freezer or a chilled gel pack and gently press it against your hickey. This will help reduce any swelling and scatter the blood pooling under your skin, which can help minimize that bold bruise.

After using cold treatment for the first 48 hours, it’s time to turn up the heat. Switch to warm compresses to get the blood flowing smoothly again. A few minutes a few times a day invites more circulation to the hickey zone, helping you hustle through healing and clear out the blood remnants more swiftly.

It has been revealed that you can also try a dab of comfrey ointment. Research indicates it may reduce bruise size and coloration for some peeps.

Sources indicate that caught off guard? A little concealer or foundation over the hickey makes it less noticeable.

Industry observers note that not into makeup? Scarves and high-necked shirts are also great accessories for your camouflage arsenal.

Typically, a hickey will last anywhere from 5 days to 2 weeks, depending on its severity and your body’s healing capabilities.

Recent findings suggest that communication is key! Let your partner know your feelings about receiving a hickey — some might find it fun, while others may prefer to keep their necks clear.

While generally harmless, hickeys can sometimes lead to complications like skin infections or, very rarely, blood clots. It’s best to keep the affection gentle to avoid any challenges.

Hickeys are nothing more than bruises in disguise. They start as bright red to purple love stamps and gradually fade over several days to a couple of weeks. Speed up the process with heat and cold packs or a splodge of comfrey cream.

Remember, the best approach to handling hickeys — like all aspects of relationships — is communication and care. So go forth, love responsibly, and keep a scarf handy, just in case!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Japanese wedding chapel, an Indian university and a reformed monument to an Albanian dictator are among these public buildings where stairs help to create a dramatic facade.
  • Some, like the MVRDV’s Pyramid of Tirana and Snøhetta’s Shanghai Grand Opera House, were designed specifically to give the public unrivalled access to their architecture.
  • The one thing they all have in common is that they make their stairs the main event.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Japanese wedding chapel, an Indian university and a reformed monument to an Albanian dictator are among these public buildings where stairs help to create a dramatic facade.

Some, like the MVRDV’s Pyramid of Tirana and Snøhetta’s Shanghai Grand Opera House, were designed specifically to give the public unrivalled access to their architecture. Others, like the Ribbon Chapel (top image), use stairs to serve as both a viewpoint and a metaphor.

The one thing they all have in common is that they make their stairs the main event.

Prestige University, India, by Sanjay Puri Architects.

More than 460 stepped platforms are arranged on top of Prestige University in Indore, Madhya Pradesh, which was recently crowned education project of the year at the 2026 Dezeen Awards.

Its 9,000-square-metre walkable roof gradually steps up from the ground to its full height of 28 metres, reducing the visual heft of the building while providing gathering space for all of the university‘s 3,000 students at the same time.

Drawing on the ancient tradition of Indian stepwells, the staircases are organised around courtyards that help to draw sun and ventilation deep into the building, reducing its dependence on artificial light and air conditioning.

Shanghai Grand Opera House, China, by Snøhetta.

Snøhetta has had a thing for walkable roofs ever since its seminal design for the Oslo Opera House in 2008.

Now, China has received its own take on the theme with the Shanghai Opera House, defined by a giant spiral staircase that curves out of the facade and dramatically cantilevers at its peak.

Much like the slanted roof in Oslo, the stairs were designed to make the building radically accessible to the public – although Dezeen revealed earlier this month that access to the roof is now restricted to paid ticket holders.

Pyramid of Tirana, Albania, by MVRDV and IRI Architecture.

Stairs serve both a practical and symbolic function in MVRDV‘s renovation of the Pyramid of Tirana – a monument built for Albanian dictator Enver Hoxha in the 1980s.

The Dutch architecture studio added steps to the pyramid on all sides to allow people to climb and reclaim the building.

“The first time I saw the Pyramid being walked all over by the youth of Tirana, I was deeply touched by its symbolism and by its incredible optimism,” said MVRDV founding partner Winy Maas.

Ribbon Chapel, Japan, by Hiroshi Nakamura.

Intertwining staircases spiral around the glazed core of this wedding chapel in Onomichi, designed by Tokyo-based architect Hiroshi Nakamura.

The stairs, representing the joining of two people in marriage, meet at the top to create a small viewing platform overlooking Japan‘s Seto Inland Sea.

“Just as two lives go through twists and turns before uniting as one, the two spirals seamlessly connect at their 15.4-metre summit to form a single ribbon,” Nakamura explained.

Hisao & Hiroko Taki Plaza, Japan, by Kengo Kuma and Associates.

This student hub was designed by Kengo Kuma and Associates to resemble a natural landform growing out of the Tokyo Institute of Technology campus.

Wooden bleachers and plants help to conceal the building, which is partially sunken into the ground to retain views of the university’s historic clock tower.

The external staircase that descends into the building is also mirrored inside, helping to blur the boundary between interior and exterior landscape.
