#102947. Having ‘Boring’ Conversations Is Really Good for You, Psychologists Say

📅 15 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (889 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Having ‘Boring’ Conversations Is Really Good for You, Psychologists Say

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s tempting to try to bypass coworkers in the break room or limit small talk with the person waiting next to you in an effort to avoid what you suspect will be a dull conversation.
  • The study, which was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that people who actually engage in these conversations thought that they were much more interesting and enjoyable than they expected.
  • In a recent development, “These moments are small, but they are not trivial,” Nicholas Allan, PhD, psychologist and assistant professor in the department of psychiatry and behavioral health at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it’s tempting to try to bypass coworkers in the break room or limit small talk with the person waiting next to you in an effort to avoid what you suspect will be a dull conversation. But upcoming research makes a solid argument for leaning into these “boring” chats.

The study, which was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that people who actually engage in these conversations thought that they were much more interesting and enjoyable than they expected. But beyond that, there is data to suggest that having these “boring” conversations could do your mental and physical health a solid.

In a recent development, “These moments are small, but they are not trivial,” Nicholas Allan, PhD, psychologist and assistant professor in the department of psychiatry and behavioral health at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. Here’s why.

In a recent development, the research focused on nine experiments featuring 1,800 participants. During the experiments, participants were asked to predict how much they would enjoy talking about a range of topics they identified as boring. These included World Wars I and II, nonfiction books, math, onions, the stock market, cats, and vegan diets. These chats happened with either strangers or friends, and were in person or online.

Sources indicate that the researchers discovered that while participants remarked they expected the conversations to be pretty lame, they reported afterward that they enjoyed them much more than they thought they would. This even happened when both people in the conversation thought a topic was boring.

“We decided to conduct this research because so many people avoid conversations they think will be boring. We cancel small talk, dread networking events, and assume that certain topics, like the weather, commuting, or daily routines, just won’t be interesting,” Elizabeth Trinh, lead study author and a doctoral student at the University of Michigan, tells SELF. “If conversations are generally good for us, why do we so often expect them to be dull or draining?”.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, the researchers found that being engaged in the conversation was what really mattered. “Engagement drives enjoyment more than topic does,” Trinh indicates. “People assume that interest comes from having a fascinating subject. But in reality, what makes conversations enjoyable is the sense of connection like feeling heard, responding to each other, and discovering unexpected details about someone’s life. Even a mundane topic can become meaningful when two people are actively engaging with each other.”.

People are social creatures by nature and connecting over a topic that feels boring, like onions, is still a social connection, Aaron P. Brinen, PsyD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, tells SELF. Thea Gallagher, PsyD, clinical associate professor of psychology at NYU Langone Health, agrees. “Sometimes people will predict that a conversation will be awkward or uncomfortable. But if you try to connect and listen in a conversation, there can be great benefits,” she tells SELF.

Industry observers note that as a result, Dr. Gallagher notes she encourages her patients to have conversations everywhere they go. “Being a lifelong learner can be very powerful,” she says. “At the end of the day, connecting with humans can make us feel good.”.

In a recent development, these chats can seem pointless, but experts stress that they’re actually not. Not only will you likely find that you enjoy “boring” conversations more than you expected, it could keep you from feeling lonely.

“Loneliness is not just about how many people someone sees. It is about whether interactions feel connecting and meaningful,” explains Dr. Allan. Side-stepping a “boring” chat is likely to increase your sense of loneliness, Dr. Brinen indicates. “Even if you didn’t want to be a part of that conversation, you’re still lonely,” he points out.

Loneliness on its own is a horrible feeling, but it can also have a significant impact on your health. Feeling lonely or socially isolated raises the risk of a slew of serious health conditions, including heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, depression, anxiety, dementia, and early death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). “When we find a way to be engaged with other people, it meets that need to connect with others,” Dr. Brinen says.

Over time, those small “boring” moments can build on each other, Dr. Allan indicates. With that, your feelings of loneliness—and health risks that can come with them—decrease.

It has been revealed that of course, some interactions with others aren’t great. “Not all social contact is beneficial,” Dr. Allan claims. “More contact is not automatically better. What seems to matter most is whether the interaction feels respectful, reciprocal, and emotionally safe. Positive connection helps. Depleting or hostile interactions do not.”.

Ultimately, Trinh recommends keeping an open mind when it comes to future conversations. “We may be missing out on connection because we misjudge how conversations will feel,” she indicates. “If we avoid talking to someone because we assume it will be boring—like a coworker at the coffee machine, a stranger at an event, or a neighbor in the elevator—we may be unnecessarily depriving ourselves of small moments of connection that could improve our mood and sense of belonging.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, cutting back on calories but not losing weight? You might wonder if you’ve gotten stuck in the twilight zone of so-called “starvation mode.”.

Everyone from your personal trainer to your grandma may have warned you about this metabolic frenemy that keeps your body holding onto weight. But is starvation mode really a thing — or just an urban legend?

The concept of starvation mode is that when you restrict calories, your body has a “hold it right there” response. To prevent you from losing weight rapidly, your metabolism slows, conserving energy by reducing the calories it burns.

In a recent development, research shows starvation mode — formally called adaptive thermogenesis or metabolic adaptation — is a legit phenomenon. It’s well documented that sometimes, the more weight you lose (and the more rapidly you do so), the more your body resists the process.

Evolutionarily speaking, this may be a holdover from when humans faced food scarcity and needed a mechanism for self-preservation. But in today’s world, starvation mode can be a frustrating roadblock to weight loss.

Sources indicate that what does this metabolic hiccup look like? These symptoms may indicate that starvation mode is becoming a problem for your health:.

Starvation mode isn’t the same thing as actual starving. In today’s modern food environment, true starvation is rare. If you’re eating regularly, you won’t experience life-threatening starvation.

According to recent reports, however, your body might exhibit some of the same early signs as real starvation. These include the symptoms listed above.

Most commonly, though, starvation mode involves stalled weight loss. You may have hit the wall of adaptive thermogenesis when restricting calories and increasing physical activity without losing weight.

Getting into starvation mode can take just a few days, especially if those days involve severe calorie restriction.

Recent findings suggest that so what counts as severe calorie restriction? Many experts advise not going below 1,200 calories per day for women and 1,500 calories per day for men unless supervised by a doctor. Anything below these numbers could land you in starvation mode faster.

Fortunately, getting your body out of starvation mode isn’t complicated.

First, there’s the obvious solution: Eat a few more calories. But we don’t mean just any calories. By adding a few more nutrient-dense foods (especially those with fiber and protein), you may find weight loss becomes easier, not harder. Both of these nutrients have links to weight loss — so they might help you get out of starvation mode without gaining weight.

If you’re feeling extremely depleted, you might take a temporary break from a weight loss diet to replenish your nutrient stores.

Recent findings suggest that choosing the proper exercise could also bump you out of starvation mode. Resistance exercises like weightlifting, yoga, push-ups, squats, and others build muscle, which increases your metabolic rate.

According to a 2014 study, people who participated in a 9-month resistance exercise program increased their resting metabolic rate — aka how many calories they burned at rest — by an average of 5%.

In a recent development, weight loss is a balancing act. It’s normal to experience physical and emotional ups and downs.

In a recent development, that mentioned, it’s time to see a doctor if you’re noticing symptoms like extreme fatigue or lethargy, constipation that lasts more than a few days, sensitivity to cold, or unusual mood changes. Your healthcare team can help you hit the sweet spot of weight loss without lingering in starvation mode.

Industry observers note that despite its name, being in starvation mode doesn’t mean you’ll starve. Instead, it’s a state in which your body has adapted to your weight loss efforts, giving you pushback on how many calories it burns. With strategies like tweaking your calorie intake and adding strength training, you can get out of this mode and back on the path to sustained weight loss.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Swiss watchmaker Mondaine has expanded its Doppio collection with the Solar Skeleton, a timepiece that brings solar technology into the foreground of its design.

Rather than concealing the solar plates beneath the dial, the watch reveals them through a precisely cut circular opening, turning a functional component into a defining visual feature.

The design builds on the distinctive visual language of Mondaine‘s Doppio collection, which is characterised by double-line hands and indexes, a concave dial and a double-domed sapphire crystal.

Mondaine explained that these elements establish a sense of repetition, rhythm and structural clarity, while the exposed solar plates introduce an additional layer of depth and visual interest.

While solar technology is typically hidden from view, Mondaine has taken a different approach with the Doppio Solar Skeleton.

A carefully positioned circular opening around the centre of the dial offers a controlled view of the solar movement, while the outer section retains the indexes to ensure clear readability.

By making the technology visible, Mondaine aimed to bridge the watch’s technical function with its aesthetic identity, without compromising the “clarity and legibility” that define the collection.

Powered by a Swiss Ronda solar movement, the watch converts natural and artificial light into electrical energy, which is stored in a rechargeable battery.

According to Mondaine, a few minutes of sunlight can reactivate a fully discharged movement, while a full charge provides a power reserve of up to eight months in complete darkness.

The brand explained that this technology eliminates the need for regular battery replacements, offering a more resource-conscious approach to timekeeping.

The Doppio Solar Skeleton is available in two versions, each offering a different interpretation of its distinctive design.

The first combines a polished silver 316L stainless steel case with a vegan grape leather strap, bringing together traditional watchmaking materials and a contemporary material alternative.

The second features a polished black stainless steel case paired with a matching mesh bracelet, creating a more monochromatic appearance that emphasises the watch’s clean lines and geometric detailing.

Both versions feature a 41-millimetre case, a discreet date window and a precisely laser-etched Mondaine logo and solar markings.

A double-domed sapphire crystal and water resistance of up to 5 ATM complete the design, “combining refined aesthetics with everyday practicality”.

“With the Doppio Solar Skeleton, we wanted to make solar technology part of the design itself,” remarked Mondaine.

“By revealing the cells beneath the dial, we have created a watch where functionality becomes a defining aesthetic feature, while staying true to Mondaine’s principles of clarity, precision and Swiss design.”.

The Doppio Solar Skeleton reflects Mondaine’s commitment to iconic Swiss minimalist design, where form and function work together.

By integrating visible solar technology into the collection’s established design language, the watch intends to demonstrate how a functional element can become an integral part of a timepiece’s aesthetic identity.

To find out more about Mondaine and the Doppio Solar Skeleton, visit the brand’s website.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Incline walking and running are commonly framed as opposites: one is low impact, the other is high-intensity.
  • Understanding those differences can help you decide which one deserves a spot in your fitness routine, or how to incorporate both.
  • At their core, incline walking and running share a common foundation: they get your body moving in a rhythmic, repetitive way that challenges your cardiovascular system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Incline walking and running are commonly framed as opposites: one is low impact, the other is high-intensity. But in reality, they’re both effective cardio options that challenge your body in distinct ways—from the muscles you recruit to the impact on your joints. Both workouts can boost your heart health, build endurance, and leave you seriously sweaty, but they place different demands on your body, according to Gab Reznik, CPT and Tone House coach. The question isn’t which is better across the board—it’s which is better for you depending on your goals.

Understanding those differences can help you decide which one deserves a spot in your fitness routine, or how to incorporate both.

At their core, incline walking and running share a common foundation: they get your body moving in a rhythmic, repetitive way that challenges your cardiovascular system.

“Any movement is better than no movement at all—whether that’s incline walking or running,” Reznik tells SELF. “They’re both effective at increasing blood flow, elevating heart rate, and improving overall aerobic capacity.” That means stronger heart and lung function over time—which are key markers of long-term health.

They also both demand muscular effort. Running requires you to generate power with every stride, while incline walking emphasizes controlled, deliberate steps against gravity (thanks to the incline). “Over time, the repetitive impact and loading can help strengthen joints and support long-term durability when done properly,” Reznik says.

While they may look similar on the surface, incline walking and running are different in two major ways: how hard they push your body, and how much stress they place on your joints.

Recent findings suggest that running is the higher-impact option. With each stride, your joints absorb roughly two to three times your body weight. That added force typically translates to higher intensity—and more calories burned per hour, Reznik explains.

Industry observers note that incline walking, on the other hand, keeps one foot on the ground at all times, reducing overall joint load. “Incline walking is more sustainable for longer durations,” Reznik notes. “At the same fitness level, someone will typically be able to maintain an incline walk longer than a run due to the lower per-step demand.”.

It’s easy to think of incline walking as purely cardio—but that’s only part of its benefits.

In a recent development, “Incline walking can absolutely build strength, just not in the same way as lifting weights,” Reznik says. Instead of maximizing muscle growth by picking up heavy weights, incline walking improves muscular endurance, particularly in the lower body (think: glutes, hamstrings, and calves).

Sources indicate that the steeper the incline, the greater the challenge. And if you want to level up even more, try adding external load, like a weighted vest, Reznik suggests. “It can increase the strength stimulus without significantly increasing joint impact.”.

Still, it’s notable to keep your expectations realistic. If your goal is to build maximal strength or increase muscle size, traditional strength training should still be your primary focus.

Industry observers note that one of the biggest misconceptions about incline walking is that it’s somehow inferior to running. Reznik is quick to shut that down.

“Walking isn’t less effective—it’s simply a different type of stimulus,” she indicates.

In a recent development, in fact, incline walking can be deceptively tough. Imagine this: a 15% incline at 3 mph for 30 minutes, without holding onto the treadmill. “That’s extremely challenging—even for a trained runner,” Reznik says.

In a recent development, both workouts can improve cardiovascular fitness and support fat loss when programmed appropriately. The key is understanding that “effective” doesn’t mean “hardest”—it means the movement is aligned with your fitness goals.

In a recent development, if you’re aiming to maximize calorie burn in a shorter amount of time or really test your cardiovascular endurance, running may be the more efficient choice, Reznik says. Its higher intensity makes it ideal for pushing your limits.

In a recent development, but if you’re looking to reduce joint stress while still building aerobic fitness (and even some muscular endurance), incline walking may be the smarter pick. “If you treat them as complementary, you can unlock a higher level of performance and longevity,” Reznik says.

Deciding between incline walking and running ultimately comes down to three factors: your goals, your current fitness level, and what you actually enjoy enough to stick with.

Recent findings suggest that beginners might start with a light jog at a conversational pace or a slight incline (around 2% to 3%) at a comfortable walking speed, Reznik suggests. From there, it’s important to progress either the speed or incline, but not both at once.

“Incline walking isn’t the ‘easy’ option—it’s the smart option when used correctly,” Reznik says. “Running isn’t the ‘better’ option—it’s the specific option when it aligns with your goals.”.

A well-rounded routine might include both: running for higher-intensity days when you want to challenge your cardio limits, and incline walking for longer, lower-impact sessions that still deliver a serious burn.

Ultimately, there’s no clear winner between incline walking and running because they aren’t rivals. Both movements can be tools for improving heart health, building endurance and strengthening key muscle groups. The better workout is the one that helps you move consistently and safely. And in many cases, the smartest approach isn’t choosing between them—it’s using both.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there are many possible causes for bumps inside your nose — some as harmless as a pimple, others that might need more attention. It’s easy to imagine the worst, but the truth is usually less alarming.

If you’ve got a painful, annoying, or strange bump in your nose, keep reading to learn what it might be, whether it’s worth worrying about, and how to deal with it.

So, what’s behind these bothersome nose bumps? Here are some common culprits:.

This is inflammation of the nasal vestibule, the area just inside your nostrils, often caused by bacterial infections. It can lead to painful, red bumps sensitive to the touch. Common triggers include frequent nose-picking, blowing too hard, or even plucking nose hairs.

Sources indicate that like on your face, the pores inside your nose can become clogged with oil, dirt, and bacteria, leading to pimples. These can be painful and may swell, especially in such a sensitive area.

Non-cancerous growths can develop in the nasal passages or sinus lining due to chronic inflammation, allergies, or infections. While they’re usually painless, larger polyps can cause blockages, leading to breathing difficulties, a reduced sense of smell, or recurrent sinus infections.

When you pluck or trim nose hairs, the hair can sometimes grow back into the skin instead of out, causing an ingrown hair. If this becomes infected, it can result in a painful bump inside the nose.

A bump can also form inside the nose due to trauma, such as a blow to the nose, or even from something as simple as aggressive nose-picking. The trauma can cause the tissue to swell or become bruised. In some cases, a hard bump may form as the tissue heals.

Fluid-filled sacs that can form in your nose, usually harmless but sometimes uncomfortable.

A hard bump inside the nose might be due to problems with the cartilage, such as a deviated septum or cartilage overgrowth.

Small, benign bumps that may appear on or in the nose are often mistaken for pimples but are fibrous tissue growths.

"Sacred" archaeological finds become raw materials for design in Ex Situ exhibition

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (980 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Upcoming objects made from mammoth bone, leather from the middle ages and stumps from a road built under Roman Emperor Hadrian feature in the Ex Situ project, set to be exhibited soon in The Hague.
  • Initiated and curated by Dutch designer Marisa Klaster, working in concert with archaeologist René Isarin, the project makes use of materials that many in Isarin’s profession and the broader public might consider off-limits for latest designs: the finds from archaeological digs.
  • However, while these finds, such as 40,000-year-old mammoth bone and 14th-century ship wood, sound like they belong in a museum, they are in fact deselected – not chosen for inclusion in any archives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Upcoming objects made from mammoth bone, leather from the middle ages and stumps from a road built under Roman Emperor Hadrian feature in the Ex Situ project, set to be exhibited soon in The Hague.

Initiated and curated by Dutch designer Marisa Klaster, working in concert with archaeologist René Isarin, the project makes use of materials that many in Isarin’s profession and the broader public might consider off-limits for latest designs: the finds from archaeological digs.

However, while these finds, such as 40,000-year-old mammoth bone and 14th-century ship wood, sound like they belong in a museum, they are in fact deselected – not chosen for inclusion in any archives.

Deselected finds are duplicates, common in type, poorly preserved or otherwise judged to have limited future research value.

“The material that you see here is the lowest of the lowest quality,” said Isarin at a preview of Ex Situ at this year’s Dutch Design Week. “It’s not preserved. It doesn’t belong in a museum. It doesn’t belong in a depot.”.

In fact, if it is not going to be used for educational purposes or reference collections, deselected archaeological finds are required by Dutch law to be carefully destroyed, as they are in many places around the world, mentioned Isarin and Klaster.

In a recent development, although the materials may be of low value to archaeology, the designers both found this something of a waste. With Ex Situ, they aim to explore a newly introduced category of use and preservation for these materials, believing artists and designers have the capacity to tell stories of heritage in a different way to museums.

With the permission of the province of South Holland, they gave deselected materials to nine Dutch practitioners with expertise in crafts such as ceramics, woodwork and glassmaking.

One of the most finished pieces, exhibited in a preview showcase at October’s Dutch Design Week in the Klokgebouw, was by footwear designer and materials researcher Judith Sanders.

She crafted the foundation posts from a section of the Roman Limes border road, dated to 125AD and built under the emperor Hadrian, into the heel of a pair of high-heeled shoes. Sanders was intrigued by the notion that they could perform structurally once again – this time bearing the load of just one person.

Bold numbers on the sides of the shoe denote where on the dig site the material came from, while a second pair of shoes works leather from the middle ages into a modern-day sneaker silhouette.

Another piece is by designer-maker Daan Simons, who worked with 14th-century wood fragments from a ship that was wrecked and then subsequently used in the construction of Rotterdam.

The texture and existing peg holes in the wood are preserved in his Remembrance Pots, which he imagines holding the ashes of a loved one or a keepsake of theirs, compounding the layers of memory in the vessel.

Klaster and Isarin started on the path to Ex Situ after meeting accidentally at their timber drying kiln, where she was having some wood dried for a furniture project, and he was having the deselected Roman posts dried in the hope they would find another life.

“Intrigued by their blackness”, Klaster asked Isarin if she could have them, and went on to make a series of tall vases. That was five years ago, and they have been discussing the potential intersection of archaeology and design ever since.

Klaster claims that the Ex Situ designers were supported with information about heritage and the finds they were working with, but that the project naturally inspired some trepidation.

According to recent reports, “In the work that they have made so far, you see that they have thought it through, and there is respect in what they made,” said Klaster. “But the first cut with a scissor or a bandsaw is, of course, a scary thing.”.

“[One of the designers] was like, can I really saw that in two? And I stated yes, you can. If you have a proposal as a designer, yes, it’s yours.”.

That worry will be echoed among some archaeologists, Isarin adds, and he and Klaster’s aim is for the exhibition to promote discussion among the profession.

“For archaeologists, this material is in a sense sacred,” remarked Isarin. “But it’s deselected, so nobody wants it.”.

Sources indicate that he said that while reactions have so far been positive, the glitch becomes more thorny if the design were to take place in a commercial context – for instance, if Sanders’ shoes were sold by a fashion brand. In that sense, some archaeologists may see this project as opening a Pandora’s box.

“As soon as we enter the commercial world, then I think for many archaeologists it will be, even though it’s deselected material, an interesting debate ethically,” said Isarin.

Industry observers note that “Suppose that all this matter, which has no value at all, that somebody gets rich out of it. That would be a disaster for many archaeologists.”.

Nevertheless, Klaster and Isarin think it is a debate worth having.

Pieces in the exhibition come from practitioners ranging from glass artist Bernard Heesen, working with 17th- and 18th-century glass, to conceptual material designer Shahar Livne, working with mammoth bone, and ceramicist Lotte Douwes, working with Roman pottery.

“We have so much rich material beneath our feet, with amazing stories from 40,000 years up to today,” said Klaster.

The exhibition was previewed at Dutch Design Week, alongside the maximalist installation Everything Moist Seems Alive installation by Maison the Faux and Boris Acket and design collective Show Not Show’s Table of Power exhibition.

It has been revealed that ex Situ: Matter in Translation will be on at See Lab, The Hague, from 5 February to 7 March 2027, with discussion events as part of its programming. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Temperatures are starting to rise, with some parts of the US facing a record-setting early heat wave this week.
  • That’s the major takeaway from new research published in the journal Neurology: The study uncovered three lesser-known factors that can trigger migraine—and these triggers can crop up even more in the late spring and summer.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you’re one of the 12% of Americans who deals with these headaches, this is information to keep in your back pocket.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Temperatures are starting to rise, with some parts of the US facing a record-setting early heat wave this week. But while you’re probably focused on staying cool, there’s one more thing that should be on your radar: a higher-than-usual risk of migraine headaches.

That’s the major takeaway from new research published in the journal Neurology: The study uncovered three lesser-known factors that can trigger migraine—and these triggers can crop up even more in the late spring and summer.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re one of the 12% of Americans who deals with these headaches, this is information to keep in your back pocket. Here’s what the study found, plus how doctors who treat patients with migraine recommend protecting yourself.

It has been revealed that for the study, researchers followed 7,032 people living in Israel for about a decade who suffered from migraines. During the study period, researchers looked at participants’ daily exposure to air pollution, along with tracking weather conditions. They also looked at how often and when people visited the hospital or their primary care doctor with a migraine. That data was compared to the levels of pollution and weather conditions on that particular day, along with seven days before that.

During the study period, 2,215 people (or 32%) had at least one visit to the hospital or a clinic with a migraine. The researchers also found that 47% of participants in the study bought triptan medications at one point or another—fast-acting prescription medications that are designed to stop a migraine—with most using at least two tablets a month.

Ultimately, the researchers discovered a link between three weather-related factors and migraine: air pollution, temperature (including UV exposure), and humidity. First, they found a correlation between higher levels of air pollution and the most number of visits to a hospital or clinic for a migraine. They also found that the day with the least visits to the hospital or clinic also had lower-than-average pollution levels. People with short-term exposure to high levels of nitrogen dioxide (a common pollutant from traffic exhaust) were 41% more likely to go to the hospital or clinic for migraine than people who weren’t exposed to high levels of the gas.

The study also revealed that people who were exposed to high levels of UV rays from the sun on a given day were 23% more likely to visit a healthcare provider for migraine symptoms than those who weren’t. High temperatures and low humidity appear to be linked to more migraine headaches, likely because they amplify the effect of nitrogen dioxide, the researchers said.

With climate change intensifying how often we deal with heat waves and pollution, it’s important to consider these risk factors when it comes to migraine, the researchers wrote.

It’s important to note that the study didn’t prove that air pollution, heat, and lower humidity levels cause migraines—it just found a link between them. But doctors say there’s likely something here.

Air pollution can spark neuroinflammation (the immune system’s inflammatory response in the brain and spinal cord), which is a risk factor for migraine, Sana Ghafoor, MD, neurologist at Tufts Medical Center, tells SELF. This may cause a release of pain chemicals like calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and substance P that can lead to a migraine, Dr. Ghafoor notes.

In a recent development, air pollution may be particularly problematic for people with allergies who also struggle with migraines, Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, California, tells SELF. The body may see air pollution as an allergen and mount an immune response, which can spark a migraine in people who are sensitive to this trigger, he explains.

Then, there’s the fact that heat can impact blood vessels and nerves. “When people heat up, nerves and blood vessels in tight locations can become irritated, as the diameter of a blood vessel or nerves increases with heat,” Dr. Segil says. That, too, can trigger a migraine. You’re also more susceptible to getting dehydrated when it’s hot out, Dr. Ghafoor says: “If you're overheated and dehydrated, those can also trigger migraines.”.

Dr. Segil points out that high humidity common in the spring and summer (and not just that related to air pollution) can trigger migraines too. High humidity causes you to sweat and lose water, which can decrease the amount of blood in your blood vessels (if you don’t replace it), Dr. Segil notes. “This decreases the diameter of blood vessels and can cause headaches, just like an increased blood vessel diameter,” he says.

Dr. Ghafoor says she often sees more patients have migraine headaches when high humidity strikes. “Even with small [atmospheric] pressure changes, it can activate nerve endings and sinuses, which can lead to the release of pain chemicals,” she says.

These are some of the most common migraine triggers, according to the US National Library of Medicine:.

These foods and ingredients can also trigger migraines, per the US National Library of Medicine:.

Migraine triggers are personal, making it important to do what you can to figure out yours and then try to avoid them as best as possible. (Dr. Ghafoor recommends keeping a headache diary to try to narrow things down.) But factors like air pollution, heat, and humidity can be tough to avoid.

If levels of air pollution are high in your area, Dr. Segil recommends wearing a face mask like an N95 when you need to be outdoors. Keeping your windows shut and running an air purifier can also help tamp down on pollution indoors. If you’d like, you can track pollution levels throughout the day and try to stay inside during peak times, Dr. Ghafoor states.

Sources indicate that when heat and humidity strikes, Dr. Ghafoor recommends doing what you can to stay well hydrated. “Make sure that it’s not just water, but electrolytes too,” she indicates. “All of that is a very key part of lifestyle management for patients who have migraine.”.

Ultimately, doing your best to try to figure out your triggers (and avoid them) can go a long way toward helping to keep you more comfortable on a regular basis. “Knowing and identifying migraine triggers is very important,” Dr. Ghafoor claims. “It’s empowering the patient to understand their disease.”.

Images courtesy of Sturdy.

A nine-metre-tall replica of a town hall in Fayetteville, North Carolina, takes centre stage at American rapper J Cole’s world tour set, which has been created by production organization Sturdy.

The set for The Fall Off Tour was designed by Los Angeles-based Sturdy to realise J Cole’s ambition to take his hometown, Fayetteville – or “the ville”– “to the world”.

Industry observers note that to do this, the studio drew on the historic, two-storey Market House building, which has stood as a local landmark in the city since 1832. Sturdy created a weathered, ivy-covered replica of the structure, which is neoclassical with gothic revival details.

“The Market House was chosen because it’s an iconic piece of architecture historically as well in the town that J Cole’s from,” Martinez told Dezeen.

“I think a substantial part of the intention is that he takes home with him wherever he goes; conceptually, the idea was to take ‘the ville’ to the world,” he continued.

“And what better way to do that than something that lives basically at the centre point of the entire city?”.

Other nods to the rapper’s life in Fayetteville include the presence of a Honda Civic car, which Martinez describes as a “supporting actor in the show”.

Positioned in front of the building at centre stage, the car is supported on ties that allow it to be suspended above the stage during specific moments of the performance.

“The car is like a supporting actor in the show that adds a little bit of an authentic take to the performance,” he remarked.

“His fans know the black Civic, and, at least from my perspective, with this being The Fall Off, the car needs to have a place in the story. It’s part of ‘the ville’,” Martinez added.

The set was designed by Sturdy to be easily dismantled, shipped and rebuilt between highlights across the US, Europe, South Africa, Australia and Newly introduced Zealand.

This determined the scale and design of the neoclassical Market House replica, which stretches just over 15 metres and is composed of easy-to-assemble wood and metal components.

The materiality of the structure also allows for J Cole’s performance to extend to the building’s first-floor terrace.

Alongside the structure is a 23-metre-long walkway lined with grass, rocks and a tree stump that doubles as a seat for the artist.

“Any show that we are doing, especially of this scale, has to be designed from a ‘rigging perspective’ to how this thing breaks down,” Martinez explained.

It has been revealed that “That all has to be thoroughly thought out because we’ve got to be able to have the proper Legos. We can’t really just show up and hope that it’s going to piece together,” he added.

Also contributing to the set is a large LED screen, which, according to Martinez, is used “rather sparingly” throughout the performances to bring the stage design to the fore.

“I think for a long stretch of time demonstrates were just about crazy visuals and putting stuff on screens and just letting people see stuff moving in the background,” he said.

“We never use the entirety of the screen for the whole show,” Martinez continued. “It’s to add a little bit of depth to what we have going on scenically on stage.”.

Recent findings suggest that J Cole’s The Fall-Off World Tour has been running since July, with recent indicates at London’s O2 Arena. The tour will end in December in Johannesburg, South Africa.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • During my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal.
  • At the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy.
  • If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal. It was sharp, persistent, and unsettling in a way I couldn’t ignore. As a former labor and delivery nurse, I understood the risks in a way many patients do not. I knew what to watch for. I knew my history. I knew when something felt wrong. Yet when I raised concerns, they were not met with the urgency they deserved.

At the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy. I knew that the vertical incision on my uterus could put a future pregnancy at risk. I spoke up. I asked questions. I paid attention to my body. Still, when I experienced a uterine rupture, I was navigating a system that did not respond with the level of care and urgency that the moment required.

If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?

Conversations during Black Maternal Health Week often center around one urgent truth: Black women are still far more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes in this country than white women. This is not an assumption. It is a proven fact, and it should stop all of us in our tracks. It also does not only impact one socioeconomic group. It affects everyone, including some of the most visible and resourced women in the world.

According to recent reports, as the founder of Mielle, my mission is to empower women, especially Black women, to express their authentic selves. At its core, that mission is about care, agency, and visibility, which is why conversations like this matter. It’s about showing up for every part of Black women’s experience. We need to talk more candidly about what happens to Black women who survive the trauma of miscarriage or stillbirth, and the prolonged mental health challenges that can follow, including postpartum depression.

In a recent development, black women are expected to remain “strong” while navigating medical emergencies. We’re dismissed, told to wait, to calm down, and to trust a system that has not always earned that trust. We survive experiences that change our families and us forever. And then, too often, we are expected to do something just as impossible: keep going as if survival is the end of the story. It is not.

That is why Black Maternal Health Week cannot be about mortality alone. It must also be about what it means to live after trauma, preventable harm, and loss that reshapes your life.

In a recent development, the data make clear that this crisis is ongoing. Black women are about three times more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes than white women, and more than 80% of those deaths are considered preventable. Black infants also die at more than twice the rate of white infants. These are not random gaps. They reflect a healthcare system and a culture that too often normalizes Black women’s pain instead of responding to it.

Research shows that one in five women, or about 20%, report mistreatment during maternity care, but for Black women, that figure climbs to nearly 30%, reflecting more frequent experiences of bias, disrespect, and lack of autonomy in clinical settings. Nearly half of women say they have held back from asking questions or sharing concerns. In one of the most vulnerable moments of a person’s life, too many are already calculating whether speaking up will make things worse.

In my own life, grief did not arrive quietly. It entered my marriage, my motherhood, my body, my faith, and eventually my work. In my book, The Glory In Your Story, I write about how grief does not follow a timeline. It becomes part of who you are, and healing begins not by outrunning it, but by acknowledging it.

According to recent reports, that matters because so many Black women are praised for being strong when what we actually need is space to be human. After losing Milan, I returned to work. I kept moving. I built Mielle. From the outside, it can look like a story of resilience. And in many ways, it is. But we have to be honest about the lessons we take from stories like mine.

According to recent reports, the lesson should not be that Black women are uniquely equipped to carry devastating grief and still perform at a high level. It should not be that our resilience makes systemic failures acceptable. And it should not be that we have to turn survival into something productive just to make our pain legible.

Too often, we celebrate the comeback without sitting long enough with the conditions that made it necessary.

Sources indicate that faith carried me. Purpose helped me rebuild. But none of that changes the reality that more listening, better care, stronger hospital systems, and greater urgency might have changed my story. If we are serious about maternal health, we have to be just as serious about saying that clearly.

Sources indicate that black Maternal Health Week gives us an opportunity to think more broadly about what justice looks like. It looks like hospitals are equipped for emergencies. It looks like providers who listen to Black women the first time, without requiring patients to fight to be believed. It looks like support for families after loss–not just during a crisis. And it looks like making space for grief without expecting Black women to turn it into inspiration before we are ready.

It’s time that we honor not only the women we have lost, but also the women still here carrying what the system could not or would not hold for them. Survival is not the finish line. Being heard, protected, and cared for should be.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a LinkedIn post, Williamson said he was rejoining the Architects Registration Board’s (ARB) register because he no longer wanted “to face the prospect of legal action”.
  • Specifically, he mentioned he feared the potential “legal proceedings and financial penalties” from referring to himself as an architect, which ARB does not permit if a person is unregistered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The president of the Royal Institute of British Architects, Chris Williamson, has decided to renew his membership with the Architects Registration Board, nearly a year after terminating it.

In a LinkedIn post, Williamson said he was rejoining the Architects Registration Board’s (ARB) register because he no longer wanted “to face the prospect of legal action”.

Specifically, he mentioned he feared the potential “legal proceedings and financial penalties” from referring to himself as an architect, which ARB does not permit if a person is unregistered.

Williamson’s post comes nearly a year after he revealed he was not going to renew his membership to draw attention to what he called the “absurdity of the current regulatory framework”.

This ARB framework presently only regulates the protected title “architect” and the competence of those on its register, meaning it does not oversee the competence of unregistered providers of architectural services.

His withdrawal from ARB last year aligned with the launch of a campaign by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) calling for a new regulatory model for UK architects.

Though he has now rejoined the ARB register, Williamson said his position on the need to reform remains unchanged.

“Today, I have decided to rejoin the ARB register,” he posted on LinkedIn on Friday.

It has been revealed that “Over the last year, I have sat in meetings and roundtables with Ministers, MPs and Peers, spoken at party conferences and COP31, and had the pleasure of awarding the Stirling Prize,” he continued. “Throughout, I have felt the fear of legal proceedings and financial penalties all for referring to myself, in these settings, as an architect – something that’s so fundamental to my identity.”.

Williamson, the co-founder of Weston Williamson + Partners, began his two-year term as president on 1 September 2025.

In the LinkedIn post – a shortened version of an open letter shared with RIBA members – he said he will now continue to “push for a stronger system” for regulation.

The current RIBA campaign calls for three steps to reform architects’ regulation, including repealing the Architects Act – a UK law that sets the framework for the regulation of the title architect, under which ARB is the regulator.

According to recent reports, it also proposes new legislation outlining reserved activities, such as submitting full planning applications, and who can execute them. The final step calls for the introduction of a Built Environment Council to oversee the competence of individuals and companies working in the construction industry.

“I know my decision to return may surprise or disappoint some of you, particularly those who followed my lead,” concluded Williamson.

“I want to stress this is not a step backwards and it does not reflect a change in my views. In fact, the year I’ve spent outside of the Register has only cemented my commitment to reform,” he continued.

“While my title may change, RIBA’s campaign for regulatory reform will not. I will use my experience on both sides to push for a stronger system that protects what we call ourselves – and what we do.”.

Williamson was selected as RIBA president in 2024. Prior to this, he held several roles within the RIBA, including the vice president international from 2017 to 2019.

In 2014, ARB gave Dezeen 14 days to amend an article describing John Pawson as an architect, claiming it was “in the public interest” for Dezeen to use an alternative description, as Pawson is not registered with the board.

  • Although revealed by IKEA US as part of its 2027 Style Guide, keen eyes would’ve already seen the shade pop up earlier this year in the sell-out floor lamp created by Dutch designer Lex Pott for IKEA’s PS Collection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of IKEA (unless stated otherwise).

Swedish retailer IKEA has unveiled its prediction for 2027’s Color of the Year – a dark, reddish-purple shade called Wild Fig.

Although revealed by IKEA US as part of its 2027 Style Guide, keen eyes would’ve already seen the shade pop up earlier this year in the sell-out floor lamp created by Dutch designer Lex Pott for IKEA’s PS Collection.

The firm describes Wild Fig as “a deep, botanical shade with a rich purple tone”, although in certain lights, it looks closer to an earthy oxblood red.

“Full of character and the unexpected, it brings depth and a daring mindset to everyday spaces,” said Abbey Stark, home furnishing direction leader at IKEA US.

Used across furnishings and accessories, it can provide a subtle touch of colour without being overly aggressive, especially paired with warm woods and neutral shades, IKEA US suggests.

But the company equally pictures it being splashed across entire walls and argues it “unexpectedly fits in” with even brighter colours like baby pink and electric blue – IKEA US’s previous colours of the year.

The manufacturer’s Style Guide also pulled out a number of other interior design trends to look out for in 2027, including pattern clashing and Japandi minimalism.

Interior designers have already started making liberal use of Wild Fig, as seen in Note Design Studio’s scheme for the Lammhults showroom in Stockholm, where it blankets walls, floors and ceilings in the entrance, as well as an entire kitchen.

Other predictions for 2027’s colour of the year are set to start rolling in any minute, with Pantone’s set to be unveiled at the start of December.

Paint brand Dulux got ahead of the game when it named a muted green called Soulful Sage as its contender in September.

Some interiors industry insiders, including Dezeen columnist Michelle Ogundehin, have argued at least since the end of the pandemic that “it’s time to reconsider the whole colour of the year carnival”, which was originally invented as a marketing stunt for Pantone’s colour-matching system, much like the Michelin Guide was invented to sell more tyres.

Photography courtesy of IKEA (unless stated otherwise).

#102932. Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on.
  • According to recent reports, if you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone.
  • There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on. But these symptoms, as vague as they are, could actually stem from a health condition that’s historically been deemed a “male disease”: obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA.

According to recent reports, if you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone. It wasn’t until the ’90s that researchers first recognized that OSA, which causes you to repeatedly stop breathing while asleep, often presents differently in women than it does in men. For starters women with the condition may not even snore.

There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.

In a recent development, “The disease itself was defined in men,” explains Jennifer Martin, PhD, a behavioral sleep medicine specialist and professor at Florida International University’s Herbert Wertheim College of Medicine in Miami. “The way men and women breathe when they’re asleep is not the same, and our definition of the disease doesn’t account for that.”.

Although obstructive sleep apnea appears to be less common and typically milder in women (at least before menopause), studies suggest that the consequences of the disease, if left untreated, can be similar, if not worse, for us, making it vital to learn the signs and seek help. Here’s what we know about obstructive sleep apnea and its impact on women. Plus, experts explain how to advocate for the best care if you think you may have the condition.

According to recent reports, sleep apnea is one of several conditions that fall under the sleep-disordered breathing umbrella. The most common type is OSA, which happens when your upper airway repeatedly collapses during sleep, making it harder for air to reach your lungs, claims Anita Valanju Shelgikar, MD, a sleep medicine physician with University of Michigan Health and president of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

Industry observers note that the textbook symptoms of this condition—which, for the record, were determined based on studies mostly involving men—include loud snoring and dramatic gasps for air as a person tries to continue breathing while asleep. But this often isn’t the case for women, Dr. Shelgikar tells SELF. Instead, women with OSA are more likely to have nightmares, wake up multiple times a night, have trouble staying asleep, and deal with insomnia, which then causes symptoms like daytime fatigue, morning headaches, and mood swings. Women also have more hypopneas (shallow breaths with less oxygen flow), whereas men tend toward apneas (complete pauses in breathing).

Some experts speculate that it’s possible snoring isn’t commonly reported among women with this disorder because they’re embarrassed to talk about it, given society expects them to sleep like Disney princesses. But a growing body of research suggests that biology may better explain this and other sex-related differences in symptoms. For example, compared with men, women have smaller, more stable airways that are less likely to collapse (and in turn vibrate, making you snore) during sleep. Women also tend to have less fat around their necks, and before menopause they seemingly benefit from the protective effects of estrogen and progesterone, which interact with the respiratory system in a way that aids breathing.

Industry observers note that all things considered, it makes sense why more men than women in the US have this condition, making up about 59% and 41% of obstructive sleep apnea patients, respectively. However, once women go through menopause, which causes their estrogen and progesterone levels to drop, the rate of OSA and the severity of symptoms in this group increases dramatically, Dr. Martin states. Studies have found that anywhere from 47% to 67% of postmenopausal women have obstructive sleep apnea, which is about the same as men in this age range (50 and older). The number of women who actually get diagnosed with the condition is a different story, though—more on that shortly.

Industry observers note that regardless of age, however, women still deal with more sleep apnea–related symptoms than men, Dr. Martin adds, even if they have a less severe form of the condition. This is likely because women have more “subtle breathing disturbances” during sleep that hurt the overall quality of their rest compared with men, Dr. Martin notes.

Because women often don’t experience “classic” OSA symptoms, they end up being misdiagnosed or dismissed. “When [men] walk into a physician’s office and say they’re sleepy and they snore, they get a diagnostic test right away,” Dr. Martin states. “When a woman walks in and says, ‘I don’t sleep well, and I’m very fatigued during the day,’ they don’t often get referred” for screening. In fact, research suggests that men are nine times more likely to be referred for diagnostic testing than women.

Women with OSA commonly have their symptoms misattributed to conditions like depression, anxiety, insomnia, and menopause or even medication side effects, notes Dr. Shelgikar, who is also a neurology professor at the University of Michigan Medical School. Not to mention women can have these other conditions as well, which might make their sleep apnea not only harder to detect but also worsen it. Take the double whammy that is insomnia and OSA: Having both of these disorders at the same time is more common among women than men, Dr. Martin says, and in some cases they may be given a sleep aid (such as diphenhydramine or a benzodiazepine) that can further relax their throat muscles, exacerbating their sleep apnea and leaving them even more oxygen-deprived.

According to recent reports, and it doesn’t help that, as we talked about earlier, the diagnostic criteria for OSA are largely based on how the condition presents in men. “When we diagnose sleep apnea, we require one of two things to happen: A breathing interruption has to be associated either with a drop in oxygen levels or a brief awakening from sleep,” Dr. Martin indicates. “Women don’t have those very deep drops in oxygen levels that men do. So that means that the way we define the disease itself kind of biases us towards diagnosing it more in men than women.” What’s more, Medicare, which the vast majority of Americans ages 65 and older rely on for health insurance, only recognizes a sleep apnea diagnosis if a person has those steep drops in oxygen, Dr. Martin says. Those typical mid-slumber wake-ups don’t count on their own. So even “the criteria that Medicare forces people to use to define sleep apnea is very male-centric,” she adds.

Industry observers note that home sleep apnea tests, which are becoming increasingly common as a cheaper alternative to the gold standard in-lab exams, are also more prone to miss the condition in women. Because women tend to have fewer and milder events than men, these at-home tests may not be able to diagnose sleep apnea as accurately in this population, Dr. Martin notes. They can be even more inaccurate in women with insomnia. These individuals “may not get enough sleep to get an accurate diagnosis,” she says, “so if they wear [the monitor] for six hours, but they’re only sleeping for four of them, it may look like they have less sleep apnea than they really do.”.

That’s all to say that sleep apnea is likely much more common among women than the available data suggests, experts tell SELF. And that reality reveals a sobering point: A lot of women with this condition probably aren’t receiving the care they need, a delay that can, for some people, snowball into an avalanche of additional yet preventable health challenges.

Industry observers note that if left untreated, sleep apnea can have downstream effects on your health, particularly your heart, says Atul Malhotra, MD, research chief of pulmonary, critical care, and sleep medicine at UC San Diego Health. Every time you stop breathing, your body responds to the lack of oxygen by releasing the stress hormone adrenaline to jolt you awake so you take a breath. This happens really rapidly; you are typically up for just a few seconds and probably won’t even remember it the next morning.

Over time this constant stress strains your cardiovascular system, Dr. Malhotra states, which may increase your risk for high blood pressure, heart attack, stroke, irregular heartbeat, and heart failure. Although the evidence is mixed, some research suggests that it’s more common for women with severe sleep apnea to experience cardiovascular complications than it is for men. Studies also show that women tend to have more health conditions upon diagnosis than men do, including thyroid disease, asthma, and depression. This raises the classic “chicken or the egg” question, but either way treating OSA can only help.

In a recent development, because obstructive sleep apnea leads to low-quality shut-eye, it is also associated with memory and cognition complications and poor daytime alertness, which can boost the likelihood of car and workplace accidents (for certain high-risk jobs like those in the transportation and construction industries), Dr. Shelgikar claims. Perhaps less discussed is how untreated sleep apnea affects our ability to care for ourselves and maintain relationships. “We don’t do a good job thinking about sleep apnea as a potential cause of mental health symptoms,” Dr. Martin says. In fact, research shows that managing OSA could actually help some people dealing with anxiety and depression improve their symptoms.

Industry observers note that as researchers continue searching for answers, Dr. Martin points to a silver lining: There’s good evidence to suggest that women “benefit at least as much as men, if not more” from sleep apnea treatment, which is why it’s important to know what to look out for.

Although you’re quite literally working against decades of medical bias, it’s still possible to receive a sleep apnea diagnosis if you’re equipped with the right intel.

Industry News: Meet AMAA, Neri&Hu’s pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1403 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated.
  • An innovative approach to the reuse of existing buildings defines the output of Italian architecture office AMAA, which Neri&Hu has selected as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design as part of Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.
  • Led by Marcello Galiotto and Alessandra Rampazzo, over the past 14 years AMAA has become known for its approach to the reuse of post-industrial structures in northern Italy, with the transformation of a former factory building into its own studio, a typical example of its approach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated.

An innovative approach to the reuse of existing buildings defines the output of Italian architecture office AMAA, which Neri&Hu has selected as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design as part of Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.

Led by Marcello Galiotto and Alessandra Rampazzo, over the past 14 years AMAA has become known for its approach to the reuse of post-industrial structures in northern Italy, with the transformation of a former factory building into its own studio, a typical example of its approach.

According to Galiotto, these buildings are a taste of what the studio wants to achieve.

“What we have done in the past 10 years is really just a sketch of what we can do in the future,” he told Dezeen.

“Our research is still growing, and it can be applied to various programmes and contexts,” he continued, “but in 20 years we will both be 60 so we want the studio to be able to evolve and grow in upcoming directions.”.

The preservation and adaptation of existing buildings, which is central to AMAA’s practice, is a key reason why architects Lyndon Neri and Rossana Hu selected the studio for Dezeen’s 20×20 series.

“AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse,” remarked the duo, adding that the studio’s ability to repurpose historic structures “positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture”.

AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse, [which] positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture.

Galiotto and Rampazzo met Neri and Hu when they participated in the 2023 Venice Biennale and have since been invited to host lectures at the University of Pennsylvania, where Hu is chair of the architecture department.

“We have a long relationship with Lyndon and Rossana who we consider to be both amazing people and great architects so it’s truly an honour to be selected by them,” remarked Galiotto.

Rampazzo added that she saw a clear overlap between Shanghai-based Neri&Hu’s work, which also has a focus on adaptive reuse approach, and their approach at AMAA.

“I’m a fan of their work and I see similarities in the way we do architecture and also the way we teach, despite our different cultural backgrounds,” she remarked. “I also love how they really support students and young architects by sharing their knowledge. We have a lot to learn from them but I hope we can have the same kind of legacy.”.

Rampazzo and Galiotto have known each other for more than 20 years after meeting while studying architecture at the Iuav University of Venice.

The studio now has offices in Venice and in the industrial town of Arzignano, and has gradually become established among Italy’s most respected architecture firms thanks to projects such as their own office and a cafe housed within a 19th-century town hall.

We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice, so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio.

The pair studied together at Iuav under the professorship of Massimo Carmassi, who they cite as an crucial influence on their approach to restoration and reuse.

After graduating in 2010, they assisted Carmassi and briefly set up a studio with friends to work on competitions. Then Galiotto went to Japan to work for Sou Fujimoto, while Rampazzo travelled to India for her PhD studies.

“We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice,” mentioned Galiotto, “so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio.”.

This global travel and work experience helped open their minds to alternative approaches and opportunities, as well as giving them the confidence to set up their own studio back in Venice.

“We’re still evolving, and evolving our identity,” said Galiotto. “But the important thing was to find ourselves. That’s why the path was complicated.

It has been revealed that “Stay in Italy… going outside of Italy… travelling the world as much as we can to see things. That was the key, I think, to the position that we are covering right now in the panorama of architecture in Italy.”.

In 2015, they opened a branch office in Galiotto’s hometown of Arzignano, which has been described as an “AMAA playground” due to the number of projects the practice has completed there.

Galiotto pointed out that their work in the town is part of an ongoing research into how architecture can blur the line between private and public spaces, with the Caffe Nazionale project providing a good example.

“Although the cafe is privately owned, it also forms the edge of a plaza so we wanted to give the space back to the people,” the architect explained, adding that the studio has coined the term “super public” to describe this aspect of their practice.

Alongside their work in Arzignano and Venice, AMAA now has commissions across Italy, including hospitality and residential projects, as well as schools and a theatre. Along with a focus on reuse, especially industrial buildings, Galiotto believes that the studio’s work is united by its considered eclecticism.

“We’re influenced by art, artists, travels and whatever we can be – by curiosity,” he mentioned. “I would say it’s something that’s very vital and it gives us this kind of eclecticism. Our architecture in this moment is very eclectic and at the same time has a strong direction.”.

“It’s like a piano symphony, very complicated and very up and down, but at the same time very right like a poem, very well taught and very well executed, but very complicated in terms of ingredients.”.

The studio’s expanding list of projects has caused it to swell in size to approximately 30 members of staff, which Galiotto suggested is necessary to facilitate their detailed, research-led approach.

We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects.

Looking ahead, the architects mentioned their main objective is to continue developing their team and consolidating their approach so that others can carry it on in the coming decades.

One concern they have is maintaining the same quality of output as demand for their services grows and they take on an increasing number of projects.

In just the past year they have completed 10 projects – as many as they delivered during the first decade of their practice – with public commissions now joining their work for private clients.

Despite the rapid growth, Galiotto and Rampazzo insisted their approach remains consistent whatever scale of project they are working on, whether it’s a chair, a public plaza or a museum, which they both agree would be a dream next project.

Asked for her view on the future of architecture over the coming decades, Rampazzo noted there is a trend in Italy towards involving other creatives in the design process, which represents an alternative to the more autocratic approach of the past.

“Sharing ideas and opinions leads to more interesting outcomes,” she claimed. “We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects.”.

In their teaching roles at institutions including Kent State University and Universidade do Minho in Portugal, Galiotto and Rampazzo are responsible for helping to shape the attitudes of the next generation of architects, who they recognise are entering the workplace in challenging times.

Galiotto remarked if there is one thing he tries to pass on to his students and the staff in his studio it is to “have passion and to keep pushing for what you believe in.”.

“If you are humble, passionate and curious then you can find success,” he added. “Sometimes it can be tough, but when you love what you do you can live your life feeling like you never worked for a single day.”.

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Kilian O’Sullivan.

A collection of brick-clad buildings containing over 450 homes forms Kidbrooke Park Road in London, which architecture studio HTA Design claims is the largest new-build council housing development in the UK.

Built on a formerly disused site in Greenwich, the development contains 452 homes, all of which are social housing.

Construction manufacturer Durkan delivered Kidbrooke Park Road for the Royal Borough of Greenwich as part of its council housing programme, Greenwich Builds.

HTA Design said the project “demonstrates what can be achieved when local authorities take an ambitious approach to housing delivery”.

“Our main goal was to demonstrate that council housing delivered at scale does not have to come at the expense of good design,” HTA Design managing partner Simon Bayliss told Dezeen.

“We wanted to create a neighbourhood where the homes are generous and adaptable, where landscape is integral rather than an afterthought, and where streets and public spaces feel active, welcoming and safe,” he continued.

“Together, the two phases have delivered the UK’s largest council housing development and one of the most significant social housing projects completed in recent years. We hope it serves as a benchmark for how future generations of affordable housing can be delivered across London and the UK.”.

HTA Design recently completed the second phase of the scheme, which adds eight housing blocks with 330 homes to the three blocks completed in phase one.

Ranging from six to 15 storeys, the housing comprises one-, two-, and three-bedroom apartments and family maisonettes, most of which are dual-aspect.

The buildings at Kidbrooke Park Road have a reinforced concrete frame, clad in brick chosen to reference red-brick buildings in the local area.

Arched entrances, patterned brickwork and exposed concrete elements were designed to add visual interest among the development’s green spaces, which include tree-lined streets, community gardens, wildflower meadows, play areas and gardens designed for rainwater runoff.

“A key challenge was ensuring that two phases delivered separately would ultimately come together as one place,” mentioned Bayliss.

“Through simple buildings and typologies with repetitive architectural components, combined with a landscape strategy that runs throughout the development, we set out to create a neighbourhood with a clear identity that worked within its context.”.

It has been revealed that elsewhere in the development are a nursery, community facilities and green roofs. The housing is complete with air-source heat pumps, electric boilers and rooftop photovoltaics.

“We hope residents feel proud to live here,” Bayliss concluded.

“Beyond the homes themselves, the project has been designed to support everyday life, with play spaces, shared green areas, a nursery, community facilities and local amenities all contributing to a strong sense of community,” he mentioned.

“Those are often the things that transform a housing development into a genuine neighbourhood.”.

The deputy mayor of London for Housing and Residential Development Tom Copley said the project represents how London is “leading the way nationally on council home building”.

“The new development at Kidbrooke Park Road is the perfect example of what we’re achieving, with 452 council homes forming the largest single entirely new-build council housing development in the country,” he said.

“We recently announced that 60 per cent of the funding from the first round of the mayor’s new Social and Affordable Homes Programme will go to London boroughs, and we look forward to that decision delivering even more new council homes in future.”.

Last month, the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) announced the brick-clad Lion Green Road housing by Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, which contains a mix of private and socially rented homes, as the winner of this year’s Stirling Prize.

RIBA also awarded its Neave Brown Award for Housing to Rowan Court, a cluster of brick-clad social housing blocks in Seven Sisters designed by Satish Jassal Architects.
