7 Tips for Building a Healthy Diet With Canned, Frozen, and Packaged Goods

📅 17 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1496 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Certain influencers have built entire social media empires out of making everything from scratch.
  • Industry observers note that but this suggestion is hardly fair.
  • In a recent development, besides the lower price point, canned, frozen, and packaged foods have one other major advantage: their staying power.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Certain influencers have built entire social media empires out of making everything from scratch. Oftentimes, their videos carry an implicit sense of moral superiority, suggesting that you’re not a good parent (or at least not as good as them) if you’re resorting to pre-packaged store-bought items. Those who pick their own produce and painstakingly hand-craft their own candy necklaces simply work harder, love their children more, are fundamentally better.

Industry observers note that but this suggestion is hardly fair. For the vast majority of people—meaning those who don’t make their living off of wellness content or have near-endless amounts of time and money to burn—canned, frozen, and packaged stuff is almost always a far more practical option. “Groceries are a fortune,” after all, Anthea Levi, MS, RD, a Brooklyn-based health writer and the founder of Alive+Well Nutrition, tells SELF—and fresh items tend to be the most expensive, as a trip to the produce section of the supermarket will readily prove.

In a recent development, besides the lower price point, canned, frozen, and packaged foods have one other major advantage: their staying power. “You can keep them in your freezer for months, so that often gives people confidence” in the purchase, since they know they don’t have an expiration date hanging over their head, Desiree Nielsen, RD, a recipe developer with a focus on plant-based nutrition, tells SELF. This, in turn, leads to reduced food waste: “Fresh salad greens are notorious for going slimy in the fridge, but you’ll never have that glitch with frozen spinach. Ditto for fish. Fresh fish needs to be cooked ASAP before it turns, while frozen fish and canned or tinned fish last until you’re ready to use them,” Levi says.

Sources indicate that nielsen also takes problem with the basic idea that these options are somehow inherently inferior—“a substantial, big misconception,” in her eyes. “There has been a lot of confusion about the nature of these foods in general. Just because something is processed or packaged does not mean it’s unhealthy,” she notes.

In a recent development, in other words, canned, frozen, or packaged items are often perfectly fine to include in your diet—and you shouldn’t feel embarrassed, ashamed, or inadequate if they make frequent appearances in your meals (or if they’re your first resort over fresh). “Constant access to fresh foods is, unfortunately, a luxury. If canned, frozen, or packaged items are the only way you’re able to put a fruit or vegetable on your plate, go for it,” Levi indicates. But if you’re still concerned about the health aspect, there are a few key ways to maximize the nutritional value and improve the overall experience. Here’s what to know to make the most of your freezer stash.

“Typically, the fewer ingredients, the better,” Levi claims—a rule of thumb to consider while shopping. While canned, frozen, and packaged items have a reputation for being ultra-processed—rife with additives and lower in nutritional value—there are actually plenty out there “that are made from just one or two whole-food ingredients, such as canned peas, frozen fruit, and canned salmon,” Levi says. “These are as close to fresh foods as you can get, and just as nutritious.” Many jarred peanut butters only contain dry roasted peanuts and salt, for example. (By contrast, Ritz peanut butter crackers, which have an ingredients list several rows long, are a very different story.).

Recent findings suggest that that mentioned, this problem can be nuanced. “Just because an ingredient looks fancy or technical or like a chemical does not necessarily mean that it's bad for you,” Nielsen points out. Many processed foods—including bread, milk, and breakfast cereal—are fortified with healthy vitamins and minerals that you might not otherwise consume enough of in your diet. Take vitamin C—which may appear under the name “ascorbic acid”—as an example. “You might not recognize that what you’re looking at is vitamin C, so you don't want to scare yourself off of potentially nutritious and valuable food because you see things on the ingredients label that you don't recognize,” Nielsen states.

Industry observers note that in Nielsen’s experience, canned foods are often considered even less “healthy” than frozen, but the stigma isn’t necessarily warranted. Canned beans, which boast fiber, plant-based protein, and minerals like iron and zinc, are an excellent example of a canned food that amounts to an “incredible nutrition source,” she notes. Still, this category does have one major drawback: Staples like veggies, soups, and, yes, beans can contain a significant amount of sodium, a mineral that can cause high blood pressure and related complications like heart disease and stroke when overconsumed. Tinned fish like TikTok’s beloved sardines can suffer from the same concern, as the brine inside the tin can be heavy on added salt as well.

Given that many brands offer sodium-sensitive alternatives, try to prioritize those options instead to keep your sodium intake in check and avoid potential health consequences, according to Nielsen. Look for labels like “No salt added,” “Low sodium,” or even “No sodium” to steer you in the right direction. If you can’t find anything fitting that bill at your local store, draining and rinsing canned products before use can also drastically cut down on the sodium content—by up to 40%, according to some estimates. (Just keep in mind this method may also cause losses in other nutrients, like vitamin C.).

“In terms of packaged and processed foods, I'm always looking for a couple of nutrients to minimize and a couple of nutrients to optimize,” Nielsen says. Sodium is one to limit or avoid, as we’ve already covered, but there are others too—like added sugars and saturated fat. “Peaches that come canned in sugary syrup aren’t as nutritious as peaches that come canned in water, or are purchased frozen or fresh,” for example, Levi says.

Industry observers note that on the other hand, when you’re reading over a nutrition facts label, “what you want to see is fiber,” Nielsen notes—and “protein is a significant bonus.” Multiple vitamins and minerals in a product is also often a positive sign. Even breakfast cereals, which are often thought of as unhealthy, “can be incredible sources of minerals like iron and zinc—things that we need that help to keep our metabolism running, that keep us energized,” Nielsen says.

Sources indicate that trying to decide between two (or more) similar products? Comparing and contrasting the ingredients can help you narrow it down, according to Nielsen. Take breakfast cereal: You’ll want to ask yourself, “‘Which one of these cereals gives me the most fiber, the most protein, has the least sugar?’” she notes. In this case, the relative content of vitamins and minerals can also be a helpful clue. Seeing that a cereal contains 10% to 20% of your recommended dietary allowance, as many do, can be “your sort of gut check that this is actually a really nutritious food,” Nielsen says.

Even though frozen veggies are affordable and durable, they do have one big downside compared to fresh: Their taste and texture can take a hit—and, in turn, “you do have to adjust your cooking somewhat,” Nielsen says. To prevent sogginess, cook frozen veggies from frozen rather than letting them defrost first, according to Levi. And you’ll want to use heat-based cooking methods (like air-frying, baking, roasting, and stir-frying) “as opposed to water-based methods like boiling or steaming,” she says.

In a recent development, “Many of us are working more than ever before—maybe working two or three jobs—and we don't have a lot of time to put a home-cooked meal on the table,” Nielsen claims. Strategically pairing your canned, frozen, and packaged items is an easy way to boost efficiency in the kitchen without sacrificing nutritional value. If you’re having canned soup for dinner, you can dump in a can of lentils to boost the fiber and protein, for example. (Bonus tip: You can also use this approach to stretch out your leftovers. Need a batch of spaghetti to last longer? Toss some frozen peas on top or some frozen broccoli on the side.).

In a recent development, “Stocking your freezer and pantry with budget-friendly canned, frozen, and packaged items can help make balanced meals a breeze,” Levi claims. Follow the tried-and-true “plate method” to guarantee a nutritious result, according to Nielsen: Reserve a quarter of your plate for whole grains or starchy vegetables, another quarter for protein, and the remaining half for fruits and non-starchy veggies. You could make rolled oats with chia seeds, frozen berries, and peanut butter for breakfast, or pasta with tinned sardines and frozen broccoli for dinner, for example, Levi says. “It sounds way too simple, but it is backed by so much science to help you balance your diet without counting anything,” Nielsen says. “As long as you stick to that plate method, you will be eating a nourishing diet”—yes, even if your ingredients don’t come to you direct.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Simply called Doha Pavilion, the psychedelic structure was conceived a work of both art and architecture for MIA Park – a public space outside the Museum of Islamic Art by IM Pei.
  • It serves as a permanent pavilion for the site and as a gallery for Richter’s own work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Iwan Baan.

Kaleidoscopic patterns adorn the exterior of this pavilion in Doha, Qatar, designed by artist Gerhard Richter with US studio Selldorf Architects as an art gallery.

Simply called Doha Pavilion, the psychedelic structure was conceived a work of both art and architecture for MIA Park – a public space outside the Museum of Islamic Art by IM Pei.

It serves as a permanent pavilion for the site and as a gallery for Richter’s own work.

Richter designed the Doha Pavilion with Selldorf Architects as a reference to his Strip paintings – a series that involved digitally dividing his Abstract Painting artwork into vertical stripes, building on his earlier explorations of colour, pattern and repetition.

“My trip to Doha in 2013 came two years into developing my Strip paintings, and the city’s architecture and history sparked an idea for a pavilion that could unite the thematic threads of that body of work,” said Richter.

“The pavilion’s exterior features decorative tiles based on the patterns that first led me to the Strips,” he continued. “Doha is the right place and the only place for my pavilion.”.

Doha Pavilion has a six-sided form, wrapped in psychedelic tiles displaying repeating, kaleidoscopic patterns that recall geometries seen in Islamic art, nodding to the project’s context.

Selldorf Architects founder Annabelle Selldorf noted the design reflects a “profound culmination of many years of [Richter’s] research into abstraction”.

“I am grateful for the welcome that Gerhard Richter extended to me, and for the wonderful dialogue that ensued, as my studio made manifest the work that had existed in his mind,” she stated.

“This pavilion is the profound culmination of many years of his research into abstraction, with intensely physical patterns that invite you to immerse yourself in their endlessness,” she continued.

“The more I look at them, the more fascinating they become to me as an architectural space to experience.”.

In a recent development, inside, Richter’s paintings and sculptures are displayed throughout the hexagonal gallery space. This includes both archival and newly introduced works made especially for the pavilion.

Among the new works is the Strip Tower – a freestanding tripartite sculpture.

The opening of Doha Pavilion coincides with the inaugural edition of Rubaiya Qatar 2026, which is an international visual arts quadrennial.

Elsewhere, Selldorf Architects recently completed the controversial remodel of the National Gallery’s Sainsbury Wing. In an interview with Dezeen after the opening, founder Selldorf stated that “what matters is I know why we did things”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) concluded on November 22, 2026, in Antalya, Türkiye, following negotiations that extended beyond the scheduled closing date. Hosted by Türkiye with Australia leading the negotiations, the summit brought together representatives of nearly 200 Parties, alongside researchers, businesses, climate organizations, and civil society, to advance international climate action. While countries reached decisions on climate finance, adaptation, just transition, and other agenda items, they failed to agree on the proposed overarching Antalya Pact, with disagreements over fossil fuels, finance, and the level of ambition in the final text. For the built environment, COP31 advanced several initiatives addressing building energy performance, electrification, urban resilience, and climate investment, while leaving broader questions of implementation and international coordination unresolved.

In a recent development, the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) concluded on November 22, 2026, in Antalya, Türkiye, following negotiations that extended beyond the scheduled closing date. Hosted by Türkiye with Australia leading the negotiations, the summit brought together representatives of nearly 200 Parties, alongside researchers, businesses, climate organizations, and civil society, to advance international climate action. While countries reached decisions on climate finance, adaptation, just transition, and other agenda items, they failed to agree on the proposed overarching Antalya Pact, with disagreements over fossil fuels, finance, and the level of ambition in the final text. For the built environment, COP31 advanced several initiatives addressing building energy performance, electrification, urban resilience, and climate investment, while leaving broader questions of implementation and international coordination unresolved.

Buildings and construction remain central to climate action, accounting for a significant share of global energy consumption and emissions while also being exposed to rising temperatures, flooding, and other climate-related risks. At COP31, the Turkish Presidency introduced the Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings, a voluntary framework targeting a 25% reduction in the operational energy intensity of the global building stock by 2035, compared with 2020 levels. Discussions on urban resilience also addressed the relationship between national climate commitments and investment at the local level, particularly in housing, infrastructure, and adaptation. While these initiatives provide frameworks for further action, their implementation will depend on national policies, financing, and coordination across public and private sectors.

Below are four developments from COP31 relevant to architecture, cities, and the built environment.

Related Article COP31 to Take Place in Antalya, Turkiye, as SP Architects Adapts Former Expo Grounds.

The Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings.

One of COP31's most direct initiatives for the building sector was the Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings, launched by the Turkish Presidency on October 29 in collaboration with the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP)-hosted Global Alliance for Buildings and Construction (GlobalABC). The voluntary framework supports two of the Presidency's 2035 objectives: pursuing a 25% reduction in the operational energy intensity of the global building stock compared with 2020 levels, and accelerating efficient electrification in buildings in support of the 35-by-35 target, which seeks to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035. At the second ministerial meeting of the Intergovernmental Council for Buildings and Climate (ICBC), held during COP31, 24 countries, the European Commission, and 38 non-Party stakeholders expressed support for or endorsed the Compact.

One of COP31's most direct initiatives for the building sector was the Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings, launched by the Turkish Presidency on October 29 in collaboration with the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP)-hosted Global Alliance for Buildings and Construction (GlobalABC). The voluntary framework supports two of the Presidency's 2035 objectives: pursuing a 25% reduction in the operational energy intensity of the global building stock compared with 2020 levels, and accelerating efficient electrification in buildings in support of the 35-by-35 target, which seeks to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035. At the second ministerial meeting of the Intergovernmental Council for Buildings and Climate (ICBC), held during COP31, 24 countries, the European Commission, and 38 non-Party stakeholders expressed support for or endorsed the Compact.

The framework identifies six areas for action, including integrating energy efficiency and electrification into national strategies, strengthening building energy and carbon performance, accelerating renovation of existing buildings, reducing energy demand, improving buildings' flexibility within energy systems, and mobilizing finance and technical capacity. Its proposed measures range from stronger building energy codes and renovation strategies to electrified heating and cooling, energy management, passive cooling, and investment in public buildings and social infrastructure. While the Compact does not establish binding targets for individual countries, it provides a shared framework for governments and industry to advance building decarbonization, linking operational energy performance with renovation, affordability, and long-term resilience.

Climate-Resilient Cities: Housing, Infrastructure, and Local Implementation.

Cities and urban resilience were also prominent at COP31, with the Turkish Presidency and UN-Habitat convening a High-Level Dialogue on Urban Resilience, Adaptation and Climate Action on November 12. The discussions addressed how national climate aims and adaptation strategies can be translated into investments at the local level, with housing, infrastructure, urban regeneration, informal settlement upgrading, and post-disaster reconstruction identified as areas requiring stronger implementation. Participants emphasized the importance of connecting national climate commitments with local development priorities while strengthening coordination between governments, municipalities, financial institutions, and development partners. The dialogue also highlighted the financing gap facing cities, with climate-resilient infrastructure and services requiring investment beyond current levels.

Participants emphasized the importance of connecting national climate commitments with local development priorities while strengthening coordination between governments, municipalities, financial institutions, and development partners. The dialogue also highlighted the financing gap facing cities, with climate-resilient infrastructure and services requiring investment beyond current levels.

Recent findings suggest that the discussions positioned housing and basic urban services as part of climate adaptation, highlighting the need for homes that can withstand floods and extreme heat, infrastructure that can continue functioning during climate-related disasters, and urban development strategies that address the needs of vulnerable communities. Rather than treating resilience as a separate technical objective, the discussions linked it to housing conditions, public services, reconstruction processes, and the capacity of cities to respond to climate risks. The emphasis on implementation also highlighted the challenges of moving from planning to investment, particularly for municipalities that lack the financial or technical capacity to develop large-scale climate projects.

Financing Urban Resilience Through the Sustainable Urban Resilience Financing Facility.

It has been revealed that alongside discussions on climate adaptation, COP31 highlighted the Sustainable Urban Resilience Financing Facility (SURFF), an initiative developed through Türkiye's İLBANK in partnership with UN-Habitat and the World Bank. Launched ahead of the summit during Fresh York Climate Week, the initiative aims to help cities and countries translate climate commitments into investment-ready urban resilience projects, addressing the gap between national climate strategies and implementation at the municipal level. It is structured around three pillars: country-led Resilient Cities Platforms, a Resilient Cities Centre of Excellence, and an international dialogue intended to facilitate cooperation, share experience, and improve access to climate finance.

Rolled out ahead of the summit during New York Climate Week, the initiative aims to help cities and countries translate climate commitments into investment-ready urban resilience projects, addressing the gap between national climate strategies and implementation at the municipal level. Industry observers note that SURFF was presented as an approach to strengthening project preparation, local institutional capacity, and access to public and private financing for urban climate investments. Its priorities include resilient infrastructure, climate adaptation, and projects that respond to the needs of cities and their communities. Rather than operating as a newly introduced financing fund, the facility aims to connect cities with existing financing mechanisms, technical assistance, and implementation partners. Its effectiveness will therefore depend on the development of investment pipelines, the availability of finance, and the ability to translate its framework into financed and completed urban interventions.

Fossil Fuels and Electrification: An Unresolved Transition.

It has been revealed that the transition away from fossil fuels remained one of the most contested concerns at COP31. Countries were divided over whether the final political text should include an explicit commitment to move away from coal, oil, and gas. The proposed Antalya Pact did not include a clear reference to fossil fuels, prompting objections from the European Union, the United Kingdom, and several climate-vulnerable nations, which argued that the text did not adequately address the primary drivers of climate change. Disagreements over the language of the energy transition, climate finance, and the level of ambition required prevented the draft from reaching consensus. The outcome leaves the commitment made at COP28 to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems without a new collective roadmap at COP31.

Outside the formal negotiations, efforts to advance electrification continued through voluntary initiatives. Around 80 countries supported the Presidency's 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge, which seeks to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035. For the built environment, electrification connects the transition to buildings through heating, cooling, cooking, and energy systems, while energy efficiency and passive design strategies can reduce demand. The Antalya Compact similarly addresses building energy use through renovation, efficient systems, and measures to reduce operational demand. However, electrification targets and building efficiency initiatives do not replace a negotiated global commitment to phase out fossil fuels, leaving the pace of transition dependent on national policies, energy infrastructure, investment, and further international cooperation.

Latest Update: 6 Signs Your Skin Needs Medical Attention, Stat

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your skin is your most visible organ, so it’s easy to notice when something seems off.
  • Many of these skin challenges get better with the right at-home remedies or changes in your skin care routine.
  • But if skin symptoms don’t go away with a little self-care — or they return frequently — a chronic skin condition might be the culprit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your skin is your most visible organ, so it’s easy to notice when something seems off. It’s normal to experience some skin issues from time to time, like itchiness, breakouts, or ingrown hairs. But when these skin symptoms stick around, it could be a sign that something more serious is going on.

Many of these skin challenges get better with the right at-home remedies or changes in your skin care routine. For example, if dryness pops up when Old Man Winter comes along, slathering on a more intense moisturizer may help.

But if skin symptoms don’t go away with a little self-care — or they return frequently — a chronic skin condition might be the culprit. However, just because you have a lasting symptom or two doesn’t necessarily mean you have a chronic health glitch.

According to recent reports, here are the symptoms you should watch for and what they might mean. And if they don’t improve, consider checking in with a dermatologist for a proper diagnosis and a plan of action.

It has been revealed that if you wish you had cat claws to satisfy your skin itch, you could be dealing with eczema. Eczema is an umbrella term for several conditions that impact the skin, with atopic dermatitis being the most common.

With most forms of eczema, your skin may show signs of inflammation, such as:.

These symptoms may flare up occasionally and then go into periods of remission, where your skin isn’t as irritated.

Allergies can also lead to itchiness. For example, if you’re allergic to a skin care ingredient, a fabric type, a pet, or another allergen, your skin might react as a way to tell you to avoid this trigger.

Ongoing or regular periods of itchiness are a reason to see a dermatologist.

A rash can affect the skin in various ways, including:.

A one-off or temporary rash might result from friction or chafing from a new outfit item. It could also be a heat rash when sweat gets trapped in skinfolds or bodily creases.

According to recent reports, A persistent rash could be a sign of eczema or allergies. However, different types of rashes can be a sign of other things. For example, a butterfly-shaped (malar) rash across the face is a common sign of an autoimmune disease known as lupus.

If you frequently experience skin rashes, talk with a dermatologist to help you get to the bottom of the issue.

Sources indicate that dry skin can be just that — dry skin. Common causes include:.

But if your skin is so dry it makes you want to bathe in a vat of thick moisturizer, it could be a sign of psoriasis.

In a recent development, psoriasis is an inflammatory skin condition potentially caused by an overactive immune system. It can lead to dry, cracked, or scaling skin. In fact, psoriasis often involves a buildup of scales or plaques on areas like the elbows or knees — though they can occur anywhere.

It has been revealed that psoriasis and eczema are different conditions, but they have overlapping symptoms that mimic each other. So if you experience these symptoms, it’s key to see a dermatologist to identify and treat the underlying cause.

Recent findings suggest that changes in skin color — including red, brown, gray, or purple patches of skin — can be a sign of various skin complications, including eczema, psoriasis, or allergies. But it can also be a sign of rosacea.

Rosacea typically involves persistent redness that looks like a sunburn or blushing. It may also lead to skin thickening.

It has been revealed that the good news? Rosacea is highly treatable. So working with a dermatologist can help you address it.

Recent findings suggest that no one is immune from developing the occasional pimple or ingrown hair. But sometimes, skin bumps can be a sign that something else is going on.

Acne is one of the most common skin conditions that could bring skin bumps like pimples.

Recent findings suggest that hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is another condition that causes painful, boil-like lumps to form underneath the skin. These bumps can turn into pus-filled pockets that may connect via tunnels. HS typically reveals up in areas of high friction or where skin meets skin, such as the armpits or groin.

Other types of skin bumps may include ingrown hairs, which can get infected and turn into folliculitis.

Talk with a dermatologist to help you address any bothersome skin bumps you may experience.

According to recent reports, common moles are growths that develop when pigment cells (melanocytes) grow in clusters. The average adult has between 10 to 40 common moles.

An irregular mole, also known as a dysplastic nevus, is a type of mole that looks different from your common moles. If you have a dysplastic nevus (or several), schedule regular skin checks with a dermatologist to look for anything suspicious. Be sure to mention any changes in:.

These types of changes could be a sign of a form of skin cancer such as melanoma, which occurs in melanocytes. Melanoma can develop anywhere, including on normal-looking skin, a common mole, or a dysplastic nevus.

In a recent development, skin symptoms — like rashes, bumps, discoloration, dryness, or itchiness — may come and go. But if symptoms stick around or return frequently, consider seeing a dermatologist for an evaluation. Your skin may be telling you that there’s an underlying issue that needs to be addressed.

Sources indicate that A dermatologist can provide a proper diagnosis and treatment proposal to help reduce, or, in some cases, resolve your skin symptoms. If you don’t currently have a dermatologist, your primary care physician or nurse practitioner can refer you to one.

Latest Update: Dezeen reports from Latest York's new November design week

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A collection of showcases, old and newly introduced, took place in New York this November, effectively adding a second design week to a city already loaded with events.
  • The as-yet-unofficial design week in the first weeks of November came into focus earlier this year, when trade fair ICFF, anchor fair of NYCxDesign, announced that in 2027 it will take place simultaneously with sister fair BDNY, which has been held in November for years.
  • The move has prompted questions in the city about the future of the NYCxDesign festival in May and what a November design week would look like.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A collection of showcases, old and newly introduced, took place in New York this November, effectively adding a second design week to a city already loaded with events. Dezeen’s US editor Ben Dreith explores the offerings.

The as-yet-unofficial design week in the first weeks of November came into focus earlier this year, when trade fair ICFF, anchor fair of NYCxDesign, announced that in 2027 it will take place simultaneously with sister fair BDNY, which has been held in November for years.

The move has prompted questions in the city about the future of the NYCxDesign festival in May and what a November design week would look like.

While BDNY and high-end showcase Salon Art + Design have always been held in November, other design fairs have sprouted to take advantage of the opportunity to show during this busy period.

The week is positioning itself, without any explicit organisation, as a massive event in the New York design calendar.

Even NYCxDesign, still scheduled for May as usual in 2027, held a November event bringing in designers Ross Lovegrove, Karim Rashid and Rem D Koolhaas for a talk moderated by Upcoming York-based design writer Camille Okhio.

The panellists spoke about the potential for AI and derided the inclusion of craft in conversations about design. However, as writer Debika Ray noted in an opinion piece for Dezeen, crafted, one-off pieces have lately come to dominate design shows.

NYCxDesign staking out a talk with well-known industrial designers suggests that its May event could be devoted to industrial design, while November complements it with a focus on collectible furniture.

This was definitely true this year, when collectible designs dominated the November showcases.

Recent findings suggest that among these was the Brussels-founded design fair Collectible. For its third New York iteration, it moved from office tower-turned creative hub WSA to a defunct movie theatre on the Upper East Side that is being developed by entities related to WSA.

While the unfinished theatre fit the experimental nature of the work, the execution was, by some accounts, chaotic, with one worker being sent to the hospital after an unstable light fell onto her head.

Collectible called it an “isolated occurrence involving an exhibitor’s equipment”.

“The safety of our exhibitors, staff and visitors is a priority, and we take any reported incident seriously,” a representative for Collectible told Dezeen.

“Collectible maintains safety procedures for the fair and expects all exhibitors to ensure that their own equipment is installed and secured appropriately.”.

It has been revealed that despite some chaos, including recently laid cement, there were strong showings. Philadelphia-based Dudd Haus indicated a pared-down booth with its usual mix of conceptual one-offs. Particularly of note was a milled-aluminium floor lamp by Jordan Maurice and a paravent made with telephone cords by Overt Cove.

Also eye-catching was a booth of droopy glass lamps and shades with erotic overtones by Upstate Newly introduced York gallery Freaks, and another sensual booth with drapes and lacquered furniture by Iitem studio.

The fair’s scenography carried the sleek, modern, USM-laden feel from the prior additions. Curators Alex Tieghi-Walker and Lynette Nylander designed special sections.

Bas-reliefs were popular on otherwise modern furniture, including a battened screen by Polish studio Wiktoria & Filip Bielicki for Objekt Gallery and a coffee table with raised ceramic on its base by Small Things Studio for Salon 21.

At Collectible, Montreal design collective Ensemble showcased its members’ work on nooks in a wall made with USM panels.

This was just a taste of what Ensemble had in store for the week. The collective brought their signature experimentation to Yabu Pushelberg’s Tribeca studio, creating a plywood room-within-a-room to showcase work, including new lamps by Zebulon Perron, sculptural glass lamps by Alex Joncas, metal works by Jérémy Paguet, leather lamps by Jeta Studio and brass-lined mirrors by Jeremy Le Chatelier.

It was an extremely focused showing that proved sometimes you can do more with less.

At Salon Art + Design, a few younger galleries stuck out from the historical work and ultra-high-end designs that usually characterise the fair.

Brooklyn-based Zarolat’s showing included ash-wood lamps with cellulose shades by Natural Urbano and Polybion, while New York-based hub for Brazilian furniture, Bossa Furniture, showcased a greatest hits of mid-century São Paulo makers, including Joaquim Tenreiro.

BDNY was, as usual, where most of the actual commerce took place during the week. While the interior designers and architects descended on the sample-forward showing, a few brands demonstrated stand-out collections, including Sancal’s showing of Júlia Esqué’s playfully fringed armchairs and Santa & Cole’s modern, fun lighting.

According to recent reports, later in the week, LA-based Basic Space, run by the organisers behind Design Miami, returned to SoHo. With artistic direction by Alexander May, the stark, white-cube approach differed from the in-situ, multi-room afair that characterised the first Latest York Basic Space in 2025.

The fair featured a focus on big names and multiple co-curators competing for attention on the promotional materials and in the execution.

Standout pieces included the live-edge wood furniture with small metal connective elements by Brooklyn-based designer Gregory Beson, as well as Daniel Swarilov’s metal credenzas, in a section curated by Marquel Williams.

Paris-based Harry Nuriev created a metallic take on first-class airline seats as a standalone installation. Another booth featured an oversized sofa by NFL player Stefon Diggs’ luxury furniture brand Si Vis Pacem, illustrating the fair’s mix of design with celebrity culture.

Finally, Mexico City-based creative studio Fábrica, run by artist Darryl Richardson and partner Maryah Ananda, held its La Sala showcase in a loft near Penn Station.

With a focus on international Black designers, the showcase featured art and design, with the space shaped like a living room by interior designer Johnathan Bailey.

Furniture pieces of note included a slim metal chair by Kai Avent-deLeo and an armchair by Mark Grattan.

The social focus of the event gave it an aesthetic heft, and a few of its stated goals, “community over curation” and “warmth over spectacle”, made it stand out from many of the other offerings from the week.

Judging by the willingness of the different fall fairs to join in, it seems likely that the November design week will fully take off.

#102900. How Taking a GLP-1 Could Affect Your Bone Health

📅 19 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1576 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

How Taking a GLP-1 Could Affect Your Bone Health

📅 19 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1576 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When it comes to treating obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other chronic health conditions, GLP-1 agonist drugs—such as Ozempic, Zepbound, and Wegovy—have been a game changer for literally millions of Americans.
  • But as with any medication, these drugs can deliver unwelcome side effects.
  • Recent findings suggest that the research, which was presented at the 2026 American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons annual meeting in March and has not yet been peer-reviewed, found a link between GLP-1 use and increased risk of bone complications, including osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones) and osteomalacia (soft bones).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When it comes to treating obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other chronic health conditions, GLP-1 agonist drugs—such as Ozempic, Zepbound, and Wegovy—have been a game changer for literally millions of Americans.

But as with any medication, these drugs can deliver unwelcome side effects. And a recent study that just garnered a bunch of attention raised the possibility of fresh ones.

Recent findings suggest that the research, which was presented at the 2026 American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons annual meeting in March and has not yet been peer-reviewed, found a link between GLP-1 use and increased risk of bone complications, including osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones) and osteomalacia (soft bones). The study also found a link between GLP-1 use and heightened risk of gout, a type of arthritis that causes pain and swelling in the joints.

Recent findings suggest that the lead study author said he became interested in whether GLP-1s might affect bone and other connective tissue after some of his patients “developed serious tendon tears following relatively minor injuries,” according to NBC News. After analyzing five years of medical records from nearly 147,000 adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity, the study authors concluded that GLP-1 use was associated with a “significantly increased” risk of osteoporosis, osteomalacia, and gout.

Of course, this news is likely unsettling for anyone on these medications. But should we be legit worried about these findings? And how exactly could GLP-1s harm bone health in the first place? We tapped two experts for answers, along with practical tips for protecting bone health while taking GLP-1s.

First, some relieving news: As of now, there is “no sound scientific evidence” that suggests GLP-1s directly increase the risk of osteoporosis or osteomalacia, Marci Laudenslager, MD, an obesity medicine physician with The Johns Hopkins Healthful Eating, Activity & Weight Program, tells SELF. (Same goes for gout, she adds.).

Dr. Laudenslager, who was not involved in the study, points out that it was observational in nature, meaning it looked at correlation…not causation. “While well-conducted observational studies can reveal a potential relationship between a medication and a clinical outcome, they cannot determine whether a medication directly causes that clinical outcome,” she explains.

Recent findings suggest that another limitation of the study is that it relied on medical records alone, which means it assumed that all patients who were prescribed GLP-1s, as noted in their medical records, were actually taking the drug. In reality, many patients who are prescribed GLP-1s are unable to take them because of cost or medication shortages, Dr. Laudenslager claims. Moreover, people who do start taking don’t always continue due to insurance, cost, or problems tolerating the drug, she adds.

Beyond that, the study didn’t take into account factors that commonly impact bone health, like exercise habits, nutritional habits, and other lifestyle factors, Kelyssa Hall, an exercise physiologist and certified strength and conditioning specialist at Hospital for Special Surgery, tells SELF. “These factors can play a huge role in bone health with or without the addition of GLP-1s.” The study also didn’t account for certain endocrine conditions, cancers, alcohol use, family history, and steroid use–all of which can also play a role in bone health, Dr. Laudenslager adds. And the study didn’t note which specific GLP-1 drug people used and the dosage, she adds.

Recent findings suggest that lastly, the study findings have not yet been peer reviewed–a step that Dr. Laudenslager describes it as “essential” in the scientific process. As Hall puts it: The study “highlights the need for more research on these topics.”.

Industry observers note that okay, so that particular study has its limitations. But other research supports the notion that these drugs may be linked with declining bone health. So…is there actual cause for concern?

Sources indicate that according to Dr. Laudenslager and Hall, taking GLP1-s can indeed decrease bone density for some people. But that’s likely due to the volume and rate at which people lose weight while on these drugs—and not anything specific to the medication itself, Dr. Laudenslager indicates.

“When you take GLP-1s, there can be rapid weight loss which means there is less load being carried around on the skeleton,” Hall says. “Bone formation or strengthening is improved with load to the skeletal system,” she explains, “so losing weight decreases the regular load on the bones overall.”.

Industry observers note that over time, this decrease in loading can translate to a decrease in bone density, Dr. Laudenslager claims. But, again, this isn’t unique to GLP-1s: “Significant weight loss through any mechanism—lifestyle change, medications, or surgery—can impact metabolism as a whole and bone metabolism, in particular,” she says. Basically, whenever you lose a bunch of weight—regardless of how you lost those pounds—there’s always a risk of bone loss.

In a recent development, in short, while it’s true that some people taking GLP-1s have had changes to their bone health, these changes seem to “be driven primarily by magnitude of weight loss rather than a direct, negative consequence of the medications themselves,” Dr. Laudenslager states. That said, the use of GLP-1s and bone health “is an active area of study,” she adds. More research is needed to fully understand the impact of GLP-1s on bone density.

In a recent development, resistance training is important for pretty much everyone—and that includes folks on GLP-1s. One of its many benefits is that it’s been shown to improve bone density, Hall says. That means it can be a helpful strategy to bolster bone health when you’re on a GLP-1. Plus, strength training can help guard against muscle loss that can happen when you’re losing weight. “Retaining muscle mass is important for strength and stability,” she says. And it can also help support your overall metabolism, she adds, which can help your body sustain weight loss results for the long haul.

In a recent development, if you’re new to strength training, Dr. Laudenslager recommends gradually building up to a routine of two to three sessions a week, with at least a day off in between each workout to allow your muscles the time they need to recover. Before getting started though, make sure to check with your doctor or other medical provider so they can advise what type of workouts are safe and recommended for you.

Industry observers note that A common side effect of GLP-1s is appetite suppression, which can sometimes lead people to follow a really low calorie diet. Calorie restriction can suppress bone growth and increase the risk of fractures, according to research, which is one of the reasons you want to make sure you’re still eating enough to support your overall health while on a GLP-1. “Hunger is an essential hormonal cue we all need in order to sustain health,” Dr. Laudenslager states. The ideal amount of calories is highly individualized, but if you’re unsure that you’re getting what you need, bring it up with your doctor or another qualified expert, such as a registered dietitian.

According to recent reports, protein is often touted for its muscle-building benefits, but it’s also vital for bone health, as it helps to build bone mass. The recommended dietary allowance for adults is 0.8 grams of protein per kilograms of bodyweight a day—a general guideline that Dr. Laudenslager also suggests for people taking GLP-1s. She suggests a slightly higher intake for people at greater risk of bone health problems (such as older adults and postmenopausal women) and lesser amounts in people with kidney disease. Just make sure that as you prioritize protein, you don’t skimp on key components of a well-rounded diet, including fiber, water, healthy fats, and essential vitamins, minerals, and nutrients, she adds.

According to recent reports, rapid weight loss can be harmful for bone health, so to mitigate this risk, strive for a more gradual reduction in pounds. The recommended rate of weight loss depends on your starting weight, but as a general guideline, Dr. Laudenslager recommends losing 5% to 10% of your total weight over the course of about six months. This translates to an average of about 0.5 to 2 pounds lost a week. So if you notice that taking a GLP-1 is causing you to lose weight at a faster pace, bring it up with your doctor. They may want to adjust your medication dosing to help slow your weight loss rate into a more ideal, gradual range.

Bone loss isn’t an overnight thing. In fact, clinically significant bone loss typically happens over the course of years, Dr. Laudenslager indicates. “This means there are a wealth of opportunities throughout a person’s weight loss journey to prevent and treat bone loss early on if it’s detected through surveillance.” So if you have any bone health concerns, mention them to your doctor (though hopefully your provider is proactively thinking about this too).

Industry observers note that on that note, Dr. Laudenslager strongly encourages people interested in obesity treatment to seek care from a board-certified obesity medicine physician. She recommends the American Board of Obesity Medicine and the Obesity Action Coalition websites as resources for finding a board-certified provider.

Recent findings suggest that GLP-1s can be a true game-changer for people struggling with chronic health conditions. Unfortunately, there’s still a lot of societal stigma and misunderstanding surrounding obesity, including the misconception that “anti-obesity medications are dangerous and should be avoided,” Dr. Laudenslager notes. In truth, though? “The medication side effects are quite manageable when prescribed by providers who are well-versed in current practice guidelines,” she says.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy Studio Gang.

Architecture practice Studio Gang has completed a women’s conference centre overlooking Geneva Lake in Wisconsin, with three irregularly shaped buildings informed by the site’s oak forest.

Located outside of Chicago on a lakeside hill, the Women’s Leadership Center contains meeting spaces for established and emerging women in leadership roles to gather and “ideate solutions to complex issues within their industries”.

“Women leaders spend much of their careers in rooms that weren’t designed with them in mind,” remarked the center’s founder Ann Drake, former CEO of supply chain provider DSC Logistics. “I wanted to build one that was.”.

Studio Gang stated key elements of the design were sustainability – with strategies such as a mass timber structure – and responding to the ecology of the site through gently curving volumes and wide-open windows.

“We designed the Women’s Leadership Center to respect and learn from its surrounding forest ecology while allowing community, leadership, and collaborative problem-solving to thrive,” said Studio Gang founding partner Jeanne Gang.

“Locally sourced materials, mass timber, and low-carbon concrete minimise the buildings’ carbon footprint, while the landscape helps to repair the site’s ecology and enhance its biodiversity.”.

The campus contains three main buildings — the circular Council building that functions as the main meeting space, the Lodge, which is made of three interconnected volumes, and the Cabin, a smaller building that contains accommodations.

White oak wood harvested on-site, a dark wood cladding and natural Wisconsin stone were used throughout all three buildings to “reflect the tones and textures of the forest”, according to the studio.

The Council building is arranged around a central courtyard and garden that doubles as a rainwater-collection site.

Its rooms, including a larger lecture hall and meeting room, fan outwards around the courtyard and are lined with floor-to-ceiling windows, while a heavy timber structure creates a series of skylights at the entrance.

A walkway leads out the back of the Council building towards the Lodge. The building contains more casual meeting and socialising spaces, such as a Great Room arranged around a fireplace.

According to recent reports, it also contains a mass-timber structure above this space, which is lined with skylights. Outdoor terraces overlook Geneva Lake, while the building’s green roof contains a “coffee nook” and patios for seating.

Tucked off into a corner of the site, the Cabin building contains several bedrooms across two levels, as well as utility spaces such as a laundry room.

Its lower level contains a dining area and living area, which double as additional, more intimate gathering spaces.

Fully accessible ramps interconnect all three structures and lead down to the water bank, where they end in a pier.

Elsewhere, Studio Gang recently completed an open-air theatre in upstate New York and a Denver hotel.

Photography courtesy Studio Gang.

According to recent reports, picture this: you board a Japan Airlines Boeing 787-9 at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, turn left, and settle into your own private suite. That's the experience this redemption delivers — and the math behind it is what makes the ChooseFI community absolutely love it. A JAL Business Class ticket from Seattle (SEA) to Tokyo Narita (NRT) typically retails between **$5,000 and $10,000** in cash. That's a real number — pull up JAL.com on any given date and you'll see it. Yet Alaska Mileage Plan prices this exact award at just **60,000 miles** one way. On a $5,000 ticket, that's **8.3 cents per point**. On a $10,000 ticket — which is common during peak travel periods — that's a staggering **16.7 cents per point**. The ChooseFI benchmark for a "good" redemption is typically 1.5 to 2 cents per point. This blows past that by a factor of five to ten. Why does this gap exist? Because Alaska Mileage Plan uses a **fixed award chart** to price partner redemptions. They set the JAL Business Class rate years ago and haven't moved it in step with rising cash fares. As international business class prices have climbed, the points cost has stayed anchored — and that's the pricing inefficiency that savvy travelers exploit. This isn't a loophole that disappears tomorrow. JAL and Alaska have a deep, long-standing partnership. Alaska has consistently maintained this pricing as one of the crown jewels of its partner award chart. For anyone building toward financial independence who also wants to see the world in comfort, this redemption represents exactly what the FI travel rewards philosophy is about: using the system's own rules to access experiences that cash-wealthy people pay enormous sums for, nearly free.

A sweet spot that punches far above its weight in cents-per-mile value.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you see it, and understanding it will help you recognize similar opportunities across the loyalty landscape.

Alaska's Fixed Award Chart Is the Key.

It has been revealed that most major airline programs have shifted to dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate with demand, just like cash prices. Alaska Mileage Plan has largely resisted this for its partner awards. JAL Business Class from North America is priced at a flat 60,000 Alaska miles one way, period. It doesn't matter if it's Golden Week in Japan or a random Tuesday in February. The chart price holds.

According to recent reports, this creates an extraordinary opportunity because JAL cash fares are not fixed. They respond to demand, fuel costs, seasonality, and competitive dynamics. When those fares rise — as they have substantially in recent years — your 60,000 miles buy proportionally more value. The inefficiency widens the more expensive the cash fare becomes.

According to recent reports, here's a detail that separates Alaska from many other programs: Alaska Mileage Strategy charges zero fuel surcharges on any partner award booking. This is significant. Some programs (looking at you, British Airways Avios) pass through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $400–$800 to a theoretically cheap award. With Alaska, your out-of-pocket is taxes only — typically $50–$150 on a transpacific itinerary. Your 60,000-mile redemption costs you 60,000 miles plus roughly $100. Full stop.

The Transfer Path: Marriott Bonvoy® Is Your On-Ramp.

Alaska Mileage Blueprint has no direct credit card transfer partners in the traditional Chase/Amex/Citi sense. This is the most notable nuance of this redemption to understand. You cannot transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards directly to Alaska. Instead, the primary transfer path runs through Marriott Bonvoy®.

The ratio is 3 Marriott points to 1 Alaska mile, and transfers typically take 1 to 5 days to complete. There's also the well-known Marriott bonus: transfer 60,000 Marriott points and receive 5,000 bonus miles, meaning 60,000 Marriott points nets you 25,000 Alaska miles. This makes earning Alaska miles via Marriott cards (like the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless or Brilliant) a viable — if not the most efficient — path.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A contemporary take on Ukrainian vernacular buildings and a preschool in Estonia are among the winners of the Thermory Design Awards 2026, which celebrate the versatility of thermally modified wood.
  • Of 78 submissions from 23 countries, four winning projects have been selected in the competition’s fifth annual edition, covering the categories of interior, tiny and private house, residential, commercial and public building, and wellness and spa.
  • Thermory thermowood is wood that has been modified using heat and steam with no added chemicals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A contemporary take on Ukrainian vernacular buildings and a preschool in Estonia are among the winners of the Thermory Design Awards 2026, which celebrate the versatility of thermally modified wood.

Of 78 submissions from 23 countries, four winning projects have been selected in the competition’s fifth annual edition, covering the categories of interior, tiny and private house, residential, commercial and public building, and wellness and spa.

Thermory thermowood is wood that has been modified using heat and steam with no added chemicals.

The treatment enhances the material’s dimensional stability and reduces moisture uptake compared with untreated wood, according to Thermory.

The winner of the interior category is a trio of Ukrainian guesthouses collectively named Under the Reed Roof, designed by Kyiv-based studio YOD Group.

Each guesthouse comprises a glass-walled volume at the base, topped by a tapered thatched roof with exaggerated proportions.

While the exterior of these roofs is made with traditional reeds, the interiors are lined with thermo-ash shingles, arranged to create a tactile effect that is repeated on the front doors.

These highlight the interplay between the interior’s traditional and contemporary design elements, contrasting materials, and the balance between the structure’s openness and enclosure.

“The project stood out to the jury for its exceptionally coherent concept, in which architecture and interior elements come together to form a harmonious whole,” stated Thermory.

Winning in the tiny and private house category was Marker Architecture‘s Flooded Gums project, a flood-resilient dwelling built on working farmland.

The building features thermo-ash cladding and thermo-spruce decking, owing to the materials’ robustness and aesthetic merits.

“What particularly impressed the jury was the honesty and clarity of the architecture,” said Thermory of the project.

“Rather than concealing its construction, the project makes its structural logic visible, with every element serving a purpose: the result is a modest yet highly refined building that strikes a compelling balance between aesthetics, functionality and its natural setting,” it added.

Estonia’s Rakke Kindergarten secured the win in the residential, commercial and public building category, thanks to what Thermory describes as local studio Arhitekt Must‘s “cohesive and imaginative design”.

Thermo-spruce cladding, thermo-pine posts and thermo-pine decking all feature in the design, enhancing both its functionality and visual appeal.

The building’s function as an educational environment is made distinctive by the space’s inventive ceiling, which is composed of the short thermo-pine posts, arranged in a way that creates an engaging optical illusion.

“This unexpected architectural gesture elevates a functional space into something distinctive, demonstrating how thoughtful detailing can shape the character and experience of an entire building,” said Thermory.

Finally, the winner of the wellness and spa category is a sauna within the Estonian Embassy in Berlin, designed by interior studio AERIS.

The interiors feature statement walls covered in custom-made oak shingles, which, being circular and slightly overlapping, resemble fish scales.

These are joined by thermo-alder benches and walls, creating a cohesive scheme of timber details that integrate neatly with the lighting design.

“The harmonious interplay of materials, surfaces and light imbues the space with a contemporary edge while retaining the intimacy and warmth of a traditional sauna,” noted Thermory.

“Although vastly different in character and purpose, the winning projects share a creative and unconventional approach to design,” it added.

“Each places wood at the heart of its architectural expression, combining imaginative thinking with meticulous attention to detail.”.

The 2026 instalment of the competition was judged by a diverse international jury of architects and Thermory representatives, including Kärt Kanarbik, Thermory’s architectural project manager; Lars Skjølstrup Østergaard, lead design architect at Henning Larsen; Sami Rintala, professor and architect at Rintala Eggertsson Architects; Jaan Port, architect and partner at PIN Arhitektid; and Tõnis Kalve, architect at ByKalve and Thermory project sales architect.

To learn more about Thermory, visit its website.

For Some Women, Weight Loss Drugs Are a Secret They Keep From Their Partners

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The first time Caroline went on Wegovy, it wasn’t a secret: She told her boyfriend, mother, and close friends.
  • “I had tried every way under the sun to lose weight,” Caroline tells SELF.
  • Industry observers note that so she went online and found a doctor who prescribed the medication over the phone, unaware of how much Caroline actually weighed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first time Caroline went on Wegovy, it wasn’t a secret: She told her boyfriend, mother, and close friends. Over the course of six months, they watched as she shed 30 pounds, going from 130 back to what she calls her “healthy original weight” of 100 pounds. Even still, her loved ones worried about the extent of her weight loss and didn’t want her to lose even more.

“I had tried every way under the sun to lose weight,” Caroline tells SELF. The 34-year-old, who lives in Montreal, asked to use only her first name to protect her privacy. “I was really tired of trying.” At five feet four inches, she wasn’t obese and didn’t think her primary doctor would approve a prescription.

Industry observers note that so she went online and found a doctor who prescribed the medication over the phone, unaware of how much Caroline actually weighed. Immediately after starting Wegovy, she says, “the weight started coming off incredibly fast.” After six months she decided she wanted to stop. But as soon as she got off Wegovy, the weight came back: She gained 10 pounds in a month. “I realized, I can’t stop,” Caroline says.

Recent findings suggest that so for the past six months, she has been taking Wegovy again, this time at a maintenance-level dosage. But there’s one big difference: This time, she’s keeping it a secret from her boyfriend and family. “Now that we’re talking about kids, he’s seen all the impacts [of the drug] and he’s done with it,” she says. Since she lives alone, hiding her medication from him is relatively easy—she stashes it in the back of the fridge, since it needs to be kept cold. But she’s still worried he’ll see it, and when they travel together, she has to hide the medication in the hotel room fridge—or, if they’re visiting his parents, in their refrigerator. “So imagine, I’m hiding stuff in my parents-in-laws’ fridge, hoping they won’t see them,” she says. “It’s super awkward.”.

Industry observers note that caroline isn’t the only woman going to great lengths to keep her GLP-1 use a secret. On a recent thread on the r/GLP1microdosing subreddit, women shared their tips and tricks for hiding medication from their partners. One stashes them in a tomato paste box. Another uses a play food container from a child’s pretend kitchen. Still others have turned to an opaque feta cheese container, butter stick box, anchovy paste box, empty bottles of women’s probiotics and Alani Nu supplements, a plastic to-go container, a metal water bottle, a box of wine, and a baking soda box in the back of the fridge—all to conceal the weight loss medication.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s a real thing,” Kia Mitchell, MD, who specializes in family and obesity medicine, tells SELF. She has seen numerous women in her Jacksonville, Florida, practice go to similar efforts to hide their medication from their partners. The first time she heard about this pattern, it was from a patient who “just didn’t want to turn this into a debate at home,” she indicates. “She just wanted to have the option” to take the medication. “A lot of my patients are similar,” Dr. Mitchell adds. “There’s this loss of control with the gaining of the weight, but being able to control the narrative around weight loss has been empowering and exciting” for her patients. “Because now they can reveal it on their own terms. That’s where the control comes back.”.

The reasons women want to reveal their weight loss medications on their own terms are palpable in that subreddit thread. “If my husband found out, it would just be a series of lectures,” wrote a user called Vivid-Act-6442. “Just don’t want to hear any negative or critical opinions,” wrote another user called [deleted]. “After 52 years of marriage, one knows one’s mate.” One woman chimed in to say she was hiding her meds from her teens—because she didn’t want them telling her ex-husband. “I just don’t feel like the questions,” she wrote.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Mitchell has mixed feelings about this type of secrecy. Anyone on a health journey benefits from having a “network that’s really cheering for you,” Dr. Mitchell states. “Dealing with something like this, I want people to have community.” But, she continues, it’s “empowering and protective” for women to get to decide who knows about their weight loss drugs—even if, ideally, “you really want to be in a relationship with someone you trust completely.”.

From a medical standpoint, there are some potential pitfalls to hiding GLP-1s from a significant other. For one, it’s easier to get pregnant while taking them—Mitchell states she has “several GLP-1 babies” in her practice. There are also the drugs’ potential side effects, and hiding medication can make it more difficult for a patient to turn to her partner if she’s struggling. And more generally, secrecy can cause stress. “When someone is trying to lose weight, we want their stress hormones to be as low as possible,” Dr. Mitchell says. “If you’re trying to hide [medication], we’ll be fighting an uphill battle if you’re stressed about that.”.

According to recent reports, the bigger issue is hiding GLP-1 medications from your regular doctor, something that has become much easier thanks to the rise in telehealth companies like Hers and Ro. That’s a problem Caroline is having: She didn’t tell her doctor both times she went on Wegovy and still doesn’t want to, even though she’s concerned about how the drug may interact with the Accutane and Ritalin she takes. The idea of admitting her GLP-1 use to her doctor makes her anxious, since she doesn’t want to break their trust. But her annual physical is coming up, and her doctor will see that she’s lost a lot of weight.

“I use ChatGPT as my doctor at this point since I can’t be honest with my own doctor,” she claims. “I say, ‘Hey, this is my actual weight, what type of dosage is okay to take with other drugs?’” Admittedly, she adds, this is “probably not the best option.”.

In a recent development, caroline got her Wegovy prescription through Hers. During the process she was only asked for basic bloodwork and received no counseling, just “documentation to read.”.

Craig Primack, MD, the head of weight loss at Hers, tells SELF that the tech giant’s prescribing doctors “do ask [patients] to talk with their primary care doctor about the care they’re getting.” He acknowledges that the company doesn’t do much in the way of direct counseling but states that “we ask about mental health and anxiety and stresses.” The Hers app contains what Primack terms “psychologist-built information” about topics such as sleep management and eating personas.

Dr. Primack is “absolutely” aware that some patients hide their medication from their partners. He states that some don’t want to say anything until they’ve proven they can lose weight; some don’t want to say anything because of the medication’s cost; some worry about how it could change the way they and their partner see each other. “Your weight and persona set up a dynamic in your couple,” Dr. Primack says. “When you start changing that, sometimes spouses get very jealous—‘Oh my god, you’re becoming potentially more attractive.’ Not that weight is directly linked to that, but that’s what I hear them say.”.

And then, of course, there’s the more general stigma associated with weight and weight loss. “One benefit of telemedicine is it takes the bias and stigma away,” Dr. Primack says. “One reason we are here is because people are uncomfortable going to talk to their primary care doctor about it.”.

Sources indicate that whether or not Caroline decides to tell her doctor about her medication, she still will have to grapple with the larger issues that her Wegovy use, and her secrecy around it, have raised. “It’s very stressful,” she claims. “The fact that not only can I not talk about it, but I’m also unable to get off of it. I don’t love the idea of taking medicine like that forever, but I’m kind of stuck with it.” She doesn’t want to gain weight, she explains. “But I wonder to which extent I’m too harsh with my criticism of my body. Maybe my goals are too intense.”.

Given the incredible degree of vulnerability and sensitivity tied up with weight loss, the dilemma about whether to tell people about a GLP-1 medication is all too understandable. But how to tell people can make it easier, states Rachel Goldman, PhD, a clinical assistant professor in the department of psychiatry at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and a clinical psychologist whose areas of expertise include weight management and disordered eating, tells SELF. “Framing it around their own experience and needs can make the conversation feel more manageable and less like something they have to defend,” she says.

According to recent reports, since deciding whether to have this conversation isn’t easy, Dr. Goldman would first encourage a patient to “think about their why,” she claims. “What led them to this decision? What does this treatment mean for their health and wellbeing?” Once someone feels more grounded and confident in their reasoning, “it becomes easier to communicate it with that confidence.”.

Dr. Goldman also suggests coming up with some sample scripts before having the conversation. “I would suggest that they lead with their own personal experience and not think about others and why/how others are using it,” she claims. “I would encourage them to use ‘I’ statements.”.

It’s also helpful to think ahead of time about a partner’s potential reaction and to have a plan in place for different scenarios. Thinking about what you want from a partner is likewise helpful—is it support, understanding, “or simply space to make their own health decisions without judgement?” Dr. Goldman asks. She adds that it’s important to remember that a partner’s initial reaction might not be their final reaction—it can take time for someone to process a conversation and to work through their own biases and misconceptions.

“Ultimately,” she notes, “the goal isn’t to have a perfect conversation, but it’s to open the door to more honesty, connection, and support over time.”.

But if that fails, there’s always a box of anchovy paste.

7 Common Misdiagnoses for Hidradenitis Suppurativa (HS)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a skin condition that often gets caught up in a case of mistaken identity in a lineup of suspects.
  • With their host of bumps, rashes, flakiness, or scales, skin conditions can sometimes be tricky to diagnose.
  • Sources indicate that so, what exactly is HS?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a skin condition that often gets caught up in a case of mistaken identity in a lineup of suspects. Specifically, people confuse HS for some more common conditions.

With their host of bumps, rashes, flakiness, or scales, skin conditions can sometimes be tricky to diagnose. That’s because they often share common symptoms or have symptoms that overlap with or mimic those of another skin issue.

Sources indicate that so, what exactly is HS? It’s a chronic, progressive skin condition that typically appears as boil-like lumps in friction-prone and sweaty areas, where your skin can be sensitive. These lumps can form interconnected tracts underneath your skin (aka “tunneling”) that may become irritated or even infected.

Knowing how the symptoms of HS compare with those of other inflammatory skin conditions can help you advocate for the correct diagnosis and care, which is crucial for staving off disease progression.

Here are 7 conditions that HS commonly gets mistaken for.

Sources indicate that HS isn’t rare — it affects up to 4% of the population. But by comparison, acne vulgaris affects more than more than 9% of people worldwide. Sometimes HS can be mistaken for acne simply because acne is more common. But these two conditions are quite different.

In a recent development, acne typically highlights up as papules, pustules, or nodules, which are commonly called zits or blemishes. Acne most often appears on your face but can also affect your back, chest, arms, and buttocks. It occurs when your sebaceous glands have a hypersensitivity to circulating androgens (like testosterone).

By comparison, HS most often appears in sweat- and friction-prone areas, such as your armpits or groin. It occurs when hair follicles become blocked — though more research is needed to learn what causes these blockages.

Recent findings suggest that acne conglobata (AC) is a rare but intense form of nodulocystic acne. With AC, the cysts and nodules connect under your skin, and this can lead to infections and scarring. Since AC features a “tunneling” effect that may appear similar to HS, many people confuse these two otherwise distinct conditions.

One key difference? HS often appears in areas that are subjected to friction from skin-on-skin contact or chafing. AC, on the other hand, can appear anywhere on your body. To further complicate things, many people with HS also have AC, and some research suggests a link between the two conditions.

A cyst is a fluid-filled sac. Cysts have many possible causes, including injuries and minor infections. They often go away on their own, but some may require treatment.

HS bumps can resemble cysts — but HS is an ongoing inflammatory condition.

Sources indicate that an ingrown hair happens when a strand of hair anywhere on your body grows into your skin instead of out. Ingrown hairs commonly occur after shaving, waxing, or tweezing. After hair removal, a tiny upcoming hair can curl inward, creating a bump (often called a razor bump).

Sometimes people confuse HS bumps for ingrown hairs — especially since HS often occurs in places where hair removal is common, such as the armpits and bikini area. Another confusing factor is that HS develops from blocked follicles. However, the cause of the blockage in HS is more complicated than an ingrown hair.

Industry observers note that folliculitis is inflammation of hair follicles, usually caused by a bacterial infection. The inflamed hair follicles show up as small bumps and can look like ingrown hairs.

People commonly mistake HS for folliculitis because the conditions often occur in the same skin areas.

Mild folliculitis tends to go away on its own with at-home treatment, though more severe forms may require antibiotics. HS, on the other hand, is a chronic condition.

According to recent reports, A boil (also called a furuncle) is a bump filled with pus. The bump develops from a bacterial infection, often of a hair follicle. The infection causes a buildup of immune and skin cells, which leads to the formation of the bump. A carbuncle is a cluster of boils.

People often confuse HS with boils. However, boils are the result of an infection, and proper treatment typically resolves the matter. Meanwhile, the boil-like bumps of HS often require ongoing treatment.

Herpes is a common sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by the herpes simplex virus. It reveals up as painful sores or blisters.

Since herpes often affects the genital area and HS occurs around the groin or bikini line, people may confuse the two conditions. But while herpes can be spread through direct contact, HS is not contagious.

It has been revealed that other skin conditions can mimic HS, and vice versa. But a misdiagnosis can lead to an incorrect treatment that won’t actually ease your symptoms or slow the condition’s progression. This is true for other skin conditions as well.

That’s why, if you have symptoms of any of the above conditions, you should talk with a knowledgeable dermatologist who can properly diagnose your concerns and find the right treatment initiative.

It has been revealed that architecture reaches people through whatever medium carries it, and each fresh medium changes our picture of what a good building looks like. For example, when 3D modeling software arrived, the novelty of complex shapes drove the starchitecture era of the 2010s, and projects built on those experiments earned awards such as the Pritzker Prize. Today the medium is the social media feed. A building exists first as a model and then as a render, long before it exists as a place. Meanwhile, research in neuroarchitecture is building a different picture based on how people actually experience buildings. So how could those two seemingly unrelated topics close a loop that may lead to the profession's next creative frontier?

In a recent development, in the book Cognitive Architecture, Ann Sussman and Justin Hollander examine how the brain reacts to the built environment. In their research, people looked at photographs of buildings while their eye movements were tracked. Viewers tended to skip blank, featureless facades but lingered on details, contrast, and other people. One case study, the Stapleton Library in Newly introduced York, reveals how much fenestration patterns matter: windows provide areas of contrast that the eye seeks out and stays with. Their study suggests that architecture tuned to these cues could serve its occupants at a layer deeper than aesthetics. Sussman's broader argument is that the brain works at walking speed and eye level, hunting for faces, contrast, and activity at the ground floor.

Their study suggests that architecture tuned to these cues could serve its occupants at a layer deeper than aesthetics. Sussman's broader argument is that the brain works at walking speed and eye level, hunting for faces, contrast, and activity at the ground floor.

In a recent development, anjan Chatterjee's lab at the University of Pennsylvania adds nuance to this picture. They summarize architectural experience in three elements: coherence, or how organized and legible a space is; fascination, or how rich in information an environment is; and hominess, or how comfortable it feels. Everyone weighs these differently, but people with an architectural background seem to give coherence more weight than non-architects do. At the same time, he also makes a second point: architects often predict how a building will work, but they rarely collect post-occupancy information to test those predictions.
